interview.a: **C1** prioritizes fast compilation with moderate optimization, improving startup and early execution performance. **C2** spends more resources producing aggressively optimized code for sustained performance. Tiered compilation combines both approaches so applications can benefit from fast warm-up and high peak throughput.

interview.q: Can a method that is called only once become JIT compiled?
interview.a: Yes. HotSpot tracks loop backedges as well as method invocations. A method containing a sufficiently active loop can trigger compilation even during its first invocation, including replacement of the currently executing interpreted loop with compiled code.

cards.title: Parent Delegation and Class Identity
cards.tldr: **Parent delegation** prioritizes ancestor classloaders. A Java class is uniquely identified by its fully qualified name and the classloader that defined it.
cards.summary:
Java organizes classloaders into a hierarchy, where a loader can have another loader as its parent. The **parent delegation model** is the default strategy for deciding which loader should provide a requested class. It promotes consistent class definitions and prevents application dependencies from accidentally replacing essential Java classes. The parent relationship describes delegation between loaders, not inheritance between Java classes.

When `loadClass()` receives a class name, it first checks whether that class has already been loaded by this loader. If not, it asks its parent to load the class. This request can travel up to the Bootstrap Classloader. Only when the parent cannot provide the class does the requesting loader normally call `findClass()` to perform its own search. This explains why placing a custom `java.lang.String` on the application classpath cannot replace the standard `String`. Java also restricts custom loaders from defining classes in protected `java.*` packages.

The JVM defines **class identity** using both the fully qualified class name and its defining classloader. Two independent loaders defining `com.example.Foo` create different runtime types. Casting an instance between those types can throw `ClassCastException`. This enables **classloader isolation**, where separate applications or plugins use different library versions within one JVM. Tomcat, for example, uses a web application loading strategy that prefers local application classes in many cases, while preserving parent-first behavior for protected classes. Overriding delegation unnecessarily can create duplicate types, dependency conflicts and difficult debugging problems.
bullets: **Parent-first loading:** Ask ancestors before searching the current loader's own class locations.
**Already-loaded check:** Avoids defining the same class repeatedly within one loader.
**Class identity:** Combines the fully qualified name and defining classloader.
**Isolation:** Independent loaders can support different versions of the same library.
**Protected classes:** Core Java classes cannot be freely replaced by application-defined alternatives.
**Custom delegation:** Container-specific loading strategies must preserve important platform boundaries.

glossary.meaning: A loading strategy in which a classloader asks its parent to provide a class before searching locally.
A class name including its complete package path, such as com.example.Foo.
The classloader that actually defines a particular runtime class.
Separating runtime class definitions so independent applications can use different dependencies.

commonMistakes: Assuming classes with identical package names and bytecode must represent the same runtime type.
Confusing the classloader that receives a request with the classloader that ultimately defines the class.
Overriding parent delegation without considering shared interfaces and protected platform classes.

interview.q: How does parent delegation work in Java class loading?
interview.a: A classloader checks for an already-loaded class and normally delegates the request to its parent before searching locally. This continues through the hierarchy. **Parent delegation** promotes shared class definitions and protects essential platform classes from accidental replacement.

interview.q: Can two classes with the same fully qualified name exist in one JVM?
interview.a: Yes. Class identity includes both the fully qualified name and the **defining classloader**. Independent loaders can define classes with identical names, but the resulting classes are different runtime types.

interview.q: Why do application servers sometimes use child-first class loading?
interview.a: Application servers may prioritize application-specific dependencies so different deployed applications can use different library versions. Tomcat uses this approach for many web application classes while preserving special rules for Java platform classes and container-provided APIs.

cards.title: Object Allocation, Memory Layout and Escape Analysis
cards.tldr: The JVM makes object creation efficient using fast allocation buffers and compiler optimizations. Object size depends on headers, fields, references and memory alignment.
cards.summary:
Java normally allocates objects in the **heap**, a memory area managed by the garbage collector. In many HotSpot allocation paths, the JVM uses a bump pointer marking the next available memory address. Creating an object advances that pointer by the required size instead of searching a list of free memory blocks. Newly allocated fields must also receive their Java-defined default values, supported by zero-filled memory and optimized initialization.

A **Thread-Local Allocation Buffer** (`TLAB`) is a small region of heap memory reserved for one thread. With generational collectors such as G1, these buffers are generally allocated from young-generation space. Each thread can advance its own pointer without coordinating every allocation with other threads. Refilling an exhausted buffer requires a shared allocation path, potentially involving synchronization or atomic operations. Buffer sizes are adaptive rather than fixed percentages of Eden.

An ordinary Java 21 HotSpot object contains a **header** with a mark word, which stores information related to identity hashing, locking and garbage collection, and a class pointer that identifies its class metadata. A common 64-bit configuration uses an eight-byte mark word and a four-byte compressed class pointer. Fields follow the header, and HotSpot may rearrange their layout to reduce wasted space. With eight-byte alignment, an empty `Object` and an `Integer` typically occupy 16 bytes each. A `String` has a separate backing array, while a 1,000-element long array occupies slightly more than 8,000 bytes.

**Escape analysis** allows the just-in-time compiler to determine whether object identity must remain observable. **Scalar replacement** can replace eligible objects with their individual values, eliminating physical allocation entirely. Short-lived objects are often inexpensive to reclaim, but high allocation rates still create garbage collection work. Measure both allocation and retention before removing useful temporary objects or introducing object pools.
bullets: **Bump pointer:** Advances through available memory without a general-purpose free-list search.
**TLAB:** Provides efficient per-thread allocation without shared synchronization on every object creation.
**Zero initialization:** Java guarantees default field values, supported by optimized memory initialization.
**Object layout:** Headers, fields and alignment padding determine actual object size.
**Scalar replacement:** The compiler may eliminate allocations when object identity is unnecessary.
**Performance:** Measure allocation rate, retained memory and garbage collection costs together.

glossary.meaning: A region of heap memory reserved for efficient allocations by an individual thread.
Internal JVM information stored alongside an object's instance fields.
Compiler analysis that determines how an object can be accessed outside its creation context.
An optimization that replaces an object with individual field values and may eliminate its allocation.

commonMistakes: Assuming every `new` expression necessarily results in a physical heap allocation.
Treating typical HotSpot object sizes as guarantees across all JVM versions and configurations.
Assuming short-lived allocations are completely free or introducing object pools without measuring performance.

interview.q: Why is object allocation relatively fast in modern JVMs?
interview.a: HotSpot can allocate objects by advancing a pointer through available memory. A `TLAB` gives each thread its own allocation region, avoiding shared coordination on most allocations. Optimized memory initialization and compiler optimizations reduce additional overhead.

interview.q: What information is stored in a Java object header?
interview.a: A typical Java 21 HotSpot object header contains a mark word and a class pointer. The mark word contains information related to locking, identity hashing and garbage collection. The class pointer identifies the object's class metadata, and arrays also store their length.

interview.q: Does escape analysis always allocate non-escaping objects on the stack?
interview.a: No. HotSpot can use **scalar replacement** to eliminate eligible object allocations altogether, keeping individual values in registers or other compiler-managed locations. Escape analysis enables such optimizations but does not guarantee stack allocation or allocation elimination.

cards.title: Strong, Soft, Weak and Phantom References
cards.tldr: Java provides four reference strengths that influence object reachability. They support normal ownership, reclaimable caches, non-retaining associations and resource cleanup notifications.
cards.summary:
A reference is a value through which Java code accesses an object. The garbage collector uses **reachability** to determine whether objects are still needed. A **strong reference** is the ordinary reference created when an object is assigned to a variable. An object remains protected from garbage collection while a reachable strong reference chain leads to it. Java also provides specialized reference classes in `java.lang.ref`.

A **soft reference** allows the garbage collector to reclaim its referenced object according to memory demand and collector policy. Soft references can support reclaimable caches, but cached data must always be reloadable. A **weak reference** does not prevent collection once an object becomes only weakly reachable. When the garbage collector discovers that condition, it clears the weak reference. `WeakHashMap` uses weak keys so entries can disappear when their keys are no longer needed. Weak references also support canonicalization, which means sharing equivalent objects, and listener registries that should not retain listeners indefinitely.

A **phantom reference** supports notifications when an object reaches phantom reachability. Its `get()` method always returns `null`. The collector clears phantom references and enqueues registered references for processing, but notification does not guarantee that the object's physical memory has already been reclaimed. Soft and weak references can also register with a `ReferenceQueue`. Java 9 introduced `Cleaner`, which simplifies fallback resource cleanup using phantom reachability. Direct buffers and library leak detectors use related mechanisms.

Prefer ordinary strong references unless specialized lifetime behavior is necessary. Soft-reference caches have unpredictable eviction and should usually be replaced by explicitly bounded caches. A weak-map value that strongly references its own key prevents that key from becoming weakly reachable. For external resources such as sockets, prefer `AutoCloseable` and try-with-resources. Cleaner actions must not capture the monitored object, and automatic cleanup is not guaranteed to run promptly.
bullets: **Strong:** Keeps an object alive while a reachable strong reference chain exists.
**Soft:** Supports reclaimable data, but clearing behavior depends on garbage collector policy.
**Weak:** Allows collection when an object becomes only weakly reachable.
**Phantom:** Supports reachability notifications without exposing the referenced object.
**WeakHashMap trap:** A strongly retained value can accidentally keep its weak key alive.
**Cleanup:** Prefer explicit resource closure, with Cleaner as a fallback when appropriate.

glossary.meaning: Whether an object can be accessed through reference paths recognized by the garbage collector.
The object associated with a specialized reference.
A queue through which a program receives notifications about processed references.
A Java utility that registers fallback cleanup actions associated with phantom reachability.

commonMistakes: Using `SoftReference` for data that must remain available or assuming soft references are cleared only immediately before an out-of-memory error.
Assuming a `WeakHashMap` entry disappears even when its strongly retained value references its key.
Registering a Cleaner action that captures the monitored object, preventing that object from becoming phantom reachable.

interview.q: What is the difference between strong, soft, weak and phantom references?
interview.a: Strong references protect reachable objects from collection. Soft references can be cleared according to memory demand, while weak references are cleared when the collector discovers weak reachability. Phantom references support reachability notifications and cleanup mechanisms without allowing access to the referenced object.

interview.q: Can a WeakHashMap cause a memory leak?
interview.a: Yes. `WeakHashMap` holds its keys weakly but normally holds its values strongly. If a value directly or indirectly references its key, the key remains strongly reachable through the map and automatic entry removal cannot occur.

interview.q: When would you use Cleaner instead of a PhantomReference?
interview.a: `Cleaner` provides a simpler abstraction for registering fallback cleanup actions without managing phantom references and reference queues manually. The cleanup action must not retain the monitored object. For resources such as sockets and files, explicit closure remains the primary mechanism.

cards.title: Thread Dumps, Deadlocks and Hung Threads
cards.tldr: A **thread dump** captures thread states, execution stacks and lock information. Repeated dumps help distinguish ongoing computation, blocked threads and deadlocks.
cards.summary:
A **thread dump** is a snapshot of threads running inside a JVM. It contains thread names, execution states and stack traces, which describe the chain of method calls currently being executed. Thread dumps help investigate application hangs, deadlocks, excessive thread counts and requests that stop making progress. The standard tools are `jstack` and `jcmd Thread.print`.

A thread in `RUNNABLE` is executing or eligible to execute, but it may also be waiting inside native operations. A thread in `BLOCKED` is waiting to acquire a Java monitor, which is the lock associated with `synchronized` code. `WAITING` means a thread is waiting indefinitely for another action, while `TIMED_WAITING` means the wait has a time limit. A **deadlock** occurs when threads form a circular dependency on resources held by one another. Thread dumps can identify supported Java-level deadlock cycles. The `-l` option adds information about owned synchronizers, such as `ReentrantLock`, although not every synchronization primitive tracks an owning thread.

For an application hang, capture three to five thread dumps several seconds apart. Compare repeated stack traces and lock relationships to distinguish persistent blocking from normal waiting. For high CPU, correlate operating-system thread CPU usage with the native thread identifier shown in a dump. A `RUNNABLE` state alone does not prove high CPU consumption. Use **repeated sampling** to establish patterns rather than drawing conclusions from one snapshot. Traditional thread-dump operations can briefly pause or disrupt the JVM, so consider latency requirements and collection frequency in production.
bullets: **Thread dump:** Captures thread states, stack traces and available lock information.
**RUNNABLE:** Indicates execution eligibility, not necessarily active CPU consumption.
**BLOCKED:** Indicates waiting to acquire a Java monitor.
**Deadlock detection:** Look for circular lock dependencies and reported Java-level deadlocks.
**Lock details:** Use `-l` to include owned synchronizer information, including supported `ReentrantLock` ownership.
**Repeated snapshots:** Collect three to five dumps several seconds apart to investigate persistent hangs.

glossary.meaning: A sequence of method calls showing where a thread is currently executing.
A JVM synchronization mechanism associated with an object and used by synchronized code.
A situation where threads cannot proceed because they are waiting for resources held by one another.
A synchronization mechanism that tracks an exclusive owning thread, such as ReentrantLock.

cards.code:
# Inspect CPU usage by operating-system thread
top -H -p 1234

# Convert a decimal thread ID to hexadecimal
printf '%x\n' 5678

# Capture thread dumps with lock information
jstack -l 1234 > threads.txt
jcmd 1234 Thread.print -l > threads2.txt

# Capture five snapshots at five-second intervals
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do
    jcmd 1234 Thread.print -l > "threads-$i.txt"
    sleep 5
done

# Search for reported Java-level deadlocks
grep -i 'deadlock' threads-*.txt

# Compare states, stack traces and lock ownership
# Match hexadecimal thread IDs against nid values.
commonMistakes: Assuming every `RUNNABLE` thread is consuming CPU without checking operating-system thread statistics.
Treating normal `WAITING` threads in an idle executor pool as evidence of a deadlock.
Diagnosing persistent application hangs using only one thread dump.

interview.q: How would you diagnose a Java application that has stopped responding?
interview.a: I would collect three to five thread dumps using `jcmd Thread.print -l` or `jstack -l`, several seconds apart. I would compare thread states, repeated stack traces and lock ownership to identify persistent blocking, deadlocks or potentially expensive operations.

interview.q: What is the difference between BLOCKED and WAITING thread states?
interview.a: `BLOCKED` means a thread is waiting to acquire a Java monitor used by `synchronized` code. `WAITING` means it is waiting indefinitely for another action, such as a notification, thread completion or an explicit unpark operation. Neither state automatically indicates a problem.

interview.q: Can you identify high CPU consumption using a thread dump alone?
interview.a: Not reliably. A `RUNNABLE` thread may be executing Java code or waiting inside native operations. I would correlate operating-system thread CPU statistics with thread identifiers in the dump, or use a CPU profiler to identify expensive execution paths.

cards.title: Heap Dumps, Histograms and Native Memory
cards.tldr: **Memory diagnostics** identifies what consumes JVM memory and why it remains allocated. Heap dumps reveal object retention, while native memory tracking investigates JVM memory outside the heap.
cards.summary:
The JVM uses the Java heap for ordinary objects and additional memory outside the heap for class metadata, thread stacks and internal structures. A **memory leak** occurs when memory remains occupied even though the application no longer needs it. Investigating memory growth begins by determining which memory region is increasing rather than assuming every problem is a heap leak.

A **class histogram** reports object counts and aggregate shallow sizes grouped by class. Generate one using `jcmd GC.class_histogram` or `jmap -histo` to identify suspicious object populations. A **heap dump** captures objects, their classes and reference relationships. Generate one using `jcmd GC.heap_dump` or `jmap`, then inspect it with Eclipse Memory Analyzer, YourKit or VisualVM. Eclipse MAT provides a dominator tree and retained-size analysis. Retained size estimates memory that would become reclaimable if an object were removed. Paths to GC roots reveal references that keep objects reachable. Common causes include unbounded collections, caches without eviction, thread-local values and obsolete classloaders.

For memory outside the heap, use **Native Memory Tracking**, enabled at JVM startup with `NativeMemoryTracking`, and inspect its summary using `jcmd VM.native_memory summary`. It does not account for every native allocation. Compare process resident memory with heap usage, Metaspace and other reported categories. Use `VM.metaspace` and `jmap -clstats` to investigate classloader-related growth. Heap dumps can cause significant pauses and consume substantial disk space, while histograms can also be expensive. Prefer controlled collection during low traffic or on a representative replica. Protect dumps because they can contain sensitive application data. The obsolete `jhat` analyzer was removed in Java 9.
bullets: **Class histogram:** Identifies classes with large instance populations or aggregate shallow memory usage.
**Heap dump:** Captures object relationships for investigating retained memory and reference chains.
**Dominator tree:** Helps locate objects responsible for retaining substantial portions of the heap.
**Native memory tracking:** Reports supported JVM-managed native memory categories when enabled at startup.
**Metaspace analysis:** Use `VM.metaspace` and `jmap -clstats` to investigate class metadata and retained classloaders.
**Production precautions:** Consider pause duration, available disk space and sensitive data before capturing heap dumps.

glossary.meaning: Memory occupied directly by an object, excluding objects referenced by it.
Memory that would become reclaimable if a particular object and its exclusively retained objects became unreachable.
A representation of object relationships showing which objects control the reachability of other objects.
A HotSpot feature that tracks supported categories of memory allocated internally by the JVM.

cards.code:
# Quick heap information
jcmd 1234 GC.heap_info
# Object counts and aggregate shallow sizes
jcmd 1234 GC.class_histogram
jmap -histo 1234
# Capture a heap dump for offline analysis
jcmd 1234 GC.heap_dump /tmp/heap.hprof
jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap.hprof 1234
# Inspect class metadata and classloaders
jcmd 1234 VM.metaspace
jmap -clstats 1234
# Enable native memory tracking at JVM startup
java -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary -jar app.jar
# Inspect JVM native memory categories
jcmd 1234 VM.native_memory summary
# Compare changes over time
jcmd 1234 VM.native_memory baseline
jcmd 1234 VM.native_memory summary.diff
# Inspect process resident memory in kilobytes
ps -o pid,rss,cmd -p 1234
commonMistakes: Assuming the class with the highest instance count is necessarily responsible for a memory leak.
Expecting Native Memory Tracking to report every allocation made by third-party native libraries.
Capturing large heap dumps on latency-critical production instances without checking disk capacity or operational impact.

interview.q: How would you investigate a memory leak in a Java application?
interview.a: I would first determine whether heap or native memory is growing. For heap growth, I would inspect a class histogram and capture a heap dump when appropriate. Using Eclipse MAT, I would examine retained sizes, the dominator tree and paths to GC roots to identify what prevents objects from being collected.

interview.q: What is the difference between shallow size and retained size?
interview.a: **Shallow size** measures memory directly occupied by an object. **Retained size** estimates the memory that would become reclaimable if that object became unreachable. Retained size is particularly useful for identifying collections and caches that keep large object graphs alive.

interview.q: The Java heap is stable, but process memory continues growing. What would you investigate?
interview.a: I would investigate native memory categories such as thread stacks, Metaspace, direct buffers and JVM internal allocations. If Native Memory Tracking is enabled, I would inspect `VM.native_memory summary` and compare changes over time. I would also compare those results with operating-system resident memory because not every native allocation is tracked.

cards.title: Java Flight Recorder and GC Monitoring
cards.tldr: **Java Flight Recorder** captures JVM performance events over time. Use it to investigate latency, garbage collection, thread activity, compilation and input/output operations together.
cards.summary:
**Java Flight Recorder** (`JFR`) is a built-in JVM event-recording system that captures application and runtime behavior over time. Unlike a thread dump, which provides a single snapshot, JFR records a timeline of events. Its default configurations generally have low overhead, often around one percent or less, although actual costs depend on enabled events, sampling frequency and workload.

JFR records garbage collection pauses and heap changes through events such as `jdk.GCPhasePause` and `jdk.GCHeapSummary`. It also captures just-in-time compilation, which converts frequently executed bytecode into machine code, through `jdk.Compilation` and `jdk.Deoptimization`. Other events cover class loading, thread creation, parking, monitor contention, file operations, socket operations, exceptions, safepoints and sampled method execution. A **safepoint** is a JVM coordination point where threads can safely participate in certain runtime operations. Start recordings on demand using `JFR.start`, or maintain continuous recordings with a rolling time or size limit. Analyze recordings in **JDK Mission Control** to correlate application latency with JVM activity.

For quick garbage collection checks, `jstat -gc` reports collection counts, accumulated collection times and memory statistics. `jstat -gcutil` reports utilization percentages for supported memory regions. Polling these values helps identify allocation pressure and increasing old-generation occupancy. GC logs enabled through `-Xlog:gc*` provide additional collector details. Prefer JFR for broader investigations, while `jstat` remains useful for quick sampling and is not universally deprecated. Avoid forcing collections through `GC.run` as a routine diagnostic step because explicit garbage collection can disrupt production workloads. Use detailed profiling settings selectively because additional event collection can increase overhead.
bullets: **JFR timeline:** Correlates garbage collection, compilation, threading, input/output operations and application execution.
**Low overhead:** Suitable for continuous recording with appropriately selected events and retention limits.
**Latency analysis:** Inspect GC pauses, safepoints, monitor contention and socket or file operation durations.
**Thread growth:** Use `jdk.ThreadStart` events to investigate thread creation patterns.
**Quick GC checks:** Use `jstat -gc` and `jstat -gcutil` to inspect memory usage and collection statistics.
**GC precautions:** Use GC logs and JFR before considering disruptive explicit garbage collection.

glossary.meaning: A recorded observation of JVM or application activity, usually containing timestamps and relevant diagnostic information.
A coordinated execution point where the JVM can safely perform certain runtime operations.
A memory region used by generational garbage collectors for objects that survive earlier collections.
A graphical tool for analyzing Java Flight Recorder recordings and JVM performance.

cards.code:
# Monitor GC statistics every second
jstat -gc 1234 1000
jstat -gcutil 1234 1000
# Start a recording on demand
jcmd 1234 JFR.start name=diag settings=profile
# Save a snapshot without stopping the recording
jcmd 1234 JFR.dump name=diag filename=diag.jfr
# Stop the recording
jcmd 1234 JFR.stop name=diag
# Continuous recording with one-hour retention
java \
  -XX:StartFlightRecording=disk=true,maxage=1h \
  -jar app.jar
# Enable detailed garbage collection logging
java -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log -jar app.jar
# Inspect recorded events
jfr summary diag.jfr
jfr print --events jdk.GCPhasePause diag.jfr
# Open diag.jfr in JDK Mission Control.
commonMistakes: Assuming JFR always introduces a fixed amount of overhead regardless of enabled events or recording settings.
Interpreting cumulative garbage collection time as the duration of an individual application pause.
Running `GC.run` repeatedly to reduce heap utilization instead of investigating allocation and retention behavior.

interview.q: Why would you use Java Flight Recorder instead of collecting individual thread dumps?
interview.a: JFR provides a continuous timeline covering garbage collection, thread activity, compilation, input/output operations and method samples. This allows me to correlate events with latency spikes. Thread dumps are useful for specific snapshots, especially during hangs, but do not provide the same historical context.

interview.q: How would you determine whether garbage collection is causing high API latency?
interview.a: I would collect a JFR recording and compare request latency with GC pause events such as `jdk.GCPhasePause`. I would also inspect GC logs for pause durations and collection patterns. `jstat` can provide a quick initial view, but cumulative statistics alone cannot establish that a particular request was delayed by garbage collection.

interview.q: Can Java Flight Recorder be enabled in production continuously?
interview.a: Yes. JFR supports continuous recording with relatively low overhead under suitable configurations. I would configure rolling retention limits, validate the overhead for the workload and enable more expensive profiling events only when necessary.

cards.title: Heap Generations and Heap Memory Errors
cards.tldr: **Generational garbage collection** separates objects according to their age. Heap exhaustion occurs when the JVM cannot allocate objects within the available heap space.
cards.summary:
The **Java heap** is the memory area where ordinary Java objects and arrays are allocated. Garbage collection reclaims objects that are no longer reachable. Generational collectors organize the heap according to object age because most newly created objects become unnecessary quickly. This organization allows the JVM to reclaim short-lived objects efficiently without repeatedly examining every long-lived object.

Traditional generational collectors divide the heap into the **Young Generation**, containing Eden and two survivor spaces, and the **Old Generation**, also called Tenured. New objects normally enter Eden. During young garbage collection, surviving objects move between survivor spaces or are promoted to Old. The G1 collector, normally the default in Java 21 server environments, instead divides the heap into equal-sized regions dynamically assigned roles such as Eden, Survivor and Old. Objects at least half a region in size are classified as humongous and receive special allocation treatment. With two-megabyte regions, the threshold is approximately one megabyte. ZGC uses differently sized memory pages, colored pointers and concurrent object relocation. Java 21 also supports optional generational ZGC.

`OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space` means an allocation cannot be satisfied, commonly because too many live objects remain or the requested allocation is too large. **GC overhead limit exceeded** can occur when supported collectors spend excessive time collecting very little memory. The traditional HotSpot threshold is approximately 98 percent GC time with less than two percent recovery across consecutive collections. Investigate retained objects using class histograms, heap dumps and GC logs. Increasing `-Xmx` may help genuinely undersized heaps, but it does not repair unbounded caches or memory leaks. Disabling `UseGCOverheadLimit` merely removes a protective check.
bullets: **Young Generation:** Contains newly allocated and recently surviving objects in traditional generational collectors.
**Old Generation:** Contains objects promoted after surviving earlier collections or allocated there through special paths.
**G1 regions:** Dynamically assigned memory regions replace permanently contiguous generational divisions.
**Humongous objects:** Objects at least half a G1 region in size receive special allocation treatment.
**Heap exhaustion:** Often indicates excessive retained objects, insufficient heap capacity or an unusually large allocation.
**GC overhead limit:** Detects excessive collection activity with little memory recovery in supported collectors.

glossary.meaning: Young-generation memory where most ordinary new objects are initially allocated.
Memory used to hold young objects that remain reachable after garbage collection.
Moving an object from the young generation into the old generation.
An object large enough to require special region allocation under the G1 garbage collector.

cards.code:
# Traditional generational heap
Young: [Eden] [S0] [S1]
Old:   [Tenured              ]

# G1 dynamically assigned regions
[Eden][Old][Eden][Surv][Humongous][Free]

# Example object lifetime
Eden --> Survivor --> Survivor --> Old

# Configure a maximum heap size
java -Xmx2g -jar app.jar

# Inspect heap and object populations
jcmd 1234 GC.heap_info
jmap -histo:live 1234

# Capture objects and reference relationships
jcmd 1234 GC.heap_dump /tmp/heap.hprof

# Enable garbage collection logs
java -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log -jar app.jar

# Disabling overhead protection is not a leak fix
# -XX:-UseGCOverheadLimit
commonMistakes: Assuming all garbage collectors use the same physical Eden and Survivor memory layout.
Confusing a high allocation rate with excessive retention of live objects.
Disabling `UseGCOverheadLimit` instead of investigating why garbage collection recovers so little memory.

interview.q: How is the Java heap organized under generational garbage collection?
interview.a: Traditional generational collectors divide the heap into Young and Old generations. Young typically contains Eden and two survivor spaces, while longer-lived objects are promoted to Old. G1 implements these logical generations using dynamically assigned memory regions rather than permanently contiguous spaces.

interview.q: What is a humongous object in G1?
interview.a: A humongous object occupies at least half the configured G1 region size. G1 allocates such objects directly into special contiguous regions. Frequent humongous allocations can increase fragmentation and create additional garbage collection pressure.

interview.q: What is the difference between Java heap space and GC overhead limit exceeded?
interview.a: `Java heap space` indicates that a heap allocation could not be satisfied. `GC overhead limit exceeded` indicates that a supported collector is spending excessive time recovering very little memory. Both can result from excessive object retention, so I would investigate heap contents and garbage collection behavior.

cards.title: OutOfMemoryError Types and Thread Stack Exhaustion
cards.tldr: Different **memory errors** identify different exhausted resources. Read the complete error message before choosing heap, classloader, native memory or thread diagnostics.
cards.summary:
`OutOfMemoryError` occurs when the JVM cannot satisfy a required resource allocation. Its accompanying message often identifies the resource involved. **Java heap space** indicates a failed heap allocation. Metaspace errors indicate exhausted class metadata storage. Direct buffer memory errors indicate failed direct buffer reservations. GC overhead limit errors indicate excessive garbage collection with insufficient recovery under collectors that implement this check.

An error such as `unable to create native thread` means the JVM cannot create another operating-system thread. Each platform thread requires native resources, including a stack for method calls and local execution state. Thread creation can fail because of Linux user process limits, container process limits such as `pids.max`, or insufficient native memory. Investigate thread counts and configured stack sizes before increasing limits. Bounded thread pools reduce excessive platform thread creation. Java 21 **virtual threads**, lightweight JVM-managed threads, can support many blocking tasks without requiring a dedicated platform thread for every task.

`StackOverflowError` is a different error, not a subtype of `OutOfMemoryError`. It normally occurs when a thread's call stack is exhausted by deep or uncontrolled recursion. Increasing `-Xss`, which controls platform thread stack size, may accommodate legitimate deep call chains but can increase native memory requirements. Prefer correcting unnecessary recursion or replacing it with iteration. A process terminated by the operating-system **OOM killer** may produce no Java exception. Check container termination reasons and operating-system logs. For heap errors, inspect histograms, heap dumps and GC logs. For Metaspace errors, inspect classloader statistics. For direct memory errors or process termination, inspect native memory, RSS and container limits. Match the diagnostic tool to the exhausted resource rather than applying the same memory settings to every failure.
bullets: **Heap errors:** Inspect object populations, retained memory, allocation requirements and garbage collection logs.
**Metaspace errors:** Investigate loaded classes, retained classloaders and metadata limits.
**Direct memory errors:** Inspect native buffer ownership, configured limits and process memory usage.
**Native thread errors:** Investigate operating-system thread limits, container process limits and stack memory requirements.
**Stack overflow:** Correct excessive recursion or adjust stack size for legitimate deep call chains.
**OS termination:** Check operating-system logs and container termination information when no Java exception appears.

glossary.meaning: A Java thread backed by a dedicated operating-system thread.
A lightweight JVM-managed thread that can share underlying platform threads with other virtual threads.
Per-thread memory containing information about active method calls and their execution state.
An operating-system mechanism that terminates processes when memory constraints cannot otherwise be satisfied.

cards.code:
# Heap allocation failure
jcmd 1234 GC.class_histogram
jcmd 1234 GC.heap_dump /tmp/heap.hprof
# Class metadata exhaustion
jcmd 1234 VM.metaspace
jmap -clstats 1234
# Native memory exhaustion
jcmd 1234 VM.native_memory summary
ps -o pid,rss,cmd -p 1234
# Native thread creation failure on Linux
ps -o pid,nlwp,rss -p 1234
cat /proc/1234/limits
ulimit -u
# Example cgroup v2 process-limit inspection
# Run inside the relevant container or cgroup.
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/pids.max
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/pids.current
# Configure platform thread stack size
java -Xss512k -jar app.jar
# Smaller stacks can increase stack overflow risk.
commonMistakes: Responding to every `OutOfMemoryError` by increasing the maximum Java heap size.
Increasing platform thread stack size when the process already struggles to create additional native threads.
Assuming an operating-system memory termination must produce a Java exception or heap dump.

interview.q: What are the common types of OutOfMemoryError in Java?
interview.a: Common messages include `Java heap space`, `Metaspace`, direct buffer memory exhaustion, `GC overhead limit exceeded` and failure to create native threads. Each points toward a different resource or allocation problem. I would inspect the exact message and choose diagnostics appropriate to that resource.

interview.q: Why can a JVM fail to create a new thread even when heap memory is available?
interview.a: Platform threads require operating-system resources and native stack memory outside the Java heap. Thread creation can fail because of user process limits, container process limits or native memory exhaustion. Bounded thread pools or virtual threads can reduce platform thread requirements.

interview.q: Is StackOverflowError an OutOfMemoryError?
interview.a: No. `StackOverflowError` and `OutOfMemoryError` are separate subclasses of `VirtualMachineError`. Stack overflow typically indicates that a thread has exhausted its call stack through excessive recursion or deep method calls. Increasing heap size does not directly solve it.

cards.title: Classloader Leaks and Dynamic Proxy Classes
cards.tldr: A retained classloader can prevent its classes from unloading. Unreleased application resources and excessive generated proxy classes can cause **Metaspace growth**.
cards.summary:
**Metaspace** is a HotSpot JVM memory area that primarily stores class metadata, meaning internal information about loaded classes. Class unloading allows the JVM to reclaim metadata that is no longer needed. Classes defined by an ordinary custom classloader become eligible for unloading when their defining loader becomes unreachable. Garbage collection determines reachability by following references from active JVM structures, such as running threads and static fields.

A **classloader leak** occurs when an application stops or is redeployed but something continues referencing its old classloader or its classes. Common causes include values stored in `ThreadLocal`, which associates data with a thread, on long-lived container thread pools. Registered JDBC database drivers, registered MBeans used for application monitoring, shared-library static caches, running background threads and thread context classloaders can also retain an old application. Repeated deployments may therefore increase Metaspace usage until the JVM reports `OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace`.

Cleanup must match resource ownership. Remove thread-local values on the threads that set them, normally inside a `finally` block. Use lifecycle callbacks such as `@PreDestroy` or `ServletContextListener.contextDestroyed()` to deregister application-owned JDBC drivers, unregister MBeans and stop application-owned threads. Container leak-prevention facilities and dedicated libraries can help with dependencies outside your control. Simply increasing the Metaspace limit delays failures caused by permanently retained loaders.

**Dynamic proxies** are classes generated at runtime to intercept method calls. JDK proxies implement interfaces and are generated using a specified classloader that can see those interfaces. CGLIB generates subclasses using a suitable loader. Generated classes consume Metaspace, and unbounded generation or incorrectly managed caches can increase memory usage. Reuse proxy class definitions for compatible interface sets or target classes and classloaders instead of generating unique classes per object. Standard JDK and CGLIB facilities already provide caching mechanisms. Diagnose growth with `jcmd`, `jmap -clstats`, Eclipse MAT or YourKit. Compare class counts across deployments and inspect **GC roots**, which are starting points for reachability analysis, to identify what retains obsolete classloaders.
bullets: **Unloading eligibility:** An ordinary class becomes eligible when its defining classloader becomes unreachable.
**Common retention sources:** Pooled-thread values, JDBC registrations, MBeans, static caches and running threads.
**Lifecycle cleanup:** Release application-owned resources when the application stops.
**Dynamic proxies:** JDK proxies implement interfaces, while CGLIB generates subclasses.
**Bounded generation:** Reuse compatible generated proxy classes and avoid uncontrolled class generation.
**Diagnosis:** Compare classloader statistics and inspect reference paths from GC roots.

glossary.meaning: Native memory used by HotSpot primarily for storing class metadata.
A runtime-generated object that intercepts method calls through a generated class.
A starting reference from which the garbage collector determines reachable objects.

cards.code:
Classloader leak after redeployment:
Container thread
  |
  +--> ThreadLocal value
         |
         +--> Old application object
                |
                +--> Old class and classloader
                       |
                       +--> Retained class metadata
Diagnostics:
  jcmd <pid> VM.metaspace
  jcmd <pid> VM.metaspace show-loaders
  jmap -clstats <pid>
Heap analysis:
  MAT / YourKit classloader views
  -> Find obsolete classloaders
  -> Inspect paths to GC roots
Cleanup:
  ThreadLocal.remove()
  DriverManager.deregisterDriver(driver)
  MBeanServer.unregisterMBean(name)
  Stop application-owned background threads
commonMistakes: Calling `ThreadLocal.remove()` on a shutdown thread and expecting it to remove values stored on unrelated worker threads.
Increasing `MaxMetaspaceSize` without investigating obsolete classloaders or uncontrolled class generation.
Assuming every new dynamic proxy instance necessarily generates a new proxy class.

interview.q: Why can Metaspace usage increase after every application redeployment?
interview.a: Old application classloaders may remain reachable through pooled threads, registered drivers, shared caches or background tasks. Their classes cannot unload while those loaders remain reachable. Repeated redeployments accumulate retained class metadata and may eventually exhaust Metaspace.

interview.q: How do JDK dynamic proxies and CGLIB affect class loading?
interview.a: JDK proxies generate classes implementing specified interfaces, while CGLIB generates subclasses of target classes. Both require suitable classloaders and consume class metadata memory. Repeatedly generating unique proxy classes or retaining obsolete loaders can increase Metaspace usage.

interview.q: How would you investigate a suspected classloader leak in production?
interview.a: I would compare Metaspace usage and classloader statistics using `jcmd` or `jmap -clstats`. If obsolete loaders remain after redeployments, I would inspect a heap dump using MAT or YourKit. Paths to GC roots reveal which threads, registrations or caches retain them.

cards.title: Async-profiler, Flame Graphs and Bottleneck Analysis
cards.tldr: **Async-profiler** samples Java and native execution stacks to identify CPU hotspots, allocation pressure, lock contention and waiting time through flame graphs.
cards.summary:
**Async-profiler** is a sampling-based profiler for JVM applications. Sampling means periodically observing execution instead of recording every method invocation. This makes it possible to identify expensive execution paths with relatively low overhead. It is particularly useful when monitoring or Java Flight Recorder has identified a performance problem, but the underlying methods responsible for the problem remain unclear.

On Linux, CPU profiling can use the operating system's `perf_events` mechanism together with JVM stack-walking capabilities such as `AsyncGetCallTrace`. These mechanisms allow the profiler to inspect Java and native execution stacks asynchronously, reducing traditional safepoint sampling bias. **Safepoint bias** occurs when sampling disproportionately observes locations where JVM threads can reach coordination points. Async-profiler supports CPU profiling for active computation, allocation profiling for object creation, lock profiling for synchronization contention and wall-clock profiling for elapsed execution time, including waiting. Results can be displayed as an interactive **flame graph**, where wider frames represent a larger proportion of the selected samples or measurements. Vertical relationships show nested method calls, while horizontal position does not represent chronological execution.

Choose the profiling mode according to the symptom. Use CPU profiling when processor utilization is high, allocation profiling when excessive object creation increases garbage collection pressure, and lock or wall-clock profiling when requests are slow despite low CPU utilization. Java Flight Recorder provides complementary context through garbage collection, socket, file, monitor and safepoint events. An allocation hotspot does not necessarily indicate a memory leak because allocation measures creation rather than retained memory. Use heap dumps and retained-size analysis for actual object retention problems.

Profiler overhead and available features depend on the operating system, JVM, permissions, sampling frequency and selected event mode. Linux performance-counter restrictions or container security settings may prevent particular profiling mechanisms from working. Native stack accuracy can also depend on unwinding support and symbol availability. Start with short recordings under representative workloads and extend them only when necessary. Modern async-profiler distributions use `asprof`, while older versions commonly provide `profiler.sh`. Confirm findings with additional measurements rather than treating a single flame graph as conclusive proof.
bullets: **CPU profiling:** Identifies methods responsible for active processor consumption.
**Allocation profiling:** Identifies object creation hotspots rather than objects retained indefinitely.
**Lock profiling:** Helps locate synchronization contention and expensive lock acquisition.
**Wall-clock profiling:** Includes waiting time and helps investigate slow requests with low CPU usage.
**Flame graphs:** Frame width represents measured sample contribution, while vertical position represents call relationships.
**Complementary tools:** Use JFR for system-wide context and heap dumps for retained-memory investigations.

glossary.meaning: A diagnostic tool that periodically observes execution to estimate where resources or time are spent.
A visualization of sampled call stacks where frame width represents the relative contribution of a measured event.
Distortion in profiling results caused by disproportionately sampling locations associated with JVM coordination points.

cards.code:
# Modern async-profiler CLI: asprof

# CPU hotspots
./bin/asprof -d 30 -e cpu -f cpu.html 1234

# Object allocation hotspots
./bin/asprof -d 30 -e alloc -f alloc.html 1234

# Lock contention
./bin/asprof -d 30 -e lock -f lock.html 1234

# Elapsed time, including waiting
./bin/asprof -d 30 -e wall -f wall.html 1234

# Check supported profiling events
./bin/asprof list 1234

# Older async-profiler distributions
./profiler.sh -d 30 -e cpu -f cpu.html 1234

# Open the generated HTML flame graph.
# Wide frames indicate larger measured contributions.
# Parent frames represent callers.
# Child frames represent called methods.
# Horizontal position is not execution time.
commonMistakes: Using only CPU profiling to investigate requests that spend most of their time waiting for external services or synchronization.
Interpreting an allocation flame graph as evidence of a memory leak without investigating object retention.
Assuming the horizontal position of a flame graph frame indicates when a method executed.

interview.q: What is the difference between Java Flight Recorder and async-profiler?
interview.a: JFR records a broad range of JVM events, including garbage collection, compilation, threading and input/output operations. Async-profiler specializes in sampled execution analysis and provides detailed flame graphs for CPU, allocations, locks and wall-clock time. I use JFR for context and async-profiler when I need to identify specific expensive execution paths.

interview.q: An API has high response times, but CPU utilization is low. Which profiling approach would you use?
interview.a: I would begin with JFR to inspect socket operations, file operations, monitor contention and garbage collection pauses. I would then use async-profiler wall-clock or lock profiling if necessary. CPU profiling alone could miss the bottleneck because waiting threads may consume little processor time.

interview.q: What is safepoint bias and how does async-profiler address it?
interview.a: Safepoint bias occurs when a profiler disproportionately observes execution at JVM coordination points instead of sampling execution uniformly. Async-profiler uses asynchronous stack sampling mechanisms that can observe Java and native execution without requiring every sample to wait for a safepoint. This reduces sampling distortion, although other limitations can still affect profiling accuracy.

cards.title: Metaspace, PermGen and Off-Heap Memory
cards.tldr: **Native memory** exists outside the Java heap. Class metadata, direct buffers and native libraries consume it and can exhaust process memory independently of ordinary heap objects.
cards.summary:
**Native memory** is memory allocated from the operating system outside the ordinary Java object heap. HotSpot uses it for class metadata, thread stacks, compiled machine code and other runtime structures. Applications can also allocate native memory directly. Consequently, a Java process can consume substantially more memory than its configured maximum heap size.

Before Java 8, HotSpot stored class metadata in the Permanent Generation, called **PermGen**, a separate managed memory region with a configurable maximum size. Its `MaxPermSize` limit frequently caused `PermGen space` errors during repeated application deployments. Java 8 replaced PermGen with **Metaspace**, which stores class metadata in native memory and grows dynamically unless constrained by `MaxMetaspaceSize` or available system memory. A Metaspace exhaustion error can result from excessive generated classes, scripting engines repeatedly compiling expressions, unbounded proxy generation, retained classloaders or an insufficient configured limit. Ordinary classes become eligible for unloading when their defining classloader becomes unreachable.

Application **off-heap memory** includes NIO direct buffers created through `ByteBuffer.allocateDirect()`, memory-mapped files created through `FileChannel.map()` and allocations made by native libraries through JNI, the Java Native Interface. Direct buffers can reduce copying during native I/O. Their native allocations are normally released through cleanup mechanisms after their Java wrappers become unreachable. Memory-mapped files use operating-system mappings, while libraries such as RocksDB, compression libraries and Netty manage native allocations through their own ownership or pooling mechanisms. Netty reference-counted buffers must be released according to their ownership rules.

A direct buffer allocation can fail with `OutOfMemoryError` when its memory limit is exceeded. `MaxDirectMemorySize` controls supported NIO direct buffer reservations, not all native allocations. Its effective default in typical HotSpot configurations follows the maximum heap size. The operating system may instead terminate the process when system or container memory limits are exceeded. Monitor **resident set size** (`RSS`), which measures process memory currently resident in physical RAM. Compare it with heap usage, Metaspace, thread stacks and native memory categories. Enable **Native Memory Tracking** at startup and inspect changes using `jcmd VM.native_memory`. It does not track every third-party native allocation. Heap dumps can reveal Java wrappers retaining native resources, but they cannot directly account for the complete native memory contents.
bullets: **PermGen transition:** Java 8 replaced the bounded Permanent Generation with native-memory Metaspace.
**Metaspace exhaustion:** Investigate excessive class generation, retained classloaders and configured metadata limits.
**Direct buffers:** NIO can allocate native memory to reduce copying during input and output operations.
**Native resources:** Memory-mapped files, Netty buffers, RocksDB and JNI libraries follow different memory ownership rules.
**Direct memory limits:** `MaxDirectMemorySize` does not limit every native allocation made by the process.
**Diagnosis:** Combine RSS monitoring, native memory tracking, classloader statistics and library-specific metrics.

glossary.meaning: Native memory used by HotSpot primarily to store loaded class metadata.
The Java Native Interface allows Java code to interact with native code, commonly written in C or C++.
The portion of a process's memory currently resident in physical RAM.

cards.code:
# Bound Metaspace and NIO direct memory
java \
  -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m \
  -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=512m \
  -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary \
  -jar app.jar

# Inspect class metadata and classloaders
jcmd 1234 VM.metaspace
jmap -clstats 1234

# Inspect native memory categories
jcmd 1234 VM.native_memory summary

# Compare native memory growth over time
jcmd 1234 VM.native_memory baseline
# Wait while the application processes traffic.
jcmd 1234 VM.native_memory summary.diff

# Process resident memory in kilobytes
ps -o pid,rss,cmd -p 1234

# Compare these results with Java heap usage
jcmd 1234 GC.heap_info
commonMistakes: Assuming `-Xmx` limits the entire Java process, including direct buffers, class metadata and native libraries.
Increasing `MaxMetaspaceSize` without investigating excessive class generation or obsolete classloaders.
Expecting a heap dump or Native Memory Tracking to account for every byte allocated by native libraries.

interview.q: What is the difference between PermGen and Metaspace?
interview.a: PermGen was a separately managed memory region used by older HotSpot versions to store class metadata, with a configurable maximum size. Java 8 replaced it with Metaspace, which allocates class metadata in native memory and grows dynamically unless constrained. Classloader leaks can exhaust either mechanism.

interview.q: Why can a Java application exceed its Xmx memory limit at the process level?
interview.a: `-Xmx` limits the ordinary Java heap, not total process memory. Metaspace, direct buffers, thread stacks, compiled code and native libraries consume additional memory. A container must provide sufficient memory for both the heap and these additional allocations.

interview.q: How would you investigate growing process memory when heap usage is stable?
interview.a: I would compare process RSS with heap usage and inspect Native Memory Tracking if it was enabled. I would also investigate Metaspace, thread counts, direct buffer metrics and native library allocations. Heap dumps may reveal retained Java wrappers, but native allocations require additional diagnostic tools.

cards.title: JIT Optimizations, Deoptimization and Safepoints
cards.tldr: HotSpot optimizes code using runtime assumptions and can reverse those optimizations. **Safepoints** coordinate runtime operations that require threads to reach safe execution states.
cards.summary:
HotSpot's optimizing compiler uses runtime observations to improve machine code. **Speculative optimization** means generating faster code based on assumptions that appear valid during execution. For example, a monomorphic call site has observed only one concrete receiver type. C2 may perform inlining, replacing a method call with its implementation, or loop unrolling, duplicating loop bodies to reduce control overhead. These optimizations can improve throughput but require compilation time and additional compiler memory.

When an assumption becomes invalid, **deoptimization** reconstructs execution state so an affected thread can continue in interpreted or less-specialized code. An uncommon trap is a runtime guard failure that triggers this process. New receiver types, failed speculative null checks or invalidated class hierarchy assumptions can trigger deoptimization. Class redefinition may also invalidate compiled methods and make them not entrant, meaning new calls cannot enter that compiled version. Frequent invalidation, interpretation and recompilation can reduce performance, although polymorphic call sites are not automatically problematic.

**Escape analysis** determines how an allocated object's references can become visible beyond the allocation context. Scalar replacement can eliminate an object's physical allocation and represent its fields using compiler-managed values, registers or stack slots. Lock elision removes synchronization proven unnecessary, such as locking on an object inaccessible to other threads. Standard HotSpot C2 does not generally move complete non-escaping objects onto the stack. Returning an object from a method also does not guarantee allocation because the caller may be inlined. Use allocation measurements and `DoEscapeAnalysis` experiments to investigate optimization effects.

A **safepoint** allows threads to participate safely in coordinated JVM operations, including stop-the-world garbage collection phases, certain deoptimization operations, heap dumps and code cache maintenance. Threads executing Java code reach inserted checks, commonly around method returns and loop backedges, while threads in suitable native or blocked states may already be safe. **Time to safepoint** measures how long coordination takes before the requested operation begins. A long-running loop without sufficiently frequent checks can delay this process. Modern HotSpot uses counted-loop safepoints and loop strip mining to reduce such delays. Inspect `-Xlog:safepoint=info`, JFR compilation, deoptimization and safepoint events before changing compiler flags. Modern JFR sampling does not generally require a global safepoint for every sample.
bullets: **Speculative optimization:** C2 can optimize execution using observed receiver types and runtime assumptions.
**Deoptimization:** Invalid assumptions can trigger fallback execution and subsequent recompilation.
**Escape analysis:** Determines whether object identity or references must remain observable beyond the allocation context.
**Scalar replacement:** Eliminates eligible physical allocations by representing object fields as individual compiler-managed values.
**Lock elision:** Removes synchronization when the compiler proves it is unnecessary for correct execution.
**Time to safepoint:** Coordination delay is distinct from the duration of the requested JVM operation.

glossary.meaning: A runtime path that triggers deoptimization when an assumption made during compilation fails.
An optimization that replaces an object with its individual field values and may eliminate physical allocation.
The time required for relevant JVM threads to reach states suitable for a coordinated runtime operation.

commonMistakes: Claiming escape analysis always moves complete non-escaping objects from the heap onto the stack.
Assuming optimized machine code remains permanently valid regardless of changing runtime behavior or loaded classes.
Treating the reported garbage collection operation duration as the entire application interruption without considering time to safepoint.

interview.q: What is deoptimization and why does the JVM need it?
interview.a: C2 can optimize code using speculative assumptions, such as a call site having only one observed receiver type. If an assumption becomes invalid, deoptimization reconstructs execution state and transfers affected execution to a safe, less-specialized form. The JVM can subsequently compile the method using updated profiling information.

interview.q: How does escape analysis reduce garbage collection pressure?
interview.a: Escape analysis helps determine whether an object's identity must remain observable outside its allocation context. If the compiler proves an allocation is unnecessary, scalar replacement can represent its fields independently and eliminate the object allocation. It can also enable removal of unnecessary synchronization. These optimizations reduce allocation and garbage collection work without changing Java program behavior.

interview.q: What is time to safepoint and how can it affect application latency?
interview.a: Time to safepoint measures the coordination delay before a requested safepoint operation can begin. Relevant threads must reach safe execution states, and long-running compiled loops can sometimes delay that coordination. Even a short garbage collection operation may therefore contribute to a longer application interruption. Safepoint logs help distinguish coordination time from operation duration.

cards.title: GC Algorithms and Collectors Deep Dive: Serial, Parallel, G1, ZGC, Shenandoah — Pause Profiles and Tuning
cards.summary:
The java-gc-1 card introduced the trade-off between G1 and ZGC. This card goes deeper into the algorithms, the STW/safepoint mechanics every collector depends on, and the specific tuning levers that interviewers ask about. The mental model is that GC is fundamentally about finding unreachable objects and reclaiming their memory, and every collector makes a different trade-off between pause time, throughput, memory overhead, and CPU cost.

The four fundamental GC algorithms are the building blocks. **Mark-sweep**: traverse from the roots, mark reachable objects, sweep the rest into free lists. Simple and low overhead, but causes fragmentation (free memory is scattered in small chunks) and slows allocation (free-list search instead of a bump pointer). **Mark-compact**: mark reachable objects, then slide live objects together to eliminate fragmentation. No fragmentation, fast allocation, but compaction is expensive and requires pausing because objects move. Copying (semi-space): divide memory into two spaces, copy live objects from one to the other during collection, then swap. Fast collection (only live objects are touched) and no fragmentation, but it wastes half the memory. **Modern collectors combine these**: young-generation collection is copying (most objects die, so copying is cheap); old-generation collection is mark-sweep or mark-compact (with different strategies for controlling fragmentation and pause time).

Generational hypothesis is why this works. Empirically, most objects die young. A young-generation collection only has to scan the young generation (which is small and mostly garbage), copy the few survivors, and promote long-lived objects to old. This is cheap and frequent. Old-generation collections are expensive and infrequent. The combination means GC cost is roughly proportional to live data in old generation, not to total allocation rate. This is why increasing heap size can reduce GC overhead (fewer collections) but can also increase pause time (more live data per collection) — the trade-off is not monotonic.

**Serial GC** is the simplest: a single-threaded stop-the-world collector that uses copying for young and mark-compact for old. Its pause time is proportional to heap size and the size of the live set, and it has no concurrency overhead. It is appropriate for small heaps (a few hundred MB) on single-core or small-footprint environments (containers, CLI tools, batch jobs). It is also the fallback for small instances where the JVM chose it automatically. For a server with a multi-GB heap and any latency requirement, Serial is almost never the right choice, but it is worth knowing because it is the baseline against which everything else is measured.

Parallel GC (the default in Java 8, still available) is Serial GC with multiple threads. Young collections and full GCs are parallelized across N GC threads (`-XX:ParallelGCThreads`). It is designed for throughput, not latency: pauses are still stop-the-world, but they are shorter than Serial because the work is parallelized. It is the right choice for batch jobs and throughput-bound services that can tolerate pauses in the hundreds of milliseconds, and it is often the fastest collector for pure throughput on a large heap because it has the least concurrent overhead. The trade-off is pause time: a full GC on a 20 GB heap with Parallel can take seconds, which is unacceptable for interactive services.

G1 (Garbage-First) is the default since Java 9. It divides the heap into equal-sized regions (typically 1–32 MB) rather than fixed young/old spaces. Young collections are still stop-the-world and copying; the difference is old-generation collection. Instead of a single full-heap collection, G1 performs concurrent marking (identifying which regions are mostly garbage) and then collects a subset of regions — the ones with the most garbage, hence 'garbage-first' — during a mixed collection. The pause target is set by `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis` (default 200 ms), and G1 tries to pick a set of regions that can be collected within that target. It is not a hard guarantee: if the heap is nearly full or the allocation rate is very high, G1 can miss the target and eventually fall back to a full GC (the single worst-case pause). G1's weakness is humongous allocations (objects larger than half a region — typically >1 MB with 2 MB regions): they are allocated in contiguous humongous regions, can trigger extra collections, and are a common source of G1 fallback to Full GC in real applications. **Tuning levers**: `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis` (pause goal, lower = smaller pauses but more frequent collections), `-XX:G1HeapRegionSize` (larger regions reduce humongous overhead but increase pause granularity), `-XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent` (when concurrent marking starts; lower = mark sooner, more overhead but avoids fallback), `-XX:G1NewSizePercent` / `-XX:G1MaxNewSizePercent` (young generation size bounds), `-XX:G1MixedGCLiveThresholdPercent` (how much live data a region can have to be collected in a mixed collection).

ZGC (production-ready in Java 15, generational in Java 21+) is designed for very low pause times on very large heaps (up to 16 TB). It performs almost all of its work concurrently — marking, relocation, and reference updating — using colored pointers (bits in the object reference used to mark GC state) and load barriers (code inserted at every load that checks the object's state and may redirect to the new location if the object moved). The result is sub-millisecond to low-millisecond pauses regardless of heap size, at the cost of additional CPU and memory overhead (colored pointers cost extra memory, load barriers add a small per-access cost). ZGC is the right choice when latency is a hard requirement (`p99`.9 SLOs, real-time bidding, financial trading) or the heap is very large (100 GB+). It does not automatically give better throughput — for pure throughput, Parallel or G1 usually win.

Shenandoah (production-ready in Java 15, like ZGC) is a similar low-pause collector from Red Hat, using Brooks forwarding pointers (an extra pointer per object) rather than colored pointers. The design trade-offs are similar to ZGC: sub-millisecond pauses on large heaps at the cost of some throughput and memory overhead. The choice between ZGC and Shenandoah is mostly ecosystem and JVM-vendor-driven; both achieve the same goal of decoupling pause time from heap size. In interviews, mentioning that both are concurrent compacting collectors is enough — the specific choice rarely matters.

The safepoint connection is critical. Every stop-the-world pause requires all application threads to reach a safepoint. Even a low-pause collector like ZGC has to pause threads briefly at the start and end of each GC cycle to scan the roots and handle reference updates. Time-to-safepoint (TTSP) is therefore just as relevant for ZGC as for G1 — a thread stuck in a long counted loop without a safepoint check delays the pause regardless of collector. This is why choosing ZGC is not enough if the application has pathological safepoint behavior; the whole system has to cooperate.

**The tuning decision framework**: for small heaps (<4 GB) with no latency requirement, Parallel is fine and often the fastest. For a general-purpose service with moderate heaps (4–32 GB) and a pause budget in the low hundreds of milliseconds, G1 is the right default. For very large heaps (32 GB+) with a pause budget, G1 with tuned `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis` and `-XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent` can work, but watch for humongous allocation fallbacks and consider ZGC. For strict latency SLOs (sub-ms pauses), use ZGC or Shenandoah regardless of heap size. For batch jobs, Parallel is often best (throughput first). The worst practice is to tune blindly — always measure pause distributions (`p50`, `p95`, `p99`, `p99`.9), allocation rate, promotion rate, and CPU usage, and prefer changing one parameter at a time while watching the effect.

The interview-quality answer names the four algorithms (mark-sweep, mark-compact, copying, generational), describes the collectors with their pause profiles (Serial small single-threaded, Parallel throughput multi-threaded STW, G1 region-based pause-target default, ZGC/Shenandoah concurrent low-pause for large heaps), explains the safepoint connection (TTSP affects every collector), names the specific G1 tuning levers and the humongous allocation risk, and states the decision framework (heap size, pause budget, throughput vs latency). That demonstrates you can tune GC from data, not from folklore.
bullets: **Four algorithms**: mark-sweep (fragmentation), mark-compact (slide, expensive pause), copying (fast, wastes half the space), generational (young copying + old mark/compact — the modern default).
**Generational hypothesis**: most objects die young, so young GC is cheap and frequent, and old GC is expensive and rare; GC cost tracks live set size in old gen, not total allocation rate.

**Serial**: single-threaded STW, small heaps only. Parallel: multi-threaded STW, throughput-focused, seconds-long pauses on large heaps. G1: region-based, `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis` target (default 200 ms), mixed collections, default since Java 9. ZGC/Shenandoah: concurrent compacting, sub-ms to low-ms pauses, for very large heaps and strict latency.

**G1 tuning**: `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis` (lower = smaller pauses, more frequent GC), `-XX:G1HeapRegionSize` (larger regions reduce humongous overhead), `-XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent` (start marking sooner to avoid Full GC fallback), `-XX:G1NewSizePercent` / `-XX:G1MaxNewSizePercent`, `-XX:G1MixedGCLiveThresholdPercent`.
Humongous allocations (>half a region, typically >1 MB) are a common G1 Full GC fallback cause — watch for them and consider larger regions or a different collector.
ZGC/Shenandoah cost more CPU and memory (colored pointers or Brooks pointers, load barriers) — they win on latency, not throughput.
**TTSP (time-to-safepoint) affects every collector** — a thread in a long counted loop without a safepoint check delays even ZGC pauses.
**Tune from data**: pause distribution (`p50`–`p99`.9), allocation rate, promotion rate, CPU — not from folklore.
cards.code:
The four GC algorithms

  Mark-sweep       mark live, sweep free (free lists) -> fragmentation
  Mark-compact     mark live, slide -> no fragmentation, slow pause
  Copying          copy live to other half, swap -> fast, wastes half
  Generational     young copying + old mark/compact -> modern default

Collector comparison

  Collector     Threads      Pause type        Typical use
  -----------   ----------   ---------------   -----------------------------
  Serial        1            STW               small heaps (<1 GB), CLI, batch
  Parallel      N            STW               batch jobs, throughput-first
  G1            N + conc.    STW + concurrent  default; 4–32 GB, ~200 ms budget
  ZGC           N + conc.    sub-ms to low ms  strict latency, 100 GB+ heaps
  Shenandoah    N + conc.    sub-ms to low ms  same as ZGC (different vendor)

G1 tuning levers

  -XX:+UseG1GC                           (default since Java 9)
  -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200               (pause goal, lower = more frequent)
  -XX:G1HeapRegionSize=4m                (larger regions = fewer humongous)
  -XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent=45  (start marking at 45% full)
  -XX:G1NewSizePercent=5                 (young gen min)
  -XX:G1MaxNewSizePercent=60             (young gen max)
  -XX:G1MixedGCLiveThresholdPercent=85   (how live a region can be)
  -XX:+PrintGCDetails -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log

ZGC / Shenandoah

  -XX:+UseZGC                 (Java 15+ production-ready; generational in 21+)
  -XX:+UseShenandoahGC        (Java 15+)

  Sub-ms pauses even on 100 GB+ heaps; costs extra CPU/memory
  (colored pointers for ZGC, Brooks pointers for Shenandoah,
   load barriers). Not a throughput win.

GC log diagnosis (JFR or -Xlog:gc*)

  Allocation rate:         MB/sec
  Promotion rate:          bytes promoted to old gen per second
  Pause distribution:      p50, p95, p99, p99.9 of pause times
  Full GC events:          count and duration (should be near zero for G1)
  Humongous allocations:   object size > region/2 -> G1 Full GC risk
  TTSP:                    time-to-safepoint (JFR jdk.SafepointBegin)

Tuning decision tree

  heap < 4 GB, no latency SLO      -> Parallel (throughput)
  heap 4–32 GB, ~200 ms budget     -> G1 (default, tuned)
  heap 32+ GB, latency SLO         -> ZGC or Shenandoah
  batch / offline                  -> Parallel
  strict p99.9 sub-ms              -> ZGC or Shenandoah

Anti-patterns

  - tuning without measuring pause distribution
  - setting -Xmn (young size) too large -> long young pauses
  - ignoring humongous allocations -> G1 Full GC surprises
  - switching to ZGC to fix a memory leak (leak is a leak)
  - disabling explicit GC only and hoping
  - assuming ZGC = throughput win (it is a latency trade)

cards.title: JNI and the Foreign Function & Memory API: Safety, Pinning, and the Panama Project
cards.summary:
JNI (Java Native Interface) is the original mechanism for calling native code (C, C++) from Java and vice versa. It is a C API defined by the JVM: native methods are declared with the native keyword, their implementations are compiled into a shared library, and the JVM loads the library and links the method calls. JNI is how the JDK itself talks to the OS (file IO, sockets, threads), how high-performance libraries like Netty, RocksDB, LZ4, and database drivers reach native code, and how old enterprise integrations (hardware drivers, mainframe connectors) work.

JNI is powerful and dangerous, and the interview signal is whether you know both. **Safety**: JNI bypasses the JVM's memory safety — native code can read and write arbitrary memory, crash the JVM (a segfault in native code takes down the whole process, not just a thread), and corrupt the heap. It also requires careful reference management: local references created in JNI (for objects returned to Java) are freed automatically when the native method returns, but if a native method holds a Java object across calls, it must create a `GlobalRef` or the object may be garbage-collected while native code still has a pointer to it. **Threading**: JNI threads are attached to the JVM (`AttachCurrentThread`) and must be detached (`DetachCurrentThread`) before exiting, or the JVM leaks. **Exception handling**: a native method that throws a Java exception must check `ExceptionCheck()` after every JNI call that might throw, or the exception silently accumulates and is thrown at an unrelated point. This list of footguns is why the safe use of JNI requires discipline and testing.

Performance is the second surprise. **JNI is not free**: crossing the boundary costs on the order of tens to hundreds of nanoseconds, depending on the complexity of the call and the reference type conversions. Calling a native method in a tight loop is often slower than doing the same work in Java, because the boundary overhead dominates. The wins from JNI are in coarse-grained calls that do significant work (compress a 1 MB buffer, hash a large array, query a database) or in calls to code that cannot be reimplemented in Java (OS-specific drivers, hardware, mainframe connectors). **The rule is**: call native code in bulk, not per element.
