bullets: MVCC keeps old row versions in the heap so readers and writers never block each other — the cost is dead tuples that must be reclaimed.
`VACUUM` marks dead tuple space as reusable within the table; `VACUUM` FULL rewrites the table to return space to the OS but takes an exclusive lock.
Autovacuum runs in the background; if it cannot keep up (high writes, long transactions, throttling), tables and indexes bloat.
32-bit XIDs wrap at ~2 billion; `VACUUM` FREEZE replaces old XIDs with a permanently visible `FrozenXID` to prevent wraparound.
Without freeze, wraparound makes old rows invisible (apparent data loss) and PostgreSQL enters emergency read-only mode around 2 billion XIDs.
A long-running transaction blocks vacuum across the entire database; idle-in-transaction sessions are the worst case — set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`.
**Index entries also become dead and must be vacuumed** — index bloat is separate from table bloat and causes wasted heap I/O.
cards.code:
MVCC update

  Before:  [tuple v1: xmin=100, xmax=0]

  Tx 200 updates row:

  Heap page:
    [tuple v1: xmin=100, xmax=200]   <- dead to transactions > 200
    [tuple v2: xmin=200, xmax=0]     <- new version

  Reader with snapshot at xid 150 sees v1.
  Reader with snapshot at xid 250 sees v2.
  Neither blocks the other.

VACUUM

  -- marks v1 space as reusable within the table
  VACUUM orders;

  -- rewrites table to return space to OS (exclusive lock)
  VACUUM FULL orders;

Autovacuum

  -- triggers based on dead tuples / changes
  -- NEVER disable:
  ALTER TABLE orders SET (autovacuum_enabled = true);

XID wraparound

  32-bit XID wraps at ~2 billion
  VACUUM FREEZE replaces old XIDs with FrozenXID (always visible)
  warning at ~1.4 billion XIDs
  emergency read-only at ~2 billion

  monitor:
    SELECT datname, age(datfrozenxid)
    FROM pg_database
    ORDER BY age(datfrozenxid) DESC;

Long transaction hazard

  BEGIN;
    SELECT ...;   -- snapshot taken
    -- session sleeps for hours (idle in transaction)
  COMMIT;

  -- VACUUM cannot remove any tuple visible to this snapshot
  -- the entire database's vacuum horizon is held back

  fix:
    SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '5min';

Index bloat

  UPDATE changes indexed column -> old index entry dead, new entry added
  VACUUM removes dead index entries
  if vacuum lags -> index pages contain dead entries -> more I/O per lookup

cards.title: Cassandra Architecture: The Ring, Consistent Hashing, and Why Every Node Is a Master
cards.summary:
**Cassandra** is a peer-to-peer distributed database. There is no primary node, no leader, and no single point of failure. Every node in a cluster is identical in responsibility: any node can accept a read or write for any key, coordinate that request to the correct replicas, and return the result. This is the multi-master model inherited from Amazon's Dynamo paper. The consequence is high availability — losing any node does not lose the ability to read or write its data, because the data is replicated, and any surviving node can coordinate. The cost is complexity in conflict resolution: when multiple replicas accept writes independently, Cassandra must decide which value wins. It does this with last-write-wins, using the timestamp attached to every mutation.

Data is distributed around a hash ring using consistent hashing. Every node is assigned one or more positions on a continuous 0 to 2^64−1 ring; these positions are called tokens. To find where a key belongs, Cassandra hashes the partition key to produce a token, then walks the ring clockwise until it finds the first node that owns that token range. This is the primary replica. The next distinct nodes clockwise become the other replicas, up to the replication factor (RF). With RF=3, the key is stored on three distinct nodes. Because the ring is circular, adding or removing a node only moves a small fraction of keys — the rest of the ring is unaffected. This is the fundamental advantage of consistent hashing over naive hash-modulo partitioning.

Modern Cassandra uses virtual nodes (vnodes) to improve balance and scaling. Instead of assigning one token per physical node (which makes small clusters uneven and incremental scaling difficult), Cassandra assigns many tokens to each physical node — typically 16 or 32 in 4.x, down from 256 in older versions. Each token is a vnode, owned by the same physical host. When a new node joins, it claims a small piece of many existing token ranges, so data redistributes evenly across all nodes. When a node fails, its load spreads across many neighbors instead of dumping entirely onto one. **The trade-off is operational**: more tokens per node means more neighbors on the ring, which increases the number of failure combinations that can affect availability, and it slows down cluster-wide repair operations.

Replication strategy determines which nodes hold the copies. `SimpleStrategy` places replicas at the next RF nodes clockwise, which is fine for single-datacenter clusters. `NetworkTopologyStrategy` is the production default: it places replicas across racks and datacenters according to a topology-aware algorithm, so a rack failure or a datacenter outage does not take all replicas of a key offline. The replication factor is per keyspace, not per cluster, so different datasets can have different durability guarantees. A keyspace with RF=3 in a three-datacenter topology stores nine copies (three per DC), which tolerates the loss of any single datacenter without data loss.

The interview-quality answer treats Cassandra as a Dynamo-style system: peer-to-peer ring, consistent hashing with vnodes, topology-aware replication, multi-master writes, and last-write-wins conflict resolution. **The mental model is**: a key is hashed to a token, the token maps to a range, the range maps to a set of replicas, and every replica can accept a write independently. That model explains availability, scalability, and the need for tunable consistency and repair.
bullets: **Cassandra is peer-to-peer with no master** — every node coordinates any request and holds a subset of the data.
Consistent hashing maps partition keys to tokens on a ring; the first node clockwise from the token is the primary replica, the next RF−1 distinct nodes are the other replicas.
Virtual nodes (vnodes) assign many tokens per physical node, improving balance, incremental scaling, and failure load distribution at the cost of more ring neighbors.
**`NetworkTopologyStrategy` places replicas across racks and datacenters** — `SimpleStrategy` is single-datacenter only.
Replication factor is per keyspace; RF=3 in a three-DC topology means nine copies and tolerance for a full DC outage.
**Multi-master writes require conflict resolution** — Cassandra uses last-write-wins with per-mutation timestamps.
The ring explains availability (any node can serve), scalability (adding nodes moves little data), and the need for tunable consistency (replicas can diverge).

Hash ring (simplified)

  Tokens: 0 --------- 25 --------- 50 --------- 75 --------- 99
          |           |            |            |            |
        Node A      Node B       Node C       Node D       (wrap to A)

  Key "user:42" -> hash -> token 63 -> walk clockwise -> Node C
  RF=3 -> replicas on Node C, Node D, Node A

Virtual nodes

  Physical Node A owns tokens: 5, 22, 41, 67, 88
  Physical Node B owns tokens: 12, 30, 52, 74, 95
  Physical Node C owns tokens: 18, 37, 59, 80, 3

  Adding Node D takes a few small ranges from A, B, C
  -> data redistributes evenly, minimal movement

Replication strategy

    replicas = next 3 distinct nodes clockwise

  NetworkTopologyStrategy(DC1:3, DC2:3):
    replicas = 3 per datacenter, spread across racks

      WITH replication = {
        'class': 'NetworkTopologyStrategy',
        'dc1': 3,
        'dc2': 3
      };

cards.title: Cassandra Data Modeling: Query-First Design, Partition Keys, and Clustering Columns
cards.summary:
**Cassandra data modeling** is fundamentally different from relational modeling. In a relational database, you normalize entities first and write queries later; the query planner figures out how to join the tables. In Cassandra, there are no joins, no query planner, and no secondary-index magic that rescues a bad design. You must start with the queries, design a table for each query, and accept denormalization and data duplication as normal. This is the query-first approach: list the queries your application needs, design a table that answers each one efficiently, and duplicate data across tables when different queries need different access patterns.

The primary key has two parts with different jobs. The partition key determines which node stores the row: all rows with the same partition key are stored together on the same set of replicas. This is the unit of distribution and the unit of efficient retrieval. A query that specifies the full partition key hits a single partition on a known set of nodes; a query that does not specify the partition key must scan every node, which is almost always unacceptable at scale. The clustering columns determine the sort order within a partition and make rows unique. **They** are the only columns you can range-query efficiently inside a partition — ORDER BY, >, <, BETWEEN, and LIMIT with a sort order all work against clustering columns without extra sorting.

**Partition size** is the most important physical constraint. A partition must fit comfortably on disk and in memory for efficient reads, and Cassandra warns when partitions exceed 100 MB or 100,000 rows. An unbounded partition — for example, partitioning only by `user_id` when a user can have millions of events — grows forever and eventually causes read timeouts, compaction pressure, and memory issues. The standard fix is bucketing: add a time bucket (`year_month`, day, hour) or a hash bucket to the partition key, splitting the data into bounded partitions. A query for a range of time then hits multiple bounded partitions in parallel, which Cassandra handles well.

Denormalization is not a compromise; it is the design. If the application needs to query activities by user, by user and type, and by user and month, that is three tables, each with a primary key shaped for its query. The same activity row is written to all three. This feels wasteful in a relational mindset, but it is how Cassandra achieves predictable single-partition reads at scale. The trade-off is write amplification and the need to keep duplicated tables consistent — which the application must handle, because Cassandra does not enforce referential integrity or cross-table consistency.

The interview-quality answer states the query-first rule, explains the partition key as the distribution and retrieval unit, the clustering columns as the sort and range unit, the partition-size limit and bucketing fix, and the acceptance of denormalization. The trap is to model entities first and assume Cassandra will figure out the queries — that produces tables that cannot answer the application's access patterns without full scans.
bullets: **Cassandra modeling is query-first**: start from the queries, design a table per query, and accept denormalization.
**Partition key determines which nodes store the row** — all rows with the same partition key live together on the same replicas.
Clustering columns determine sort order within a partition and are the only columns that support efficient range queries and ORDER BY.
A query must specify the full partition key to hit a single partition; without it, Cassandra scans all nodes.
**Partition size must stay bounded (roughly under 100 MB / 100k rows)** — bucket by time or hash when a partition would grow unbounded.
**Denormalization is the design**: the same row is written to multiple tables, each shaped for a different query.
**No joins, no referential integrity** — the application is responsible for keeping duplicated tables consistent.
cards.code:
-- Query-first: three queries, three tables

-- Q1: activities for a user, most recent first
CREATE TABLE user_activities (
  user_id uuid,
  activity_timestamp timestamp,
  activity_id uuid,
  activity_type text,
  activity_data text,
  PRIMARY KEY (user_id, activity_timestamp, activity_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (activity_timestamp DESC, activity_id ASC);

-- Q2: activities for a user filtered by type
CREATE TABLE user_activities_by_type (
  user_id uuid,
  activity_type text,
  activity_timestamp timestamp,
  activity_id uuid,
  activity_data text,
  PRIMARY KEY ((user_id, activity_type), activity_timestamp, activity_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (activity_timestamp DESC, activity_id ASC);

-- Q3: activities for a user within a month (bucketed)
CREATE TABLE user_activities_by_month (
  user_id uuid,
  year_month text,          -- '2026-01'
  activity_timestamp timestamp,
  activity_id uuid,
  activity_data text,
  PRIMARY KEY ((user_id, year_month), activity_timestamp, activity_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (activity_timestamp DESC, activity_id ASC);

-- Efficient queries (full partition key specified)
SELECT * FROM user_activities
WHERE user_id = ? LIMIT 20;

SELECT * FROM user_activities_by_type
WHERE user_id = ? AND activity_type = 'purchase' LIMIT 50;

SELECT * FROM user_activities_by_month
WHERE user_id = ? AND year_month = '2026-01'
  AND activity_timestamp >= '2026-01-15'
  AND activity_timestamp <  '2026-01-20';

-- ANTI-PATTERN: query without the partition key
SELECT * FROM user_activities WHERE activity_type = 'purchase';
-- scans all nodes, no efficient path

cards.title: Cassandra Write Path: Commit Log, Memtable, SSTable, and Compaction
cards.summary:
Cassandra's storage engine is a Log-Structured Merge (LSM) tree, not a B-tree. This single design choice determines the entire write path and is the reason Cassandra excels at write-heavy workloads. An LSM tree never overwrites data in place. A write is always an append: it goes to an in-memory structure (the memtable) and to a durable append-only log (the commit log). Nothing is read before writing, and nothing is updated in place. The trade-off is that reads must merge multiple on-disk structures (SSTables) to find the latest version of a row, and background compaction must rewrite data repeatedly to keep the number of SSTables bounded.

The write path has four stages. First, the mutation is appended to the commit log on disk. The **commit log** is a write-ahead log shared across all tables on the node; it provides durability so that acknowledged writes survive a crash. Second, the mutation is written to the memtable, an in-memory sorted structure. The memtable serves recent reads without touching disk and is the source of truth until it is flushed. Third, when the memtable reaches a size threshold (or the commit log needs space to be reclaimed), it is flushed to disk as an immutable SSTable (Sorted String Table). Fourth, background compaction merges multiple SSTables into larger ones, resolving updates and deletes by timestamp and reclaiming space.

The commit log's durability is configurable. In batch mode, Cassandra does not acknowledge a write until the commit log has been fsynced to disk — the strongest durability, at the cost of latency. In periodic mode (the default), writes are acknowledged immediately and the commit log is fsynced every `commitlog_sync_period` (default 10 seconds). A crash can lose up to that period of writes. In practice, most deployments use periodic mode with RF≥3 and rely on replication for durability: even if one node loses a few seconds of writes, the other replicas have them, and read repair or hinted handoff will restore the lost data. The interview point is that durability is a combination of commit log sync mode, replication factor, and consistency level — not just one setting.

**Compaction** is the maintenance cost of the LSM design. Because SSTables are immutable, an update does not overwrite the old value — it writes a new cell with a newer timestamp, and the old value remains in its SSTable until compaction merges the two and keeps the newer one. **Deletes are writes too**: a delete creates a tombstone, a marker that says 'this cell is deleted as of timestamp T'. Tombstones are not removed immediately because the older value may still exist on a replica that has not seen the delete; they are retained for `gc_grace_seconds` (default 10 days) to give repair time to propagate the delete, then removed during compaction. An **excessive tombstone count** is a common Cassandra performance problem — it slows reads because every tombstone must be scanned, and it bloats storage.

The interview-quality answer names the LSM tree, the four-stage write path (commit log → memtable → SSTable → compaction), the durability trade-off of commit log sync modes, and the tombstone lifecycle. It also explains why writes are fast (append-only, no read-before-write) and why reads and compaction pay the cost (merging SSTables, scanning tombstones). That demonstrates you understand the engine, not just the API.
bullets: **Cassandra uses an LSM tree, not a B-tree** — writes are append-only to the commit log and memtable, never in-place overwrites.
**Write path**: commit log (durability) → memtable (in-memory sorted) → SSTable (immutable on-disk) → compaction (merge and reclaim).
The commit log is a shared write-ahead log; sync mode (batch vs periodic) determines how much data can be lost on a crash.
Memtables flush to SSTables when they hit a size threshold or when the commit log needs to reclaim space.
**Updates and deletes are new writes**: an update writes a newer timestamp, a delete writes a tombstone.
Tombstones are retained for `gc_grace_seconds` (default 10 days) so repair can propagate the delete, then removed by compaction.
Writes are fast because there is no read-before-write; reads and compaction pay the cost of merging SSTables and scanning tombstones.

Write path (LSM tree)

  Client write
      |
      v
  1. Commit log (append-only, on disk)   -- durability
      |
      v
  2. Memtable (in-memory, sorted)        -- serves recent reads
      |  (size threshold or commit log pressure)
      v
  3. SSTable (immutable, sorted, on disk)
      |
      v
  4. Compaction (merge SSTables, resolve by timestamp)

Update and delete semantics

  INSERT (user_id=1, email='a@x') at t=100
  INSERT (user_id=1, email='b@x') at t=200

  SSTable 1: [user_id=1, email='a@x', ts=100]
  SSTable 2: [user_id=1, email='b@x', ts=200]

  Compaction merges -> keeps ts=200 ('b@x'), discards ts=100

  DELETE FROM users WHERE user_id=1;   -- writes a tombstone at t=300
  SSTable: [user_id=1, tombstone, ts=300]
  -- retained for gc_grace_seconds, then removed by compaction

Commit log sync modes

  batch:
    fsync on every write before acknowledging
    strongest durability, highest latency

  periodic (default):
    acknowledge immediately, fsync every commitlog_sync_period (10s)
    can lose up to the sync period on a crash
    combined with RF>=3, replication covers the gap

Compaction

  - merges multiple SSTables into one
  - resolves cells by timestamp (latest wins)
  - removes expired tombstones
  - write amplification: data is rewritten multiple times
  - bounds the number of SSTables a read must consult

cards.title: Cassandra Read Path: Bloom Filters, Key Cache, and Merging SSTables
cards.summary:
A **Cassandra read** is a search across multiple storage layers, because the LSM design means the same row may have fragments in the memtable, in several SSTables, or in both. The **read path** is a sequence of filters designed to avoid touching SSTables that cannot contain the requested partition. The coordinator first identifies the replicas for the key, sends the read to the fastest replica (using the dynamic snitch, which tracks latency and 'badness' per node), and the replica then executes the local read path.

The read path checks caches in order. First, the row cache: if enabled, it holds fully merged rows that have been read before. A **row-cache hit** is the fastest possible read — the data is already merged and in memory, so no SSTable or memtable access is needed. The row cache is off by default because it is expensive to maintain and only helps for hot rows that fit in memory; enabling it without understanding the workload can evict useful data and hurt performance. Second, the memtable: recent writes live here, and any cell that was written after the last flush is only in the memtable. Third, the SSTables: for each SSTable, a bloom filter is checked before any disk access.

The **bloom filter** is the most important optimization. It is a probabilistic data structure that can answer 'does this partition key exist in this SSTable?' with certainty when the answer is no, and with uncertainty when the answer is yes. If the bloom filter says no, the SSTable is skipped entirely — no disk I/O. If it says yes, the SSTable may or may not contain the key, so Cassandra proceeds. Bloom filters are sized to keep the false-positive rate low (typically around 1%), and they are kept in memory. Without bloom filters, a read would have to check every SSTable, and the number of SSTables grows with the write rate until compaction catches up.

For SSTables that pass the bloom filter, the key cache is checked next. The key cache stores the offset of a partition key within an SSTable, so Cassandra can seek directly to the data instead of scanning the partition index. If the key cache misses, the partition summary is read (a sampled index that gives a starting point), then the partition index is scanned (which maps partition keys to offsets), then the data is read at the resulting offset. Finally, all fragments — from the row cache, memtable, and surviving SSTables — are merged cell by cell, comparing timestamps and keeping the latest value; tombstones are applied and ignored from the result. The merged row is returned to the coordinator and, if the row cache is enabled, stored there for future reads.

When the read consistency level is greater than ONE, the coordinator sends a digest request to the other replicas. A digest read asks each replica to compute a hash of the requested data without sending the full data. The coordinator compares the digests; if they differ, it requests the full data from the replicas that disagree, reconciles by timestamp, returns the latest version to the client, and triggers read repair in the background to bring the stale replicas up to date. This is how Cassandra provides stronger consistency on reads without a leader: the coordinator is the temporary point of reconciliation.

The interview-quality answer walks the layers in order (row cache → memtable → bloom filter → key cache → partition summary/index → merge), explains that bloom filters prevent unnecessary disk I/O, and describes digest reads and read repair for consistency levels above ONE. The trap is to describe a read as 'just look up the key' — in an LSM system, a read is a merge across multiple sources, and the optimizations exist to minimize how many sources are touched.
bullets: A Cassandra read searches the row cache, memtable, and multiple SSTables, then merges fragments by timestamp.
**The row cache (optional, off by default) holds fully merged rows** — the fastest read if the row is hot and fits in memory.
The bloom filter guarantees that a partition is NOT in an SSTable, so the SSTable can be skipped without disk I/O; a positive answer means 'maybe', not 'yes'.
The key cache stores partition offsets within SSTables, avoiding partition-index scans; the partition summary and partition index provide fallbacks.
The coordinator sends reads to the fastest replica (dynamic snitch) and, at consistency > ONE, sends digest requests to other replicas and reconciles by timestamp.
Read repair runs in the background after a digest mismatch to bring stale replicas up to date.
**Without bloom filters and caches, a read would touch every SSTable** — the number of SSTables is bounded by compaction, not by the read path.
cards.code:
Read path (single replica, simplified)

  1. Row cache?  -- hit -> return merged row (fastest)
  2. Memtable?   -- check for recent writes
  3. For each SSTable:
       a. Bloom filter says NO?  -> skip SSTable (no disk I/O)
       b. Bloom filter says MAYBE -> continue
       c. Key cache hit?         -> offset known, seek directly
       d. Key cache miss?        -> read partition summary
                                 -> scan partition index
                                 -> read data at offset
  4. Merge all fragments cell by cell, compare timestamps,
     keep latest, apply tombstones
  5. Return merged row; optionally populate row cache

Consistency > ONE

  Coordinator -> fastest replica: full read
  Coordinator -> other replicas:   digest read (hash of data)
  Compare digests:
    all equal      -> return result
    some differ    -> fetch full data from disagreeing replicas,
                      reconcile by timestamp, return latest,
                      trigger read repair in background

Bloom filter

  - probabilistic: can say "definitely not in this SSTable"
  - can say "maybe" (false positives possible, ~1%)
  - kept in memory, one per SSTable
  - prevents disk reads for SSTables that cannot contain the key

cards.title: Cassandra Tunable Consistency: ONE, QUORUM, ALL, and the R + W > RF Rule
cards.summary:
Cassandra exposes consistency as a per-operation choice, not a per-database setting. Every read and every write can specify a consistency level (CL), and the level determines how many replicas must respond before the coordinator returns to the client. This is the tunable consistency that CAP theorem discussions refer to: the same cluster can serve strongly consistent reads for one query and eventually consistent reads for another, depending on the business requirement. The levels are not free — higher consistency means more replicas must be reachable and respond, which increases latency and reduces availability during failures.

The core levels are ONE, QUORUM, and ALL. ONE requires a response from a single replica (the closest one); it is the fastest and most available, but a read at ONE may return stale data if the closest replica has not yet received the latest write. QUORUM requires a majority of replicas: `floor(RF/2)` + 1. For RF=3, QUORUM is 2; for RF=5, QUORUM is 3. QUORUM tolerates the failure of a minority of replicas while providing a consistency guarantee that ONE does not. ALL requires every replica to respond; it is the strongest consistency but the least available — if any replica is down, the operation fails. ALL is rarely used in production except for low-volume, high-criticality operations, because a single node failure (or even a slow node) makes the operation unavailable.

The consistency guarantee comes from the R + W > RF rule. If the number of replicas that must respond to a read (R) plus the number that must acknowledge a write (W) is greater than the replication factor (RF), then every read is guaranteed to see the latest write. With RF=3, W=QUORUM (2) and R=QUORUM (2) gives 2+2 > 3, so a quorum read always overlaps with a quorum write — at least one replica in the read set has the latest value, and the coordinator reconciles by timestamp. If W=ONE (1) and R=ONE (1), then 1+1 is not greater than 3, so a read at ONE may hit a replica that did not receive the write and return stale data. The classic mistake is to write at ONE and read at ONE and expect consistency — the math does not hold. The fix is either a quorum on both sides, or a read at ALL if writes are at ONE, but the former is the practical production choice.

Multi-datacenter deployments add `LOCAL_QUORUM` and `EACH_QUORUM`. `LOCAL_QUORUM` requires a quorum of replicas in the coordinator's datacenter only — it does not wait for remote datacenters. This is the standard choice for multi-DC applications that want strong consistency within a region but do not want cross-region latency on every operation. `EACH_QUORUM` requires a quorum in every datacenter, which is stronger but slower and less available. The interview point is that consistency is scoped to a datacenter in practice: `LOCAL_QUORUM` is what most production systems actually use, and it is why cross-DC replication lag does not block local reads and writes.

The trade-off matrix in one place: ONE is fastest and most available but can return stale data; QUORUM is the balanced default that provides strong consistency when R+W > RF; ALL is the strongest but least available; `LOCAL_QUORUM` is the multi-DC default for regional strong consistency. Cassandra also allows per-query overrides — a dashboard might read at ONE for speed, while a payment reconciliation job reads at QUORUM for correctness. This per-operation tunability is the defining feature, and it is why Cassandra is described as an AP system with configurable consistency rather than a fixed CP or AP database.

The interview-quality answer names ONE, QUORUM, ALL, `LOCAL_QUORUM`, and `EACH_QUORUM`, explains the R + W > RF rule with the RF=3 example, and states the multi-DC default. The trap is to say 'Cassandra is eventually consistent' without acknowledging that quorum reads and writes provide strong consistency when the math holds — the system is tunable, and the consistency level is a per-operation decision.
bullets: **Cassandra consistency is per-operation, not per-database** — every read and write chooses its CL.
ONE: fastest and most available, but a read at ONE can return stale data if the closest replica missed the write.
**QUORUM**: majority of replicas (RF/2 + 1); RF=3 → 2, RF=5 → 3; tolerates a minority of replica failures.
ALL: every replica must respond — strongest consistency but operation fails if any replica is down.
**The guarantee rule is R + W > RF**: with RF=3, W=QUORUM and R=QUORUM (2+2 > 3) guarantees the read sees the latest write.
**`LOCAL_QUORUM` is the multi-DC default**: a quorum within the coordinator's datacenter, no cross-region latency.
**`EACH_QUORUM` requires a quorum in every datacenter** — stronger but slower and less available.
**Cassandra is a tunable AP system, not a fixed CP or AP database** — the CL is a business decision per operation.
cards.code:
Consistency levels

  ANY        write only: at least one node (hint if replicas down)
  ONE        one replica responds
  QUORUM     floor(RF/2) + 1 replicas respond
  ALL        all replicas respond
  LOCAL_QUORUM  quorum within the coordinator's datacenter
  EACH_QUORUM   quorum in every datacenter

R + W > RF rule (strong consistency)

  RF=3:
    W=QUORUM(2) + R=QUORUM(2) = 4 > 3  -> strong
    W=ONE(1)   + R=ONE(1)     = 2 < 3  -> may be stale
    W=ALL(3)   + R=ONE(1)     = 4 > 3  -> strong
    W=ONE(1)   + R=ALL(3)     = 4 > 3  -> strong

Per-query usage

  -- dashboard read: speed over freshness
  SELECT * FROM metrics WHERE ... USING CONSISTENCY ONE;

  -- payment reconciliation: correctness
  SELECT * FROM ledger WHERE ... USING CONSISTENCY QUORUM;

  -- multi-DC local strong consistency
  SELECT * FROM users WHERE ... USING CONSISTENCY LOCAL_QUORUM;

Write path at QUORUM

  1. Coordinator sends write to all RF replicas
  2. Waits for QUORUM acknowledgements
  3. Returns success to client
  4. Other replicas receive the write asynchronously
  5. Hinted handoff covers temporarily down replicas

Trade-off matrix

  Level        Latency   Availability   Freshness
  ------       -------   ------------   ---------
  ONE          lowest    highest        may be stale
  QUORUM       medium    tolerates minority  strong if R+W>RF
  ALL          highest   lowest         strongest
  LOCAL_QUORUM low       high (local)   strong within DC

cards.title: MongoDB Document Model: Embed vs Reference, the 16 MB Limit, and the Array Growth Trap
cards.summary:
MongoDB stores data as BSON documents — binary JSON-like structures with a flexible schema. A **document** is the unit of atomicity: a single write to one document is atomic, and multi-document transactions exist but are not the default mental model. The schema is not declared up front; each document can have different fields, and the application enforces its own invariants. This flexibility is the appeal and the danger: without a schema, an inconsistent document can silently break readers.

The central design decision is embed versus reference. Embedding stores related data inside the parent document — a customer document contains its addresses array, an order document contains its line items. Referencing stores related data in a separate collection and links it by an ID — orders contain a `customerId`, and the customer lives in the customers collection. The decision rule from MongoDB's own guidance is: embed when the data is accessed together, forms a containment relationship, and the child is not queried independently; reference when the data grows without bound, is updated independently, is queried on its own, or would push the parent toward the 16 MB document limit.

The **16 MB limit** is a hard BSON limit, not a soft guideline. It is the single most important physical constraint in MongoDB schema design. An unbounded array — comments on a viral post, events for an active user, log lines per service — will eventually push the parent document past 16 MB, at which point writes fail with a document-too-large error. Even before the hard limit, large documents hurt performance: every read loads the entire document into memory, and every update rewrites the whole document (plus its indexes), so a 10 MB document with a small field change is a 10 MB write. The practical rule is to keep documents under 1 MB and embedded arrays around 100 elements; beyond that, reference or bucket.

The **bucket pattern** is the standard fix for unbounded arrays that are still accessed together. Instead of one document per parent with an ever-growing array, create one document per parent per time bucket (or per N items): a `sensor_readings` document per sensor per hour, a `chat_messages` document per conversation per day. Each bucket document stays small, writes are appends to the current bucket, and queries for a time range read a bounded number of buckets. This is the document-model equivalent of Cassandra's time-bucketed partition key — the same physical constraint (bounded unit) expressed in a different database.

Embedding gives three concrete benefits that reference cannot match: single-query reads (the parent and children arrive in one round trip), atomic updates across the embedded data (one write, one document, no transaction), and data locality on disk. Referencing gives the opposite trade-offs: no duplication (one source of truth), independent query and pagination of the child collection, and small parent documents regardless of child count. The interview trap is to treat one as correct and the other as wrong — the right choice is access-pattern-driven, and the same application often uses both (embed addresses in a customer, reference orders from a customer).

A second trap is normalization reflexes from relational modeling. In SQL, you normalize first and join later; in MongoDB, you model for the queries you will run. **Duplication is intentional**: a customer's name may be copied into each order so the order list renders without a join. The cost is that a name change must update every copy — which is why duplicating rarely-changing data is safe and duplicating frequently-changing data is not. When duplication is unavoidable and consistency matters, multi-document transactions or change streams are the tools, but the preferred design is to avoid the need by embedding what is read together and referencing what changes independently.

The interview-quality answer names the 16 MB hard limit, the embed-vs-reference decision criteria (access pattern, growth, independent query, update frequency), the bucket pattern for unbounded arrays, and the atomicity/locality benefits of embedding versus the no-duplication/independent-query benefits of referencing. That demonstrates schema design judgment, not just syntax.
bullets: MongoDB documents are BSON; the document is the unit of atomicity, and the schema is application-enforced, not database-enforced.
Embed when data is read together, forms containment, and the child is not queried independently — gives single-query reads, atomic updates, and data locality.
Reference when data grows unbounded, changes independently, is queried on its own, or would approach the 16 MB limit — gives no duplication, independent pagination, small parents.
The 16 MB BSON limit is hard; practical documents should stay under ~1 MB and embedded arrays around ~100 elements.
The bucket pattern splits an unbounded array into per-parent per-time-bucket documents, keeping each write bounded.
**Duplication is intentional in MongoDB** — copy rarely-changing data to avoid joins, but do not duplicate frequently-changing data without a consistency plan.
**The same application often mixes both**: embed addresses in a customer, reference orders from a customer.

cards.title: MongoDB Indexing: B-Tree Internals, the ESR Rule, and the Four Special Index Types
cards.summary:
MongoDB indexes are B-Tree structures whose leaf entries store the indexed value and a pointer to the document. Every collection has a default _id index, and any additional index must be created explicitly. Without an index, a query is a collection scan — it reads every document, which is `O(n)` and unacceptable at scale. With an index, the query seeks to the matching leaf entries and fetches only those documents. The same B-Tree fundamentals from relational databases apply: the index is ordered, leaf pages are linked for range scans, and the number of index entries equals the number of indexed values (or more, for multikey indexes).

The most tested MongoDB-specific rule is the ESR guideline for compound indexes: Equality fields first, Sort fields second, Range fields last. A query like { status: "SHIPPED", `customerId`: 42 } sorted by `createdAt` and filtered by total > 100 should be indexed as (status, `customerId`, `createdAt`, total) — the equality fields first, the sort field next, the range field last. **The reason is mechanical**: equality fields let the index jump to a contiguous region, the sort field lets the index return results in order without an in-memory sort, and the range field is applied as a scan within the already-narrowed region. Putting the range field earlier breaks the sort and forces an in-memory sort, which fails at scale. **The exception**: if the range predicate is highly selective and the equality predicate is not, ERS (equality, range, sort) can outperform ESR — but ESR is the default heuristic.

**Multikey indexes** are the MongoDB-specific mechanism for indexing arrays. When a field is an array, MongoDB creates one index entry per array element, all pointing to the same document. A query like { tags: "urgent" } can use a multikey index on tags to find every document whose tags array contains "urgent". The cost is index size proportional to total array elements, not document count, and a limitation: a compound index can have at most one multikey field (otherwise the index would need a cross-product of array elements, which MongoDB does not support). The interview trap is to assume a compound index on two arrays works — it will be rejected or behave unexpectedly.

The other special index types each solve a specific problem. TTL indexes automatically delete documents after a time: create an index on a Date field with `expireAfterSeconds`, and a background TTL thread runs roughly every 60 seconds to remove expired documents. TTL is single-field only, works on Date or array-of-Date fields, and is the standard mechanism for sessions, OTP tokens, and logs. Sparse indexes include only documents where the indexed field exists — useful for optional fields where most documents have no value and you do not want to index nulls. **Partial indexes** are a generalization: they index only documents matching a filter expression ( { status: "PENDING" } ), which is smaller and cheaper to maintain than indexing the whole collection. Text indexes support full-text search with stemming, stop words, and language rules; they are heavier than B-Tree indexes and a collection can have at most one text index (though it can cover multiple fields).

Unique indexes enforce a constraint: no two documents may have the same value for the indexed field. This is how MongoDB implements business keys (email, username, order number). A unique index on a missing field is problematic because multiple documents with no value would collide; combine unique with sparse or partial if the field is optional. Hashed indexes hash the field value before indexing, which gives even distribution for equality lookups but cannot support range queries — they are primarily used as shard keys for hashed sharding.

The **operational discipline** is the same as relational databases: index for the queries you run, not for every field. Every index adds a write cost (the index B-Tree is updated on every insert/update/delete), consumes memory (indexes compete for the WiredTiger cache), and must be maintained during compaction. Use `explain("executionStats")` to verify that a query uses an index (IXSCAN) rather than a collection scan (COLLSCAN), check `totalDocsExamined` versus `nReturned` (a large gap means the index is not selective enough), and drop unused indexes. The interview-quality answer names the ESR rule, multikey limitations, TTL/sparse/partial/text use cases, unique constraints, and the explain-driven verification loop.
bullets: MongoDB indexes are B-Trees; every collection has an _id index, and additional indexes must be created explicitly — without one, queries are collection scans.
**ESR rule for compound indexes**: Equality fields first, Sort second, Range last — this avoids in-memory sorts and narrows the scan efficiently.
Multikey indexes index array elements (one entry per element); a compound index can have at most one multikey field.
TTL indexes auto-delete documents after `expireAfterSeconds` on a Date field; the TTL thread runs roughly every 60 seconds; single-field only.
Sparse indexes skip documents missing the field; partial indexes index only documents matching a filter — both reduce size and write cost.
Text indexes support full-text search (stemming, stop words); one text index per collection, but it can cover multiple fields.
Unique indexes enforce business keys; combine with sparse/partial when the field is optional to avoid null collisions.
**Verify with `explain("executionStats")`**: IXSCAN vs COLLSCAN, and `totalDocsExamined` close to `nReturned`.

cards.title: MongoDB Replica Sets: Oplog, Elections, Write Concern, and Read Concern
cards.summary:
A **MongoDB replica set** is a group of mongod processes that maintain the same data set: one primary and one or more secondaries. All writes go to the primary; secondaries replicate the primary's oplog (an ordered log of every write) and apply the operations in order. If the primary fails, the remaining members hold an election and a secondary is promoted. The default is three members, which tolerates the loss of one — two members cannot form a majority after a single failure, so a three-member set is the minimum sensible production configuration.

The election protocol (pv1, the only supported version in modern MongoDB) is Raft-like. A candidate requests votes from the other voting members, needs a majority to win, and the member with the most up-to-date oplog is preferred. Elections are triggered by the primary becoming unreachable, by a step-down, or by a priority change. The subtle correctness point is majority commit: a write is not considered durable by the replica set until a majority of members have acknowledged it. The primary tracks `lastOpCommitted` — the latest oplog entry known to be on a majority — and a newly elected primary can only claim to be authoritative for writes up to that point. This is why a write with { w: "majority" } survives a failover while a write with { w: 1 } may be rolled back if the primary dies before replicating it.

**Write concern** is the client's durability contract. { w: 1 } returns after the primary acknowledges the write — fast, but a failover can lose it. { w: "majority" } returns after a majority of voting members acknowledge — durable across the loss of a minority, at higher latency. { w: 0 } (unacknowledged) returns immediately and provides no guarantee at all. Numeric values ( w: 2, w: 3 ) require a specific number of members. The production default should be majority for anything that must survive a failover; w:1 is acceptable only for data that is safe to lose (metrics, cache-like state).

**Read concern** is the client's freshness and isolation contract, and it is separate from write concern. "local" returns the node's latest data with no guarantee it has been majority-committed; "majority" returns only data acknowledged by a majority, so it never sees a write that could be rolled back; "linearizable" returns data reflecting all majority-committed writes that completed before the read began, and it reads only from the primary (slowest, strongest); "snapshot" returns data from a specific point in time and is used in multi-document transactions. Read preference (primary, `primaryPreferred`, secondary, `secondaryPreferred`, nearest) decides which member serves the read — reading from a secondary gives lower latency and read scaling but may return stale data unless combined with read concern majority and causal consistency.

**Causal consistency** is the mechanism that gives session-level read-your-writes across a replica set. A client session tracks an `operationTime` and `clusterTime`; after a write with majority write concern, subsequent reads in the same session with majority read concern are guaranteed to see that write or a later state. This is the correct answer to 'how do I read from a secondary without seeing stale data after my own write?' — you do not read at local from an arbitrary secondary; you use a causally consistent session with majority read concern. The interview-quality answer names the oplog, pv1 elections, majority commit (`lastOpCommitted`), the write concern ladder (0, 1, majority), the read concern ladder (local, majority, linearizable, snapshot), read preference, and causal sessions as the bridge.
bullets: A replica set has one primary and N secondaries; secondaries replicate the primary's oplog and apply operations in order.
**Three members is the minimum sensible set** — two members cannot form a majority after one failure.
**pv1 elections are Raft-like**: a candidate needs a majority of votes and the most up-to-date oplog wins.
Majority commit (`lastOpCommitted`) is the boundary a newly elected primary can be authoritative for — writes beyond it may be rolled back.
**Write concern**: w:0 (no guarantee), w:1 (primary only, can be lost on failover), w:majority (durable across a minority failure), numeric w:N.
**Read concern**: local (latest, may be rolled back), majority (majority-committed only), linearizable (primary, strongest, slowest), snapshot (point-in-time, for transactions).
Read preference decides which member serves reads; secondary reads scale reads but may be stale unless combined with majority read concern and causal consistency.
Causal consistency sessions give read-your-writes across members by tracking `operationTime`/`clusterTime`.
cards.code:
Replica set topology

  Primary  <-- all writes
    |  oplog replication
    +--> Secondary 1
    +--> Secondary 2

  majority = 2 of 3

Write concern

  { w: 0 }             fire-and-forget, no guarantee
  { w: 1 }             primary ack, may be rolled back on failover
  { w: "majority" }    majority ack, survives loss of a minority
  { w: 2 }             two members ack
  { w: "majority", j: true }  majority + journaled on disk

Read concern

  "local"         latest data on the node, may be rolled back
  "majority"      only data acked by a majority, never rolled back
  "linearizable"  primary only, reflects all completed majority writes
  "snapshot"      point-in-time, for multi-document transactions

Read preference

  primary             default, strongest freshness
  primaryPreferred    primary if available, else secondary
  secondary           read scaling, may be stale
  secondaryPreferred  secondary if available, else primary
  nearest             lowest latency member

Causal consistency (read-your-writes)

  ClientSession session = client.startSession();
  session.startTransaction();
  collection.insertOne(session, doc);                  // write
  collection.find(session, eq("_id", doc.getId()))     // sees the write
  session.commitTransaction();

  // for non-transactional reads:
  // writeConcern majority + readConcern majority
  // + session tracking = causal consistency

Failure scenario

  3-member set, primary dies
  -> remaining 2 hold election
  -> secondary with highest oplog wins
  -> writes acknowledged only by old primary (w:1) and not replicated
     are rolled back
  -> writes acknowledged by majority are preserved (lastOpCommitted)

cards.title: MongoDB Sharding: Shard Keys, Jumbo Chunks, and Targeted vs Scatter-Gather Queries
cards.summary:
Sharding is MongoDB's horizontal scaling mechanism: a collection's data is partitioned across multiple shards by a shard key. A sharded cluster has three components — shards (each a replica set holding a subset of the data), config servers (a replica set storing cluster metadata, including which chunks live on which shard), and mongos routers (the query routers clients connect to). The client never talks to a shard directly; it talks to mongos, which consults the cached metadata from the config servers to route each operation.

The **shard key** is the single most consequential design decision, and it is immutable in older versions (refinable or reshardable in newer ones). A good shard key has three properties: high cardinality (many distinct values, so chunks can be split), low frequency (no single value dominates the data), and non-monotonic growth (new documents do not all land at one end). A boolean field has cardinality 2 and can only produce two chunks; a status field with three values has the same problem. A monotonically increasing key — an auto-increment ID, a timestamp, an `ObjectId` — sends every new insert to the same chunk at the high end, creating a hot shard and a hot chunk. This is the MongoDB version of a partition hotspot, and it is the most common sharding failure in interviews.

When a shard key has low cardinality or skewed frequency, MongoDB can produce jumbo chunks — chunks that exceed the maximum chunk size but cannot be split further because every document in them has the same shard key value. A jumbo chunk cannot be migrated by the balancer, so data skews permanently and one shard fills up while others sit idle. The fixes are to refine the shard key (append a suffix field to increase cardinality), reshard the collection with a better key, or use hashed sharding to distribute values evenly. The interview signal is recognizing that jumbo chunks are a symptom of a bad key, not a balancing bug.

**Hashed sharding** is the standard fix for monotonic keys: the shard key value is hashed before being assigned to a chunk, so sequential IDs distribute uniformly across shards. The cost is that range queries on the hashed field become scatter-gather — MongoDB cannot know which shards hold a contiguous range because the hash destroys the ordering. Hashed sharding is right for equality lookups and write-heavy insert workloads; ranged sharding is right for range queries and data locality. Compound shard keys can combine both: { region: 1, `orderId`: 1 } gives zone locality by region and distribution within each region by the high-cardinality `orderId`. Zone sharding goes further, pinning ranges to specific shards (EU data on EU shards) for data-residency and latency requirements.

**Query routing** is the operational consequence of the shard key choice. A query that includes the shard key (or a prefix of a compound shard key) is targeted: mongos consults the chunk metadata and sends the query to the one shard that can satisfy it. A query that omits the shard key is scatter-gather: mongos broadcasts to every shard, each shard runs the query locally, and mongos merges the results. On a fifty-shard cluster, a scatter-gather query consumes fifty times the CPU, memory, and I/O of a targeted query. This is why shard key selection must start from the application's query patterns, not from the data model alone — a key that distributes writes perfectly but is never in the query predicate turns every read into a broadcast.

The balancer runs in the background on the config servers and migrates chunks from over-loaded shards to under-loaded ones when the distribution crosses a migration threshold. Chunk migration is not free: it copies data, updates metadata, and briefly affects the source and destination shards. The balancer can be scheduled to run only during off-peak hours, and it can be disabled during bulk loads. The interview-quality answer names the three components, the shard key properties (cardinality, frequency, monotonicity), jumbo chunks and their fixes, hashed vs ranged sharding, targeted vs scatter-gather routing, and the balancer's role.
bullets: A sharded cluster = shards (replica sets holding data) + config servers (metadata) + mongos routers (query routing).
**Shard key properties**: high cardinality, low frequency, non-monotonic growth — any violation causes hotspots or jumbo chunks.
Monotonic keys (auto-increment, timestamp, `ObjectId`) send all inserts to one chunk, creating a hot shard.
Jumbo chunks are chunks that exceed the size limit but cannot split because all documents share the same shard key value — fixed by refining the key, resharding, or hashed sharding.
Hashed sharding distributes monotonic keys evenly but breaks efficient range queries; ranged sharding preserves range locality but risks hotspots.
Compound shard keys combine locality (low-cardinality field) with distribution (high-cardinality field); zone sharding pins ranges to specific shards.
Targeted queries include the shard key and hit one shard; scatter-gather queries omit it and broadcast to every shard, multiplying cost by shard count.
The balancer migrates chunks from over-loaded to under-loaded shards; it can be scheduled for off-peak hours.
cards.code:
Sharded cluster

  Client
    |
    v
  mongos (router)  <--> config servers (chunk metadata)
    |
    +--> Shard 1 (replica set)   chunks A, B
    +--> Shard 2 (replica set)   chunks C, D
    +--> Shard 3 (replica set)   chunks E, F

Shard key properties

  high cardinality   many distinct values (userId, orderId)
  low frequency      no single value dominates (not region="us-east" at 80%)
  non-monotonic      new docs do not all land at one end (not createdAt, not ObjectId)

Bad keys

  { status: 1 }        cardinality 3 -> at most 3 chunks
  { createdAt: 1 }     monotonic -> hot chunk at the high end
  { _id: 1 }           ObjectId is time-based -> monotonic -> hot chunk

Fixes

  // hashed sharding -- even distribution, no range queries
  sh.shardCollection("mydb.events", { userId: "hashed" });

  // compound key -- locality + distribution
  sh.shardCollection("mydb.orders", { region: 1, orderId: 1 });

  // zone sharding -- EU data on EU shards
  sh.addShardToZone("shard01", "EU");
  sh.updateZoneKeyRange("mydb.users",
    { region: "EU", _id: MinKey },
    { region: "EU", _id: MaxKey }, "EU");

Query routing

  targeted (includes shard key):
    db.orders.find({ customerId: 42 })   // shard key = customerId
    -> mongos routes to the one shard owning chunk for 42

  scatter-gather (omits shard key):
    db.orders.find({ status: "SHIPPED" })
    -> mongos broadcasts to every shard, merges results
    -> cost multiplies by shard count

Jumbo chunk

  chunk max size exceeded, but every doc has the same shard key value
  -> cannot split
  -> cannot migrate
  -> one shard fills up, others idle

  fix: refine shard key (append suffix), reshard, or use hashed sharding

Balancer

  runs on config servers
  migrates chunks from over-loaded to under-loaded shards
  can be scheduled off-peak: sh.stopBalancer() / sh.startBalancer()

cards.title: PostgreSQL vs MongoDB vs Cassandra: A Decision Framework You Can Defend in an Interview
cards.summary:
The highest-signal database interview question is not 'what are the differences between PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and Cassandra?' — that is a feature-recall question. **The signal is**: 'given this workload, which would you pick, and what trade-off are you accepting?' A strong answer names the workload's access patterns first, then chooses, then states what the choice costs. A weak answer lists features from a comparison table.

**PostgreSQL** is a relational database with an ACID-compliant storage engine, a mature query planner, B-Tree and other index types, MVCC for concurrent reads and writes, and a rich ecosystem (PostGIS for geo, JSONB for semi-structured data, full-text search, extensions). **Its strengths are**: strong consistency by default, joins and multi-table transactions, a powerful planner that adapts to arbitrary queries, and a proven operational track record. **Its weaknesses are**: vertical scaling is the primary path (replication and sharding exist but are not the default model), writes must go through the primary (which limits write throughput compared to a multi-master system), and the relational model does not fit truly unbounded, denormalized data shapes. Choose PostgreSQL when the workload involves transactions, relationships, ad-hoc queries, reporting, or any data whose integrity matters more than raw write throughput — which covers the majority of backend systems.

**MongoDB** is a document database with a flexible schema, BSON storage, indexes, replica sets (one primary, multiple secondaries), and sharding. Its strengths are: documents match the shape of application objects (no impedance mismatch with JSON), embedded data gives single-query reads and atomic updates within a document, schema flexibility allows rapid iteration, and sharding scales horizontally when designed properly. Its weaknesses are: the 16 MB document limit forces design choices, joins ($lookup) are expensive compared to relational joins, multi-document transactions exist but are not the default mental model, and sharding requires a good shard key (a bad key produces jumbo chunks and hot shards). Choose MongoDB when the data is naturally document-shaped (nested, hierarchical, per-entity), the schema evolves frequently, the access pattern is per-document reads by key, and horizontal scaling is anticipated.

**Cassandra** is a wide-column, LSM-based distributed database with no master, tunable consistency, and linear write scalability. Its strengths are: write throughput that scales horizontally by adding nodes, no single point of failure, multi-datacenter replication, and a data model that supports high-cardinality, time-series, and append-heavy workloads. Its weaknesses are: query-first modeling (no joins, no ad-hoc queries, no planner), an unbounded partition is catastrophic, reads are more expensive than writes (merging SSTables, bloom filters, tombstones), consistency is tunable but not strongly guaranteed without R+W>RF, and the operational complexity is significant (ring management, repair, compaction tuning). Choose Cassandra when the workload is write-heavy, time-series or event-shaped, geo-distributed, and read patterns are known in advance and can be served from single partitions.

The decision heuristic that ties the three together: if the workload needs transactions, joins, and strong consistency by default → PostgreSQL. If the workload needs document-shaped data, rapid schema iteration, and per-document access → MongoDB. If the workload needs massive write throughput, linear horizontal scaling, and multi-DC availability with tunable consistency → Cassandra. The most important interview point is that these are not competitors for one workload — they are tools for different shapes. A strong answer never says 'Cassandra is better than Postgres' or 'MongoDB replaces SQL'; it says 'for this workload, because of X and Y, I would pick Z and accept the trade-off W.'

The follow-up question interviewers ask is 'what would you regret about this choice in two years?' The honest answers: PostgreSQL — the primary becomes a write bottleneck, and sharding requires application changes or a move to Citus/multi-primary. MongoDB — a poorly-chosen shard key produces jumbo chunks, and the $lookup-based joins that seemed fine at scale become the bottleneck. Cassandra — a query pattern that emerges later cannot be served efficiently, and the only fix is denormalizing a new table and backfilling it. Naming these regrets demonstrates that you understand the long-term operational cost, not just the happy path. That is the difference between a mid-level and a senior answer.
bullets: **PostgreSQL**: ACID, joins, transactions, mature planner, rich extensions — default for relational, transactional, ad-hoc-query workloads. Trade-off: primary becomes a write bottleneck at very high write throughput.

**MongoDB**: document model, flexible schema, embedded atomicity, sharding — default for document-shaped, per-entity, rapidly-evolving data. Trade-off: 16 MB document limit, expensive joins, shard key design is consequential.

**Cassandra**: LSM, no master, tunable consistency, linear write scaling, multi-DC — default for write-heavy, time-series, geo-distributed workloads with known query patterns. Trade-off: query-first modeling, no ad-hoc queries, reads more expensive than writes.

**Decision heuristic**: transactions + joins + strong-by-default → PostgreSQL; document shape + rapid schema iteration → MongoDB; massive write throughput + multi-DC + tunable consistency → Cassandra.
**Never say one is 'better'** — say 'for this workload, because of X and Y, I would pick Z and accept trade-off W.'

**Two-year regret**: PostgreSQL — primary write bottleneck; MongoDB — bad shard key produces jumbo chunks and expensive $lookup joins; Cassandra — a new query pattern cannot be served without denormalizing and backfilling.
The strongest answer names the workload's access patterns, the choice, the trade-off, and the future regret — that demonstrates judgment, not recall.
cards.code:
Decision framework

  Q1: Does the workload need transactions across multiple entities
      and/or joins across many tables?
      YES -> PostgreSQL
      NO  -> continue

  Q2: Is the data naturally document-shaped (nested, per-entity,
      schema evolves frequently) and accessed by key?
      YES -> MongoDB
      NO  -> continue

  Q3: Is the workload write-heavy (events, time-series, telemetry)
      or geo-distributed with multi-DC availability needs,
      AND are the query patterns known in advance?
      YES -> Cassandra
      NO  -> reconsider: PostgreSQL usually fits (JSONB covers
            semi-structured data, extensions cover special needs)

Comparative matrix

  Dimension          PostgreSQL        MongoDB           Cassandra
  -----------------  ----------------  ----------------  -----------------
  Consistency        strong by default  strong on primary  tunable (R+W>RF)
  Primary model      single primary     one primary / RS  multi-master
  Write scaling      vertical, then      sharding          linear via ring
                     sharding (Citus)                      (add nodes)
  Reads              planner-driven      per-doc + indexes  partition-driven
  Joins              native, powerful    $lookup (costly)  none
  Transactions        full ACID           multi-doc (opt.)   lightweight (LWT)
  Schema             fixed, migrations   flexible           fixed, query-first
  Query flexibility  ad-hoc anywhere     indexed fields     must specify key
  Ops complexity     mature, standard    moderate (RS,      high (ring,
                                          shard key)       repair, compaction)

Regrets in two years

  PostgreSQL: primary saturates at ~50-100k writes/sec,
              sharding requires Citus / application-level routing

  MongoDB:    shard key chosen for distribution but never in the
              query predicate -> every read scatter-gathers;
              $lookup joins that felt fine at 1M docs are the
              bottleneck at 100M

  Cassandra:  a new access pattern appears (e.g. query by status
              without the partition key) -> no efficient query
              path -> must create a new denormalized table and
              backfill the entire history

cards.title: Polyglot Persistence in Microservices: Database-per-Service, the Shared-Database Anti-Pattern, and Distributed Data
cards.summary:
**Polyglot persistence** is the practice of using different database technologies for different services or different data within one application, chosen to fit each workload rather than forcing every workload into one engine. In a microservices architecture it is the natural consequence of database-per-service: each service owns its data and selects the database that fits its access patterns. An order service might use PostgreSQL for transactional order state, a product catalog might use MongoDB for flexible document-shaped product data, a recommendation service might use Cassandra for high-write behavioral events, and a search service might use Elasticsearch for full-text indexing. The same company, four engines, each chosen deliberately.

The alternative — a single shared database for all services — is the shared-database anti-pattern, and interviewers love to probe why it is problematic. The first problem is coupling: if every service reads and writes the same tables, then a schema change by one team breaks another team's code. The 'database' becomes an implicit, unowned API shared across teams, and it evolves at the pace of the slowest consumer. The second problem is coupling of failures: a slow query from the analytics team can exhaust connections and take down the checkout service, because they share the same connection pool. The third problem is coupling of scaling: the entire database must scale for the sum of all workloads, and you cannot right-size each workload independently. The fourth problem is coupling of technology: every service is stuck on the same engine, even when a different engine would fit better. The fifth, and the one interviewers most often want to hear, is that a shared database makes it impossible to define clear service boundaries — if two services write to the same table, they are effectively one service with two deploy units.

The correct model is database-per-service: each service owns its schema, its credentials, and its lifecycle. Other services can only access data through the service's API (REST, gRPC, or events). No service reads another service's database directly. This is enforced by network isolation (the database is only reachable from its owning service), by credential ownership (each service has its own user with privileges only on its own schema), and by team ownership (one team is responsible for each database). The cost is that data which used to be joined in one query now requires cross-service calls — a new set of problems, but the correct set.

The first new problem is data duplication across services. If the order service needs product details, it cannot join against the product service's database. The standard solution is to consume events from the product service and maintain a local read model — the order service stores a product summary (name, price, image URL) in its own database, updated when the product service emits a `ProductUpdated` event. This is the same pattern as the outbox and CDC discussion in the messaging cards: events are the mechanism for cross-service data propagation, and each service materializes what it needs locally. The trade-off is eventual consistency — the order service's product data may lag the product service by milliseconds to seconds — and the need to handle stale reads gracefully.

The second new problem is distributed transactions. A checkout flow that debits a payment, decrements inventory, and creates an order spans three services with three databases. There is no 2PC across these databases that is acceptable in a microservices architecture, so the standard approach is the Saga pattern: each step has a compensating action, and the saga coordinates them via events (choreography) or an orchestrator (orchestration). If the payment succeeds but inventory fails, the saga issues a refund — the compensating action for the payment. This is one of the most-tested microservices interview topics, and it is directly a consequence of polyglot persistence: once data is distributed across services, atomicity across services is no longer free.

The third new problem is querying across services. A dashboard that needs order totals joined with customer names joined with product categories cannot run a single SQL query. **The standard answers are**: (1) a read-optimized projection — a separate service (or a materialized view in a dedicated read database) that consumes events from all relevant services and maintains a joined, denormalized read model; (2) an API composition layer — a service that calls multiple services and aggregates the results; (3) CQRS — separate the write model (each service owns its transactional database) from the read model (a projection optimized for queries). Each has a cost in operational complexity and consistency lag, and the choice depends on how fresh the read must be.

The interview-quality answer names database-per-service as the default, explains the shared-database anti-pattern with the five coupling problems, describes the three consequences (data duplication via events, distributed transactions via sagas, cross-service queries via projections/CQRS), and states the trade-off (eventual consistency and operational complexity in exchange for independent evolution, independent scaling, and independent failure isolation). The trap is to say 'polyglot persistence means using whatever database you want' — the point is not freedom, it is that each service owns a database it can evolve and scale independently, and the cost is that cross-service consistency and queries become explicit engineering problems instead of free database features.
bullets: **Polyglot persistence**: each service uses the database that fits its workload — PostgreSQL for transactions, MongoDB for documents, Cassandra for high-write events, Elasticsearch for search.
**Shared-database anti-pattern**: one database shared across services couples schema changes, failure domains, scaling, and technology choice — and makes service boundaries meaningless.
**Database-per-service**: each service owns its schema, credentials, and lifecycle; other services access data only through its API or events.
**Data duplication via events**: services consume events and maintain local read models instead of joining another service's database.
**Distributed transactions via sagas**: cross-service atomicity is not free; compensating actions replace 2PC.
**Cross-service queries via API composition, projections, or CQRS** — each has a consistency lag and operational cost.
**Trade-off**: eventual consistency and operational complexity in exchange for independent evolution, independent scaling, and independent failure isolation.
**The point is not 'use whatever database you want'** — it is that each service owns a database it can evolve and scale independently, and cross-service consistency becomes explicit engineering.
cards.code:
Database-per-service architecture

  Order service      -> PostgreSQL      (transactional order state)
  Product service    -> MongoDB         (flexible product documents)
  Recommendation     -> Cassandra       (high-write behavioral events)
  Search             -> Elasticsearch   (full-text index)
  Analytics          -> ClickHouse      (columnar OLAP)

  Each service owns its schema + credentials + lifecycle.
  Cross-service access only through APIs or events.

Shared-database anti-pattern (why it hurts)

  Coupling dimensions:
    1. Schema      one team's migration breaks another team's query
    2. Failure     analytics slow query exhausts pool, checkout dies
    3. Scaling     one engine must serve sum of all workloads
    4. Technology  everyone stuck on the same engine
    5. Boundaries  two services writing the same table are one service

Data duplication via events

  Product service                 Order service
  ----------------                ---------------
  products (source of truth)      orders
                                  product_snapshot  <- local read model

  product.updated event ->
    order-service.onProductUpdated()
      -> upsert product_snapshot(productId, name, price, imageUrl)

  Trade-off: product_snapshot is eventually consistent.
  Fix stale reads by tolerating short lag or reading through to
  the product service for critical views.

Distributed transactions via saga (choreography)

  Checkout flow across 3 services:

    payment.debit -> inventory.reserve -> order.create

    if inventory.reserve fails:
       -> payment.refund (compensating action)

    if order.create fails:
       -> inventory.release
       -> payment.refund

  No 2PC. Each step has a compensating action.

Cross-service queries

  API composition:
    dashboard-service -> calls order-service, customer-service,
                         product-service -> merges results

  Projection / CQRS:
    dashboard-read-db subscribes to events from all services
    and maintains a denormalized read model

  Trade-off:
    composition -> real-time, N calls per request, fragile to outages
    projection  -> fast reads, eventual consistency, more infra

When NOT to go polyglot

  - Small team, one workload shape -> one engine (Postgres) is fine
  - Postgres JSONB covers semi-structured data well
  - every extra engine = backup, monitoring, on-call, migrations,
    security review, hiring, training

cards.title: Caching Basics, Access Patterns, and TTLs
cards.summary:
Caching works like keeping the tools you use every five minutes on your workbench instead of walking back to the garage shelf every time. By storing copies of frequently read data in ultra-fast memory (RAM), applications cut response times from tens of milliseconds down to sub-millisecond reads and protect primary databases from overload.

A **cache hit** happens when requested data is found in the cache; a **cache miss** occurs when the app must fetch from the database. Four core patterns govern reads and writes. In **cache-aside** (lazy loading), the application checks the cache first, reads the database on a miss, and populates the cache. In **read-through**, the cache library itself loads missing entries from the database. In **write-through**, writes update the cache and database synchronously together. In **write-back** (write-behind), writes hit the cache immediately and flush asynchronously to the database later—blazingly fast, but risks data loss if the cache crashes.

Every cached key should carry a **TTL (Time to Live)** so stale data expires automatically. Cache read-heavy, slowly changing data (product catalogs, user profiles), and never cache rapidly mutating counters or unencrypted secrets without strict bounds.
bullets: **Cache-aside** is the most common pattern in backend apps because the application stays resilient even if the cache node goes down.
**Write-through** keeps cache and database strongly aligned at the cost of higher write latency, while **write-back** maximizes write throughput at the risk of losing unflushed memory writes.
Always attach a **TTL** to cached entries as a safety net so bugs in explicit cache invalidation never leave data stale forever.
Cache expensive computations and read-heavy entities, but avoid caching data with low reuse or strict real-time financial accuracy requirements.

glossary.meaning: Serving requested data directly from fast cache memory without querying the backing store.
Pattern where application code checks the cache first and populates it from the database on a miss.
Pattern writing to cache immediately and flushing updates to the database asynchronously later.
Expiration duration after which a cached key is automatically deleted to limit staleness.

interview.q: Compare cache-aside and write-through caching. When would you choose each?
interview.a: In **cache-aside**, the application manages both stores: it reads from the cache, loads from the DB on a miss, and typically deletes the cache key on writes. It only caches data actually requested and survives cache outages cleanly. **Write-through** updates the cache synchronously on every DB write, ensuring zero cold-miss lag for newly written items, though it pollutes the cache with data that may never be read.

interview.q: What is the main risk of write-back (write-behind) caching?
interview.a: Because **write-back** acknowledges writes as soon as they land in cache memory and flushes them asynchronously to the database in batches, any power failure or crash of the cache node before flushing permanently loses those acknowledged writes.

cards.title: Redis Data Structures and Single-Threaded Speed
cards.summary:
**Redis** is an in-memory data structure store used as a cache, session store, rate limiter, and message broker. Unlike plain key-value caches that store only opaque blobs, Redis understands rich native types directly on the server, letting you update a single field or rank millions of scores without serializing whole objects over the network.

Seven core structures cover almost every backend need: **Strings** (plain text/JSON/counters via `INCR` for rate limiting), **Hashes** (field-value maps ideal for user session objects), **Lists** (doubly-linked lists for lightweight job queues), **Sets** (unique unordered members for tags or mutual friends), **Sorted Sets (`ZSET`)** (members ranked by a float score for real-time gaming leaderboards), **Streams** (append-only consumer-group logs for event messaging), and **Bitmaps** (bit-level arrays tracking daily active users in kilobytes).

Redis achieves `100,000+` operations per second because all data lives in **RAM**, it uses non-blocking **I/O multiplexing** (`epoll`/`kqueue`), and its **single-threaded command execution** eliminates lock contention and context-switching overhead.
bullets: Redis executes commands on a **single main thread**, making multi-step commands like `INCR` or `ZADD` inherently atomic without mutex locks.
Use **Sorted Sets (`ZSET`)** for real-time leaderboards (`O(log N)` rank updates) and sliding-window rate limiters scored by timestamp.
Use **Hashes** instead of serialized JSON strings when you frequently read or increment individual fields of an object like a shopping cart.
Because Redis is single-threaded for command execution, never run `O(N)` blocking commands like `KEYS *` or huge `SMEMBERS` in production.

glossary.meaning: A collection of unique string members ordered continuously by an associated floating-point score.
An OS mechanism letting one thread monitor thousands of network sockets simultaneously for readiness.
A map of string fields to string values stored under a single Redis key.
Bit-level operations over a string key enabling compact boolean tracking for millions of IDs.

cards.code:
# Real-world Redis data structure commands
# 1. String counter for API rate limiting
INCR rate:user:42:2026112519
EXPIRE rate:user:42:2026112519 60
