Contract tests are fast (milliseconds), run in each service's CI, and fail at the deploy that caused the change — not hours later in staging.
**Contract testing scales where end-to-end tests do not**: 50 consumers = 50 small tests instead of 50 flaky environment-dependent tests.
**The contract makes the implicit interface explicit** — providers see what consumers actually use, enabling safe field removal and informed evolution.
Contract testing verifies the interface; integration testing verifies the implementation against a real dependency; end-to-end testing still validates the whole system in small quantities.
**The trap is to present contract testing as a silver bullet** — it is a targeted tool for cross-service interface drift.

cards.title: Distributed Tracing: Correlation IDs, Spans, Context Propagation, and OpenTelemetry
cards.summary:
In a monolith, debugging a slow request is straightforward: the stack trace shows every method call, and the logs are all in one place. In a microservices system, a single user request fans out into dozens of service calls, message publishes, and database queries — and each piece runs in a different process, on a different machine, with its own logs. When the request is slow, the question 'which service added the 800 ms?' has no answer from logs alone, because the logs from different services are not connected. **Distributed tracing** is the mechanism that connects them.

The **core abstraction** is the trace: one trace represents one logical request, from the moment the user clicks to the moment the response returns. A trace is composed of spans — each span represents one unit of work (an HTTP request, a database query, a message publish, a function call) and records its start time, duration, parent span, tags (metadata like `http.method`, `db.statement`), and status. **Spans form a tree**: the root span is the incoming user request, its children are the outbound calls it made, their children are the calls those calls made, and so on. The tree structure is what makes tracing useful — it shows not just how long the whole request took but how the time was distributed across the call graph, so you can see that 750 of the 800 ms were spent in one downstream call.

**Correlation IDs** are the simplest form of distributed tracing and the one every microservices system should have even if it does not use a full tracing system. A correlation ID (also called a trace ID or request ID) is a unique identifier generated at the edge (the API gateway or the first service) and propagated to every downstream service through a header (X-Correlation-ID, X-Request-ID, or the standard traceparent header). Every log line in every service includes this ID. When debugging, you search the logs across all services for that one ID and reconstruct the timeline. The correlation ID is not a trace — it has no span tree, no duration breakdown, no parent-child relationships — but it is the minimum viable tracing and it costs almost nothing to implement.

A full tracing system adds three things beyond correlation IDs. First, the span tree: each service records spans for its own work and its outbound calls, using the same trace ID and parent span ID from the incoming context. Second, timing and metadata per span: when a span started, how long it took, what the operation was, what error it produced. Third, a tracing backend (Jaeger, Zipkin, Tempo, Datadog, Honeycomb) that ingests spans and reconstructs the tree visually — a waterfall diagram showing the entire request across services, with each span as a horizontal bar. The waterfall is what makes tracing so powerful in practice: a slow request is immediately obvious as the widest bar in the diagram.

**Context propagation** is the engineering problem that makes tracing work, and it is where most tracing implementations fail. The trace context (trace ID, parent span ID, and sampling flags) must be attached to every outbound call: HTTP requests carry it in a header (the W3C standard is traceparent: 00-`<trace-id>`-`<span-id>`-`<flags>`), gRPC carries it in metadata, message queues carry it in message headers, and asynchronous executors must carry it in their task wrappers. If any hop drops the context — a custom HTTP client that does not forward headers, a Kafka producer that does not attach trace headers, a thread pool task that loses the `ThreadLocal` — the trace breaks and the downstream spans become orphans. This is why every HTTP client, message producer, and executor in the system must be tracing-aware, typically via framework integration (Spring Boot 3 auto-instruments `RestTemplate`, `WebClient`, Kafka, RabbitMQ, and executors when Micrometer Tracing is on the classpath).

OpenTelemetry (OTel) is the vendor-neutral standard for tracing, metrics, and logs. It defines the API (how applications produce spans), the SDK (how spans are collected and exported), and the OTLP protocol (how spans travel to a backend). The benefit is that applications instrument against OTel's API and can point at any compatible backend — Jaeger today, Datadog tomorrow — without code changes. Spring Boot 3 uses Micrometer Tracing, which bridges to OpenTelemetry (or Brave for Zipkin) as the underlying implementation. The interview point is that OpenTelemetry is the emerging standard, replacing the older, vendor-locked Zipkin/Brave and Jaeger clients.

Sampling is the practical constraint every production tracing system faces. **Traces are expensive**: at 10,000 requests per second, storing every trace with 50 spans each is hundreds of thousands of spans per second. Sampling records only a fraction — head-based sampling decides at the start of the trace (record 1% of requests, or 100% of errors, or 100% of slow requests), while tail-based sampling buffers the full trace and decides after seeing the outcome (record all traces with an error or with `p99` latency). Tail-based is more useful (it captures the interesting traces) but requires more infrastructure. The interview-quality answer acknowledges that production tracing is always sampled and that the sampling strategy determines what you can debug.

In an interview, the strongest answer explains the trace/span tree, insists on correlation IDs as the minimum, explains context propagation as the failure-prone part (HTTP headers, gRPC metadata, Kafka headers, executor wrappers), names OpenTelemetry as the standard with Micrometer Tracing as the Spring integration, and discusses sampling as a necessary trade-off. That demonstrates you have operated a distributed system, not just read about tracing.
bullets: A trace represents one logical request; spans are the units of work within it, forming a tree with durations and metadata.
**Correlation IDs are the minimum viable tracing**: a unique ID propagated through headers and included in every log line — no span tree, but essential for cross-service debugging.
**Context propagation is the failure-prone part**: HTTP headers (traceparent), gRPC metadata, Kafka/RabbitMQ message headers, and executor task wrappers must all carry the context.
OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard (API + SDK + OTLP protocol); Spring Boot 3 uses Micrometer Tracing bridged to OTel.
**Sampling is necessary at scale**: head-based (decide at start) is simpler; tail-based (decide after outcome) captures errors and slow traces but costs more infrastructure.

Framework auto-instrumentation (Spring Boot 3, Micrometer Tracing) covers HTTP clients, `WebClient`, Kafka, RabbitMQ, and executors — but custom clients and manual thread pools break tracing unless explicitly propagated.
**A slow request is diagnosed by the waterfall diagram**: the widest span shows where the time was spent.

cards.title: Saga Pattern: Compensating Actions, Choreography vs Orchestration, and Why 2PC Fails in Microservices
cards.summary:
A **saga** is a sequence of local transactions that together implement a business operation that spans multiple services. Each local transaction updates one service's database and publishes an event or message that triggers the next step. If a step fails, the saga executes compensating actions for the steps that already succeeded, undoing their effects. The **saga pattern** is the standard answer to the distributed-transactions problem in microservices: how do you atomically debit a payment, reserve inventory, and create an order when those three things live in three databases owned by three services?

The alternative — two-phase commit (2PC) — is the traditional distributed-transaction protocol, and it is generally rejected in microservices architectures for three reasons. First, 2PC requires a transaction coordinator and holds locks across all participants for the duration of the transaction; if any participant is slow, every participant blocks, which is unacceptable for user-facing services. Second, 2PC requires all participants to support the XA protocol, which many modern databases and message brokers do not (or support poorly). Third, 2PC couples availability: if the coordinator or any participant is unavailable, the entire transaction fails, even if the other services are healthy. The saga pattern trades atomicity for availability — the intermediate states are visible (a payment may be debited before the inventory is confirmed), but the system as a whole converges, and no service blocks on another.

The critical design rule for sagas is that every step must have a compensating action — an operation that undoes the step's effect. A debit has a refund. A reservation has a release. A shipment has a recall. Not every operation can be compensated: sending an email cannot be unsent, so the saga must either make the effect harmless (a "we'll be right back" email is followed by a correction email) or avoid the side effect until the saga is confirmed. The interview trap is to propose a saga for an operation whose steps cannot be compensated — sagas work when every step has a semantic inverse.

**Choreography** is the decentralized form: each service publishes an event when its step completes, and the next service listens and reacts. The order service publishes `OrderCreated`, the payment service listens and publishes `PaymentCharged`, the inventory service listens and publishes `InventoryReserved`, and so on. If any step fails, the failing service publishes a failure event, and the previous services listen and run their compensating actions. The advantages are loose coupling and no central point of failure — adding a new step means adding a listener, not editing an orchestrator. The disadvantages are complexity in understanding and debugging: the overall flow is implicit, spread across many services, and a new developer has to read all the listeners to understand what happens on checkout. There is also a risk of cyclic dependencies when compensation events cascade.

**Orchestration** is the centralized form: a saga orchestrator (a dedicated service or an in-process state machine) sends commands to each participant, waits for the reply, and decides the next step or the compensation on failure. The orchestrator holds the saga's state (which step is current, which steps completed, which need compensation) and is the single place to look when debugging. The advantages are clarity and control — the flow is explicit, the state machine is visible, and complex logic (conditional steps, parallel steps, timeouts) is easier to express. The disadvantages are coupling (the orchestrator must know every participant) and the risk of making the orchestrator a god service that holds too much business logic.

The choice between the two is the most-tested saga question. **The heuristic**: use choreography for short, simple flows (two or three steps) where the events are already part of the domain; use orchestration for long, complex flows (four or more steps, conditional branching, timeouts) where explicit state is worth the coupling. In practice, most teams start with choreography and migrate to orchestration when the flow becomes hard to reason about. The interview signal is not which one you pick but whether you can defend the trade-off.

A saga's steps must be idempotent, because retries and duplicate events are unavoidable in a distributed system. A compensation that runs twice must be as safe as one that runs once. This is where idempotency keys and inbox tables (covered in the Outbox card) become mandatory — the saga and the idempotency layer are the two halves of reliable distributed workflows. The interview-quality answer names the saga pattern, rejects 2PC with the lock/availability/XA reasons, insists on compensating actions and idempotency, and distinguishes choreography from orchestration with the complexity/coupling trade-off.
bullets: A saga is a sequence of local transactions across services; each step publishes an event or command that triggers the next, and failures trigger compensating actions for completed steps.
**2PC is rejected in microservices**: it holds locks across participants, requires XA support, and couples availability — one slow or down participant blocks or fails everything.
Every saga step must have a compensating action (debit → refund, reserve → release); steps without a compensable inverse cannot be safely included in a saga.
**Choreography**: services react to each other's events; decentralized, loose coupling, but the flow is implicit and hard to debug at scale.
**Orchestration**: a central orchestrator holds the saga state and drives each step; explicit and debuggable, at the cost of coupling and a potential god-service risk.
**Heuristic**: choreography for short simple flows (2–3 steps), orchestration for long complex flows (4+ steps, branching, timeouts).
**Saga steps and compensations must be idempotent** — retries and duplicate events are inevitable; idempotency keys / inbox tables are required.
cards.code:
Saga example (checkout, choreography)

  order.created    -> payment-service listens
  payment.charged  -> inventory-service listens
  inventory.reserved -> order-service listens (mark CONFIRMED)

  Failure path:
  inventory.reservation.failed
    -> payment-service listens, refunds, publishes payment.refunded
    -> order-service listens, marks CANCELLED

Saga example (checkout, orchestration)

  CheckoutOrchestrator:
    state = PENDING
    step 1: send ChargePayment -> wait for reply
    step 2: send ReserveInventory -> wait for reply
    step 3: send CreateOrder -> wait for reply
    on failure at step N: run compensations N-1 ... 1

  Compensations:
    ChargePayment   -> RefundPayment
    ReserveInventory-> ReleaseInventory
    CreateOrder     -> CancelOrder

State machine (orchestration)

  START
    |-- ChargePayment ----+--> ReserveInventory --> CreateOrder --> DONE
    |         | fail                | fail               | fail
    |         v                     v                    v
    |       CANCEL                Refund              Release
    |                             Payment             + Refund

2PC vs Saga

  2PC                          Saga
  -----------------------      -----------------------
  atomic                       eventual consistency
  locks held across services   no cross-service locks
  XA support required          no special protocol
  coordinator is a SPOF        orchestrated: coordinator, but
                               can recover from durable state;
                               choreographed: no coordinator
  blocks on slow participant   each step is a local transaction

Idempotency in sagas

  - retry of a step must not double-debit
  - use business key (orderId) as the idempotency key
  - store the key in a dedup table in the same tx as the effect
  - see Outbox card: inbox table for consumer-side dedup

cards.title: Strangler Fig Migration: Incrementally Replacing a Monolith Without a Big-Bang Rewrite
cards.summary:
The strangler fig pattern is a technique for migrating from a legacy system to a new one incrementally, without a big-bang rewrite. The name comes from a vine that grows around a tree, gradually enveloping it until the tree dies and only the vine's shape remains. In software, a new system grows around the old one, handling an increasing share of traffic, until the old system can be decommissioned. At every point in the migration, both systems are running in production, and traffic is routed between them by a facade (a proxy, an API gateway, or a routing layer) that decides which system handles each request.

The problem it solves is the big-bang rewrite's failure mode. A rewrite that replaces the entire legacy system in one release is risky because it cannot be tested against real production traffic until the cutover, it takes months or years during which the business cannot ship new features on the old system, and when it goes live, a single missed edge case can take down the whole product. The strangler fig avoids this by migrating one feature or one route at a time, in small, reversible steps — each step is tested against a slice of real traffic, monitored, and either rolled forward or rolled back. The risk is distributed across many small releases instead of concentrated in one large one.

The mechanics have four parts. First, an interception layer sits between clients and the legacy system — usually the API gateway, an NGINX reverse proxy, or a service mesh ingress. Every request goes through it. Second, routing rules decide which requests go to the legacy system and which go to the new system. A common pattern is to route by URL prefix (`/api/new/**` → new system, everything else → legacy) or by user cohort (1% of users → new system, 99% → legacy) so the new system can be validated incrementally. Third, a translation layer (often an anti-corruption layer) sits between the two systems so that data written by the new system can be read by the legacy one and vice versa. This is the hardest part and the one most migrations underestimate — the legacy system's data model is rarely clean, and the new system's model must be reconciled with it. Fourth, a decommission step: as routes migrate, the legacy code paths are removed, and eventually the legacy system is shut down.

Three techniques are commonly used alongside the strangler fig. **Branch by abstraction**: introduce an interface in the codebase that both the old and new implementations satisfy, then swap the implementation gradually via feature flags — useful when migrating within the same process. **Parallel run**: send the same request to both systems and compare responses (dark launch), so the new system is validated against real traffic without affecting users — useful for high-risk migrations where the correctness of the new system is uncertain. **Feature flags**: gate the new system by user, cohort, or percentage, so rollout and rollback are one configuration change — useful throughout the migration for gradual exposure.

The hardest problem in strangler fig migrations is shared data. If the legacy system owns a database and the new service also needs to read or write that data, the migration must decide who owns the data during the transition. There are three common approaches. **Co-existence**: both systems access the same database during the migration, with the new system reading/writing the legacy schema (painful, but sometimes the only option). **Data sync**: the new system has its own database and the two are kept in sync by CDC or an outbox-style dual-write (better long-term, more initial complexity). **Ownership handoff**: at a specific point, the new system becomes the owner and the legacy system reads from the new system's database or via API (cleanest, but requires the legacy system to change). The interview-quality answer names the trade-offs and does not pretend the data problem is trivial.

The interview-quality answer names the strangler fig's core idea (incremental migration with both systems live), explains the four parts (interception layer, routing rules, translation layer, decommission), describes the supporting techniques (branch by abstraction, parallel run, feature flags), and addresses shared data as the hardest problem with the three approaches (co-existence, sync, handoff). It also names the anti-pattern — the 'never-ending strangler' where the new system's growth stalls, the legacy system is never decommissioned, and the organization is permanently maintaining two systems. That demonstrates you understand the operational discipline the pattern requires, not just the technique.
bullets: **Strangler fig migrates incrementally**: a new system grows around the legacy one, taking over traffic gradually, until the legacy can be decommissioned.
**Four parts**: interception layer (gateway/proxy), routing rules (by URL, cohort, percentage), translation layer (anti-corruption for data), decommission.
**Supporting techniques**: branch by abstraction (interface + feature flag), parallel run / dark launch (compare responses against real traffic), feature flags (gradual rollout).
**Shared data is the hardest problem**: co-existence (same DB), data sync (CDC/outbox between two DBs), or ownership handoff (legacy reads from new).
The pattern reduces risk by distributing it across many small reversible releases instead of concentrating it in one big-bang cutover.
**The anti-pattern is the never-ending strangler** — the legacy is never decommissioned, and the org permanently maintains two systems.
**Decommission is part of the plan, not an afterthought** — if there is no decommission milestone, the migration is not really happening.
cards.code:
Strangler fig architecture

  Clients
    |
    v
  [ Interception layer: API gateway / NGINX / service mesh ]
    |                                        |
    |-- /api/new/** ----------------------> [ New service ]
    |                                        |
    |-- everything else -------------------> [ Legacy monolith ]
                                             |
                                        [ Legacy DB ]

  Routing rules evolve over time:
    phase 1:  0% to new (dark launch + parallel run)
    phase 2:  1% of users to new (canary)
    phase 3: 10% of users to new
    phase 4: 50% of users to new
    phase 5: 100% of users to new
    phase 6: decommission legacy route

Branch by abstraction

  interface OrderService {
      Order find(long id);
      void place(Order o);
  }

  class LegacyOrderService implements OrderService { ... }
  class NewOrderService    implements OrderService { ... }

  // Feature flag selects implementation per call
  @Bean OrderService orderService(FeatureFlags flags, LegacyOrderService legacy,
                                  NewOrderService modern) {
      return (order, args) -> flags.isOn("new-order-service")
          ? modern : legacy;
  }

Parallel run (dark launch)

  Request -> legacy -> response -> user
          \-> new   -> response -> compare

  Compare fields, log mismatches, do NOT return new response yet.
  Once mismatches are under a threshold, start returning the new one.

Shared data approaches

  Co-existence
    legacy and new both read/write the same DB
    fastest to start, hardest to evolve (schema is shared)

  Data sync
    legacy DB --CDC--> new DB
    new writes -> outbox -> legacy (or legacy reads via API)
    cleaner long-term, more initial complexity

  Ownership handoff
    new becomes the owner at a specific point
    legacy reads from new DB or new API
    cleanest, requires legacy changes

Decommission milestones

  [ ] route X migrated and stable for N days
  [ ] legacy code for route X deleted
  [ ] legacy DB tables for route X dropped
  [ ] legacy infra for route X scaled down
  -> if none of these happens, the "strangler" has not strangled anything

cards.title: Transactional Outbox and Idempotent Consumers: The Two Halves of Reliable Event Delivery
cards.summary:
The transactional outbox pattern solves the dual-write problem: a service must update its database and publish an event, but it cannot do both atomically. If it writes the database and then the event publish fails, downstream services never hear about the change. If it publishes the event and then the database write fails, downstream services react to a change that never happened. Wrapping both in a distributed transaction is the 2PC trap. The outbox pattern solves it by making the event publish a database operation like any other: the domain change and an 'outbox' row are written in the same local transaction, so they succeed or fail together. A separate relay process reads the outbox table and publishes the events to the broker, at-least-once. The relay can be a polling process, a CDC stream from the database's write-ahead log (Debezium on Postgres or MySQL), or a transactional message broker feature (Kafka transactions for Kafka-internal flows).

The outbox table has a stable schema: id, `aggregate_id`, `event_type`, payload (JSON), `created_at`, and optionally a status column (PENDING, SENT) for polling relays. **The write path is**: in one database transaction, update the domain table AND insert a row into the outbox. The relay reads unsent rows (or streams them via CDC) and publishes them to the broker. If the publish succeeds, the row is marked sent (or the CDC offset advances); if it fails, the relay retries. Because the outbox row is durable, a crash between the database commit and the publish is recoverable — on restart, the relay resumes and publishes the event. **The relay is at-least-once**: it may publish the same event more than once if it crashes after publishing but before marking the row sent. This is not a bug; it is the guarantee, and the consumer must handle it.

**Idempotent consumers** are the other half. Because the relay is at-least-once, and because the broker may redeliver on consumer crash, and because retries happen, a consumer will eventually see the same event twice. If the consumer is not idempotent, the effect happens twice — a double charge, a duplicate order, a double decrement. The **fix** is a stable idempotency key that is identical on every redelivery of the same logical event. The **best choice** is an `eventId` generated at the origin (a UUID placed in the event payload or a message header) or a business key (`orderId` + `event_type`). Topic-partition-offset is a bad key: offsets change across replays, cluster moves, and topic recreation.

The consumer-side pattern is the inbox table. In the same database transaction that applies the domain effect, insert the idempotency key into an inbox table with a unique constraint. If the insert succeeds, the domain effect is applied; if it fails with a duplicate-key error, the event has already been processed and the consumer returns success without applying the effect again. This makes the domain effect and the dedup record atomic — either both happen or neither does. The inbox table needs a TTL or a cleanup job that is at least as long as the maximum redelivery window (which can be days if dead-letter queues are replayed, so the TTL should be generous).

For operations that call an external system — a payment provider, an email service, a third-party API — the inbox table only guards the local database. The external call must have its own idempotency mechanism: Stripe accepts an Idempotency-Key header and returns the original response on retry; email providers usually deduplicate by message-id; a custom API must be designed with idempotency keys. The consumer stores the external system's idempotency key in the inbox record so retries reuse the same key. **This is the layering**: the outbox guarantees the event is published; the inbox guarantees the consumer does not re-apply the local effect; the external idempotency key guarantees the external side effect is not duplicated. All three layers are needed for end-to-end effectively-once delivery.

The interview trap is to think that Kafka's exactly-once semantics (EOS) removes the need for idempotent consumers. It does not. Kafka EOS guarantees exactly-once for produce-transform-produce loops within Kafka (with transactions and `read_committed` consumers). It does not cover writes to external databases or APIs. And even within Kafka, if the consumer uses at-least-once semantics (which is the default and the practical choice for most workloads), duplicates are possible. The outbox and idempotent consumers are needed whenever the sink is not a Kafka topic in the same transaction, which is almost always.

The interview-quality answer names the dual-write problem, describes the outbox table and relay (polling, CDC via Debezium, or Kafka transactions), insists on at-least-once and idempotent consumers, describes the inbox table with a unique constraint, and distinguishes local idempotency (inbox) from external idempotency (provider keys). It also notes that Kafka EOS does not replace this for external sinks. That demonstrates you understand reliable messaging as a layered problem, not a single setting.
bullets: **The dual-write problem**: a service cannot atomically update its database and publish to a broker — one can succeed and the other fail.
The outbox pattern writes the domain change and an outbox row in the same local transaction, then a relay publishes the outbox rows to the broker at-least-once.
**Relay options**: polling the outbox table, CDC from the database WAL (Debezium), or transactional Kafka producers for Kafka-internal flows.
**The relay is at-least-once** — duplicates are the guarantee, and consumers must deduplicate.
Idempotent consumers use a stable key (`eventId` UUID or business key `orderId` + `event_type`), never topic-partition-offset.
The inbox table (`idempotency_key` UNIQUE, written in the same transaction as the domain effect) makes the effect + dedup atomic.
External systems need their own idempotency keys (Stripe Idempotency-Key, message-id dedup) — the inbox only covers the local database.
Kafka EOS does not replace outbox + idempotent consumers for external sinks, and at-least-once consumers still need dedup.

cards.title: What Is a Distributed System and Why Networks Complicate It
cards.summary:
A **distributed system** is a group of independent computers connected over a network that work together so users experience them as a single coherent product—like a banking app or video streaming platform.

We build distributed systems because a single machine eventually hits hard limits in CPU, memory, storage, or geographic reach, and a single server offers zero survival if its power supply or disk dies. However, splitting software across machines introduces **partial failure**: on one laptop, either the whole program crashes or it works, whereas across ten servers, three nodes might fail or slow down while seven keep running.

Engineers new to distributed design often assume the **Eight Fallacies of Distributed Computing**—false beliefs that the network is reliable, **latency** (delay per message) is zero, and **bandwidth** (data volume per second) is infinite. Because messages can be delayed, duplicated, or lost, every distributed design becomes a trade-off between consistency, speed, and fault tolerance.
bullets: Teams adopt **distributed systems** to overcome single-machine hardware limits, serve global users locally, and survive individual server crashes.
Unlike local code, distributed software faces **partial failure**, where timeouts leave a caller unsure whether a remote action succeeded or failed.
The **fallacies of distributed computing** warn against treating remote network calls like fast, reliable in-memory method calls.
High **bandwidth** cannot fix high **latency**: shipping a hard drive across the country has huge bandwidth yet terrible latency.

glossary.meaning: Multiple networked computers coordinating via messages to appear as one unified system.
A state where some components or nodes fail while others continue operating.
The time delay required for a single message to travel from sender to receiver.
The maximum rate of data transfer across a network link, measured in bits per second.

cards.code:
# Local Method Call vs Distributed RPC Call
# Local Call (In-memory: ~10 nanoseconds, succeeds or whole JVM crashes)
OrderResult res = inventoryService.reserve(itemId);

# Distributed RPC (Over network: ~5 to 500 milliseconds, ambiguous failure)
Client ----[ reserve(itemId) ]----> Network (drop/delay?) ----> Inventory Node
Client <---[ TIMEOUT! Did Inventory commit or crash before? ]---+

interview.q: What makes debugging a distributed system fundamentally harder than debugging a single-node application?
interview.a: The biggest difference is **partial failure** and the lack of a single shared clock or memory space. When a remote call times out, the caller cannot tell whether the request was lost on the way, the server crashed before executing it, or the server executed it and the reply was dropped. Every design has to handle ambiguous outcomes safely.

interview.q: Explain the difference between latency and bandwidth with a practical example.
interview.a: **Latency** is the delay for one byte to travel from A to B, while **bandwidth** is how many bytes per second the pipe can carry. A cross-continental fiber link might have `100 Gbps` bandwidth, yet physics limits light speed so a round trip still takes `150 ms` latency—meaning chatty sequential RPCs stay slow despite huge bandwidth.

cards.title: Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling and Availability Nines
cards.summary:
When traffic grows, you have two ways to scale. **Vertical scaling** (scaling up) upgrades one machine with faster CPUs, more RAM, or bigger disks—like replacing a delivery van with a semi-truck. It requires zero code changes, but hits an expensive hardware ceiling and leaves a **single point of failure (SPOF)**.

**Horizontal scaling** (scaling out) adds more machines behind a load balancer—like hiring ten delivery vans. To scale out cleanly, web servers must be **stateless**, storing user sessions and files in shared databases or caches rather than local RAM so any server can handle any request.

Adding **redundancy** (duplicate servers across isolated power and network zones) boosts **availability**, measured in 'nines'. Reaching `99.9%` ('three nines') allows about `8.76 hours` of downtime per year, while `99.99%` ('four nines') allows only `52.6 minutes` per year—requiring automated failover because humans cannot wake up and fix outages that fast.
bullets: **Vertical scaling** is simple initially but hits hard hardware price ceilings and still leaves one machine as a **single point of failure**.
**Horizontal scaling** unlocks near-linear capacity and fault tolerance, provided application nodes stay **stateless**.
Eliminating every **single point of failure** requires **redundancy** across servers, databases, load balancers, and availability zones.
Moving from `99.9%` to `99.99%` **availability** shrinks annual downtime budget from `8.76 hours` to `52.6 minutes`, demanding automated recovery.

glossary.meaning: Adding more CPU, RAM, or storage capacity to a single existing server.
Adding more server instances to share workload behind a load balancer.
A service storing no client session data locally between requests, enabling easy scaling.
Any component whose failure brings down the entire system because no backup exists.

cards.code:
# Availability 'Nines' and Allowed Downtime
Availability | Downtime / Year | Downtime / Month | Operational Reality
-------------|-----------------|------------------|--------------------
99%   (2 9s) | 3.65 days       | 7.31 hours       | Single server, manual restarts
99.9% (3 9s) | 8.76 hours      | 43.8 minutes     | Multi-node + basic health checks
99.99%(4 9s) | 52.6 minutes    | 4.38 minutes     | Multi-AZ, automated failover
99.999%(5 9s)| 5.26 minutes    | 26.3 seconds     | Multi-region active-active

interview.q: Why must application servers be stateless before you can scale them horizontally?
interview.a: If a server stores login sessions or shopping carts in local memory, subsequent requests from that user must hit that exact instance. That prevents auto-scaling from freely adding or terminating nodes and causes users to lose sessions whenever a node crashes. Moving state to **Redis** or a database lets any node serve any request.

interview.q: You run three stateless API pods behind one database instance. What is your system's availability bottleneck?
interview.a: The single database instance is a **single point of failure (SPOF)**. Even with three redundant API pods, if that database crashes or undergoes maintenance, the whole application goes down. True high availability requires **redundancy** at every layer, including a replicated primary-standby database across separate availability zones.

cards.title: Replication Models: Leader-Follower, Multi-Leader, and Leaderless
cards.summary:
**Replication** is the process of keeping multiple copies of the same data on different machines. It exists for three reasons: durability (if one node dies, the data survives), availability (if one node is unreachable, another can serve the request), and read scaling (multiple nodes can serve reads in parallel). There are exactly three models for how writes propagate to replicas, and understanding the trade-offs among them is foundational — every later topic (consistency, replication lag, conflict resolution, quorum reads) builds on this taxonomy.

Leader-follower replication (also called master-slave or primary-replica) is the most common model. One replica is designated the leader; all writes go to the leader, which appends them to its log. Followers receive the log and apply writes in order, maintaining a copy of the leader's state. Reads can be served by any replica (often for read scaling) or only by the leader (for strong consistency). If the leader fails, a follower is promoted via an election or a manual process. This model's advantage is simplicity: there is one writer, so there are no write-write conflicts, and all replicas converge to the leader's state. Its disadvantage is that the leader is a write bottleneck — every write must pass through it — and the leader is a single point of failure (mitigated by failover, but failover takes time). This is the model used by PostgreSQL streaming replication, MySQL replica sets, Kafka (per-partition leader), MongoDB replica sets, and Redis (in non-cluster mode).

Multi-leader replication allows multiple nodes to accept writes. Each leader processes writes locally and then propagates them to the other leaders and followers. The advantage is that writes scale horizontally and each leader can serve a geographic region with low latency (writes to the Europe leader do not cross the Atlantic to reach the US leader). The **cost** is the write-write conflict problem: two leaders can accept conflicting writes to the same row at the same time, and the system must resolve the conflict somehow. The standard resolutions are last-write-wins (LWW — the write with the highest timestamp wins, which loses one of the writes and depends on clocks being roughly synchronized), custom merge functions (application-defined logic for resolving specific field conflicts), or conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs — data structures mathematically designed to merge without conflicts, such as counters, sets, and sequences). This model is used by multi-datacenter databases (CouchDB, some Cassandra configurations), Google Docs-style collaborative editors, and systems that must stay writable during a network partition.

Leaderless replication (also called quorum-based) lets any replica accept writes and reads, and the client is responsible for contacting multiple replicas to ensure consistency. When a client writes, it sends the write to multiple replicas and waits for a quorum to acknowledge; when it reads, it queries multiple replicas and takes the version with the highest timestamp (or reconciles via version vectors). The consistency guarantee is R + W > N, where N is the number of replicas, W is the write quorum, and R is the read quorum. With N=3, W=2, R=2, every read is guaranteed to overlap every write at one replica. This model has no failover — any replica can go down without a leader election — and no write bottleneck, but it pushes complexity to the client and to conflict resolution. This is the model of Cassandra, DynamoDB (in its eventual-consistency mode), and Riak. The read path must reconcile conflicting versions (Dynamo uses vector clocks for this) or accept the version with the latest timestamp.

The three models trade off write scalability, conflict complexity, and availability. **Leader-follower**: simplest, no conflicts, but write bottleneck and leader SPOF. **Multi-leader**: write scalability and partition tolerance, but conflict resolution is now an application concern. **Leaderless**: maximum availability and no leader, but the client carries the quorum and reconciliation logic. The choice depends on the workload: a bank ledger uses leader-follower (consistency and simplicity matter more than write throughput); a global cache or a user profile store uses leaderless or multi-leader (availability and locality matter); a system that must remain writable during partitions uses multi-leader.

The interview-quality answer names all three models, describes the write path for each (leader accepts all writes / multiple leaders accept writes / client writes to a quorum), explains the trade-off (write bottleneck vs conflict resolution vs client complexity), and gives real examples (PostgreSQL leader-follower, CouchDB multi-leader, Cassandra leaderless). It also explains why replication happens in the first place (durability, availability, read scaling) and how replication lag and consistency guarantees depend on whether the replication is synchronous or asynchronous. That demonstrates you understand replication as a design space, not as a single feature.
bullets: Replication exists for durability (survive node loss), availability (serve during failures), and read scaling (parallel reads).
**Leader-follower**: all writes go to one leader, followers apply the log in order — simple, no conflicts, but the leader is a write bottleneck and a single point of failure (until failover).
**Multi-leader**: multiple nodes accept writes and propagate to each other — write scalability and locality, but requires write-write conflict resolution (LWW, merge functions, CRDTs).
**Leaderless**: any replica accepts writes and reads; the client contacts multiple replicas to ensure R + W > N — no leader, no failover, but client-side quorum and reconciliation logic.
**Real examples**: PostgreSQL/MySQL/MongoDB replica sets (leader-follower), CouchDB and multi-DC databases (multi-leader), Cassandra/DynamoDB/Riak (leaderless).
**The choice depends on workload**: consistency-first → leader-follower; write throughput + locality → multi-leader; partition tolerance + no leader → leaderless.
Replication lag (covered in the next card) is what makes the difference between synchronous and asynchronous replication visible to the application.

cards.title: Replication Lag and Read Consistency: Read-Your-Writes, Monotonic Reads, and Consistent Prefix
cards.summary:
**Replication lag** is the delay between a write being committed on the leader and being applied on a follower. It exists because most leader-follower systems use asynchronous replication: the leader acknowledges the write immediately, and followers catch up in the background. Under normal conditions lag is milliseconds, but under load, network slowness, a follower restart, or a follower that falls behind on a long-running transaction, lag can grow to seconds or minutes. The consequence is that reads served by a follower can return stale data — the client sees a state that does not include a write that already succeeded. This is not a bug; it is the direct consequence of asynchronous replication, and the application must design around it.

The most important read-consistency guarantees are the ones that describe what a single client (or a causally related group of clients) is guaranteed to see. Read-your-writes (also called read-after-write): after a client successfully writes a value, subsequent reads by the same client see that value or a later one. Without this guarantee, a user updates their profile, refreshes the page, and sees the old profile — the classic 'I just saved it, why is it gone?' bug. **The usual fixes are**: (1) route reads of data the client just wrote to the leader for a short window; (2) track the client's last write timestamp/version and wait until a replica has caught up past it; (3) read from the leader for a specific session (for example, a sticky session with a 'just modified' flag). The key insight is that this is a per-client guarantee — it does not require all replicas to be caught up, only that the client's own reads see its own writes.

**Monotonic reads**: if a client reads a value and then reads again, the second read does not go backwards in time. **The classic violation**: a client reads from a replica that is caught up to T=10, then reads from a different replica that is only caught up to T=5, and the value 'goes back' to an older state. The user experiences this as flickering or disappearing data. The fix is to bind a client to a single replica for the duration of a session, or to track the client's last-seen version and route reads to replicas that are at least that caught up. This is what 'sticky sessions' at the load balancer level provide, and what Cassandra's monotonic-read consistency level implies.

**Consistent prefix**: if a sequence of writes happens in some order, a reader sees those writes in the same order (even if not with the same timing). This matters most in systems where writes happen in a sequence — event logs, chat messages, social media posts — and the reader must not see message 3 before message 2. The fix is per-partition ordering (Kafka, Cassandra) or per-replica ordering guarantees, and it is the reason ordering is scoped to a partition or key rather than to the entire dataset.

These guarantees compose into causal consistency: the strongest consistency that is still available in a partitioned system without coordination. Causal consistency says that if a write happens before another (causally), all readers see them in that order; independent writes may be seen in any order. It gives read-your-writes, monotonic reads, and consistent prefix, all at once, and it does not require a global leader or a synchronous commit. This is why CouchDB, Cassandra (with some tuning), and MongoDB causal sessions offer it as a practical middle ground: stronger than eventual, weaker than linearizable, and achievable without paying the coordination cost of strong consistency.

The distributed-systems interview question is always the same: 'A user updates their data, refreshes, and sees the old value. How do you fix it without forcing all reads to the leader?' The answer is a per-client solution: track the write (a version, a timestamp, an LSN) and route or wait until the client's own read is guaranteed to see it. **Options include**: read-your-writes routing (write to the leader, read from the leader for a short window), a monotonic version check (send the version in a header and have the replica wait for it), or a client-side cache that holds the just-written value until the replica catches up. The worst answer is 'add more replicas' — that does not fix staleness, it increases the chance of hitting a stale one. The second-worst is 'switch to synchronous replication' — that works but is a sledgehammer that couples availability to replica health.

The interview-quality answer defines replication lag, names the three per-client guarantees (read-your-writes, monotonic reads, consistent prefix), explains causal consistency as the composition of all three, gives the concrete failure scenarios (update → refresh → see old; read replica A → read replica B → see older), and gives the concrete fixes (leader routing for own writes, version-based waiting, session binding). That demonstrates you understand replication as a consistency design space, not as a feature to turn on.
bullets: Replication lag is the delay between a write on the leader and its application on a follower — usually milliseconds, but grows under load, network slowness, or follower restart.
**Read-your-writes**: after a client writes, its subsequent reads see that value or later — violated by naive read-from-follower routing.
**Monotonic reads**: a client's second read does not go back in time — violated when switching between replicas at different catch-up points.
**Consistent prefix**: writes are seen in the order they occurred — matters for sequences, event logs, chat, feeds.
Causal consistency = all three at once; it is the strongest consistency achievable in a partitioned system without coordination, and is why CouchDB, MongoDB sessions, and tuned Cassandra offer it.

**Fixes for read-your-writes**: read from the leader for a short window after writes, track the last write version and wait for the replica to catch up, or bind the client to a single replica for its session.
**'Add more replicas' and 'switch to synchronous' are both wrong answers** — the first does not fix staleness, the second trades availability for consistency unnecessarily.

Read-your-writes violation

  t=0  client writes user.name = 'Alice' -> leader
  t=1  leader acknowledges
  t=2  client reads from follower
  t=3  follower hasn't applied the write yet -> returns 'old name'

  fix: route reads of own data to the leader for the next few seconds

Monotonic reads violation

  t=0  client reads from replica A (caught up to T=10) -> sees 'value V2'
  t=1  client reads from replica B (caught up to T=5)  -> sees 'value V1'

  fix: bind the client session to one replica, or
       track last-seen version and route to replicas >= that version

Consistent prefix violation

  t=0  write msg1
  t=1  write msg2
  t=2  write msg3
  t=3  reader sees msg1, msg3, msg2  (out of order across replicas)

  fix: single-partition ordering (Kafka, Cassandra clustering key)
       or read the whole log from one replica

Causal consistency (composition)

  write(a) -> write(b)    (b causally depends on a)
  all readers see a before b

  write(c)  write(d)      (independent)
  readers may see c-before-d or d-before-c

  offered by: CouchDB, Cassandra (with causal sessions),
              MongoDB causal sessions, Riak (with per-key)

Read routing strategies

  leader-only          strong but bottleneck
  follower round-robin may be stale
  session-bound        one replica per client -> monotonic
  version-aware        client sends last-seen version, replica
                       waits if behind
  leader-for-own-data  read leader for the client's own recent writes

cards.title: Partitioning and Sharding Strategies: Range, Hash, and Directory-Based
cards.summary:
**Partitioning** (also called sharding) splits a large dataset into smaller pieces that live on different machines. It is how a system scales beyond what a single machine can store or serve, and it is the mechanism that sits underneath every distributed database. There are two related but distinct concerns: how the data is divided into partitions, and how requests are routed to the right partition. Understanding the strategies for each, and the trade-offs between them, is what interviewers are probing when they ask 'how would you shard this?'

Range partitioning assigns each partition a contiguous range of the key space. Partition 1 holds keys A–F, partition 2 holds G–M, and so on. This is the model of a sorted index: range queries (WHERE `created_at` BETWEEN x AND y) hit only the partitions that overlap the range, which makes it efficient for time-series, logs, and any query that filters by a sorted field. **The cost is hotspots**: if the key is monotonically increasing (timestamps, auto-increment IDs, `ObjectIds`), all new writes go to the last partition while earlier partitions sit idle. The standard fixes are to shard by a compound key (region + timestamp) or to periodically rebalance, but neither fully eliminates the hotspot if the workload is genuinely time-ordered.

Hash partitioning applies a hash function to the key and uses the hash to decide the partition. The hash distributes keys uniformly across partitions, which eliminates hotspots for uniformly distributed keys. The cost is that range queries become scatter-gather — because a contiguous key range maps to a random set of partitions, a query for a range must hit every partition. This is why hash-sharded collections in MongoDB and hash-partitioned tables in Cassandra are good for equality lookups and write throughput but poor for range queries. Consistent hashing (covered in sys-hashing-1) is a refinement that makes adding and removing nodes cheaper: only ~1/N of keys move instead of almost all of them.

Directory-based partitioning maintains a lookup table that explicitly maps each key (or key range) to a partition. This is the most flexible model — you can move any key to any partition at any time by updating the directory, which is useful for tiered storage (hot data on fast shards, cold data on slow shards), for data residency (EU data on EU shards), and for rebalancing when a shard grows too large. The cost is that the directory is a central component: it must be highly available, it is on the critical path of every request (or must be aggressively cached), and it must stay consistent with the actual data placement. Directory-based partitioning is used by systems like HBase (via the .META. table), Bigtable, and custom sharding layers where the routing logic is application-defined.

A fourth strategy, sometimes called geo-partitioning or tag-based, partitions by an attribute rather than by the key's hash. For example, all rows with region='EU' go to the EU shard, all rows with region='US' go to the US shard, regardless of user ID. This is a special case of directory or range partitioning, and it is the standard answer for data residency and latency requirements — a query for an EU user never crosses the Atlantic to a US shard. The cost is that a single region's growth can outpace the others, so you need to be able to further shard within a region (a two-level scheme: region first, then hash or range within region).

**Request routing** is the second concern, and it is where most sharding implementations fail. The client needs to know which shard holds a given key. The three standard approaches are: (1) the client computes the shard from the key (hash or range function replicated on the client) — fast, but the sharding function is now part of the client's code, and changing it requires a coordinated rollout; (2) a routing tier (a proxy or gateway) computes the shard and forwards the request — simpler clients, but the routing tier is now on the critical path and must be highly available; (3) a coordination service (ZooKeeper, etcd, or the database's own config) that clients query for the shard map, with the map cached locally. Most production systems use a combination: a routing tier for external clients, client-side routing with a cached map for internal clients, and a coordination service to keep the map fresh.

The most important design constraint is the shard key. A good shard key has high cardinality (many distinct values), low frequency (no value dominates the data), and aligns with the query patterns (the queries must include the shard key to avoid scatter-gather). A bad shard key produces hotspots (monotonic keys), jumbo chunks (low cardinality), or scatter-gather queries (queries that do not include the key). This is the same lesson as the MongoDB sharding card, expressed at the distributed-systems level — sharding is not a database feature, it is a data-modeling decision, and the key is the whole design.

The interview-quality answer names the three strategies (range, hash, directory), explains what each is good for (range scans, uniform writes, flexible placement), calls out the hotspot and scatter-gather failure modes, describes the request-routing approaches (client-computed, routing tier, coordination service), and insists on the shard key as the design lever. It also references consistent hashing as a refinement rather than restating it — because that card exists. That demonstrates you understand partitioning as a layered design, not as a database flag.
bullets: Partitioning (sharding) splits a dataset across machines; the two design questions are how to divide the data and how to route requests.
**Range partitioning**: contiguous key ranges — great for range scans and time-series, but hotspots on monotonic keys.
**Hash partitioning**: hash the key to pick the partition — great for uniform write distribution and equality lookups, but range queries become scatter-gather.
**Directory-based partitioning**: a lookup table maps keys to partitions — most flexible (tiering, data residency, rebalancing), but the directory must be highly available and consistent.
**Geo/tag partitioning**: partition by an attribute (region, tenant) — good for data residency and latency, at the cost of unbalanced growth.

**Request routing options**: client-computed (fast, but the shard function is in client code), routing tier (proxy/gateway, on the critical path), coordination service (ZooKeeper/etcd, cached locally).
**The shard key is the whole design**: high cardinality, low frequency, aligned with query patterns — otherwise hotspots, jumbo chunks, or scatter-gather.
Consistent hashing (covered in sys-hashing-1) is a refinement that reduces key movement on scale in/out from `O(N)` to ~1/N.

Range partitioning

  P1: id 1..1M       P2: id 1M+1..2M     P3: id 2M+1..3M
  range scan:  WHERE id BETWEEN 1500000 AND 1800000  -> P2 only
  hotspot:    INSERT id = next  -> always P3

Hash partitioning

  partition = hash(key) % N     (or consistent hashing ring)
  equality:   WHERE key = 'abc' -> one partition
  range scan: WHERE key > 'm'   -> hits every partition (scatter-gather)
  hotspot:    none if keys are uniformly distributed

Directory-based partitioning

  partition_map = {
    'user:1..1000'   -> P1,
    'user:1001..5000'-> P2,
    'tenant:euro'    -> P3,
    'tenant:us'      -> P4
  }
  request -> lookup in map -> route to partition
  flexibility: can move any range to any partition (tiering, residency)
  cost: map must be HA + consistent with actual placement

Geo partitioning

  region='EU' -> EU shard
  region='US' -> US shard

  two-level scheme for scale:
    level 1: region
    level 2: hash(userId) within region

Request routing approaches

  client-computed
    partition = hash(key) % N       (or murmur2, or range lookup)
    + fast, no extra hop
    - sharding logic is part of client code, coordinated rollout

  routing tier
    client -> router -> shard
    + simple clients, logic centralized
    - router is on the critical path, must be HA

  coordination service
    client -> ZK/etcd -> shard map (cached locally)
    + flexible, single source of truth
    - extra hop on first lookup, cache invalidation complexity

Shard key decision tree

  Q: does the workload need range scans on the key?
     YES -> range partitioning, but watch for monotonic hotspots
     NO  -> hash partitioning

  Q: does the workload need data residency or tiering?
     YES -> directory / geo partitioning

  Q: what do queries filter on?
     if queries must include the shard key to avoid scatter-gather
     -> pick a key that the application can always provide

  Q: how uniform is the natural key?
     skewed -> salt (append hash suffix) or use a compound key

cards.title: Consistency Models: Linearizable, Sequential, Causal, Eventual, and What Each Guarantees
cards.summary:
A **consistency model** is a contract between the distributed system and the client about what values reads will observe. It is not a performance metric and not a binary choice — it is a spectrum from strongest (linearizable) to weakest (eventual), with several useful intermediate models. Every interview about distributed systems eventually lands here, because the choice of consistency model determines what the system can and cannot guarantee, and therefore what the application must handle.

Linearizable (also called strict or atomic) consistency is the strongest model. It says that the system behaves as if there is a single copy of the data, and every operation appears to take effect atomically at some point between its invocation and its response. If client A writes X=1 and receives an acknowledgment, and client B reads X afterward, B must see X=1 (or a later value). No client ever sees a value that is older than one already acknowledged to another client. **Linearizability is expensive**: it requires coordination (consensus or a single leader) on every operation, and it is what CAP-theorem 'CP' systems promise during a partition (they refuse operations rather than violate linearizability). PostgreSQL with synchronous replication, etcd, ZooKeeper, and Google Spanner offer linearizable reads and writes.

Sequential consistency is slightly weaker. It says that operations appear to execute in some total order that is consistent with the order each client issued them, but that total order does not need to match real time across clients. Two clients can disagree about whether A's write or B's write happened first, as long as each client's own operations appear in the order they issued them. This is the model that multiprocessor memory often provides, and it is the model of systems that assign a global sequence number but do not require the sequence to respect wall-clock ordering. It is rarely what application developers actually want, because it does not guarantee real-time ordering.

**Causal consistency** is the strongest model that is still available in a partitioned system without coordination. It says that operations that are causally related (one happened-before another through the client's observation or through message passing) must be seen by all clients in that order, and operations that are concurrent (no causal relationship) may be seen in any order. This captures the intuitively important guarantees: you cannot see a reply before the message it replies to, you cannot see a delete before the insert that made the record exist, you cannot see an update before the read that produced it. Causal consistency gives read-your-writes, monotonic reads, and consistent prefix (from the replication lag card), all at once. It is achievable with vector clocks or dependency tracking, without the coordination cost of linearizability. CouchDB, MongoDB causal sessions, and Cassandra's lightweight transactions (via Paxos) with proper configuration approach it.

**Eventual consistency** is the weakest model. It says only that if no new writes occur, all replicas eventually converge to the same value. It says nothing about when, and nothing about what a client sees in the meantime. Eventual consistency is what you get from asynchronous replication with no ordering guarantees, and it is what most large-scale systems actually provide for non-critical data (social feeds, view counts, recommendations). It is not a defect — it is a deliberate choice to prioritize availability and latency over immediate agreement. The interview trap is to call it 'weak' dismissively; the correct answer acknowledges that it is the only model you can have at scale without coordination, and that most data does not need anything stronger.

The models form a hierarchy of guarantees, and each stronger level implies all weaker ones. Linearizable implies sequential, causal, and eventual. Sequential implies eventual (but does not necessarily imply causal in all formalizations). Causal implies eventual. **The practical decision is**: what does the application need to see? If the answer is 'the latest value, always,' you need linearizable and you will pay for it in latency and availability during partitions. If the answer is 'my own writes, and never going backwards,' causal consistency is enough and much cheaper. If the answer is 'eventually correct is fine for this data,' eventual consistency is the right choice and is the only one that scales without coordination. Naming the data per model — critical financial data needs linearizable, user-facing profile reads need causal, view counts and feeds can be eventual — is what separates a strong answer.

The interview-quality answer names the four models with the intuitive guarantee each provides (real-time single-copy for linearizable; total order per client for sequential; happens-before preserved for causal; eventual convergence for eventual), states the strictness hierarchy, ties each to a real system (Spanner/etcd for linearizable, MongoDB sessions for causal, Cassandra/Dynamo for eventual), and emphasizes that the choice is per-data not per-system. It also connects to CAP and PACELC — linearizable is what CP systems promise, eventual is what AP systems offer, and PACELC describes the latency-vs-consistency trade-off when there is no partition. That demonstrates you understand consistency as a design decision, not a label.
bullets: **Consistency models form a hierarchy**: linearizable ⊃ sequential ⊃ causal ⊃ eventual — stronger implies weaker.

**Linearizable**: behaves like a single copy of the data; every operation appears atomic and respects real time; requires coordination; offered by Spanner, etcd, ZooKeeper, PostgreSQL sync replication.
**Sequential**: a global total order consistent with each client's own operation order, but not necessarily with real time — rarely what applications want.

**Causal**: causally related operations are seen in order, concurrent ones may be seen in any order; gives read-your-writes, monotonic reads, and consistent prefix; achievable without coordination (vector clocks or dependency tracking).
**Eventual**: without new writes, replicas eventually converge — says nothing about timing or intermediate states; the only model that scales without coordination.
**The choice is per-data, not per-system**: financial data → linearizable; user-facing reads and session state → causal; view counts, feeds, recommendations → eventual.
CAP: linearizable is what 'CP' systems promise during partitions; eventual is what 'AP' systems offer. PACELC describes the latency-vs-consistency trade-off even without partitions.
