# Blue/Green: Blue (100% live) | Green (idle/tested) -> switch router
# Canary:     v1 (95% traffic) + v2 (5% traffic) -> monitor -> 100% v2
# Shadow:     v1 (100% user response) + v2 (async mirrored copy)

interview.q: How do blue/green and canary deployments differ in risk, cost, and rollback?
interview.a: Blue/green switches traffic between two full environments, giving fast rollback by flipping traffic back, but it costs extra for duplicate capacity during release. Canary ramps traffic gradually to a small slice first, limiting blast radius with lower extra capacity than a full duplicate stack. For example, high-risk payment changes often start as a canary or behind a feature flag.

interview.q: Why use a feature flag when you already have a deployment pipeline?
interview.a: Deployment puts new code onto servers, whereas a feature flag controls whether users actually hit that code path. If a new feature causes high latency or bugs, flipping the flag off disables it immediately without waiting for a full deployment or rollback. Over time, stale flags must be cleaned up to avoid code clutter.

cards.title: Infrastructure as Code: Terraform Plan, State, Drift, and Locking
cards.summary:
Clicking through a cloud console to create VPCs, databases, and queues leaves no audit trail and leads to snowflake environments that drift apart. **Infrastructure as Code** (**IaC**) defines cloud resources in version-controlled files so environments are repeatable, reviewable in pull requests, and automated in pipelines.

**Declarative** IaC (like Terraform) describes the desired end state and lets the tool figure out what to create, update, or destroy, whereas **imperative** scripts list step-by-step commands to run. Running `terraform plan` previews proposed changes against the current **state file**—which maps declared resources to real cloud IDs—and `terraform apply` executes them.

**Drift** happens when someone changes a cloud resource manually outside Terraform, causing reality to diverge from state and config. **State locking** prevents two pipelines or engineers from modifying the state file at the same time and corrupting it, while **modules** package reusable resource patterns across services.

Store Terraform state remotely in shared, access-controlled storage with locking enabled rather than on a single laptop, because state files can also contain sensitive attributes. Also watch for destructive replacements when changing immutable fields—always read `terraform plan` carefully before applying.
bullets: **Infrastructure as Code** keeps cloud setup versioned, peer-reviewed, and consistent across environments.
**Declarative** tools like Terraform target a desired state, unlike **imperative** scripts that spell out every step.
`terraform plan` previews changes and `terraform apply` updates infrastructure using the **state file**.
**State locking** stops concurrent applies from corrupting state, and **modules** standardize repeatable infrastructure.

glossary.meaning: Specifying desired end state while the engine computes required changes.
Record tracking real cloud resources mapped to declared configuration.
Difference between actual cloud resource settings and expected IaC state.
Concurrency guard preventing simultaneous writes to the Terraform state.

cards.code:
# Standard Terraform workflow: format, validate, preview plan, and apply
terraform fmt -check
terraform validate
terraform plan -out=tfplan
terraform apply tfplan

interview.q: Why does Terraform maintain a state file, and what happens without state locking in CI?
interview.a: The state file tracks metadata and real cloud IDs corresponding to your configuration so Terraform knows what exists, what changed, and what to destroy. Without state locking, two concurrent CI runs could modify state at once and corrupt it or race on resource updates. Remote state with locking prevents simultaneous writes.

interview.q: What is configuration drift, and how do you handle it?
interview.a: Drift occurs when a resource is modified manually in the cloud console or via another tool outside Terraform. Running `terraform plan` surfaces the difference between actual state and desired code. You either reconcile the drift in Terraform code or revert the manual change so environments stay consistent.

cards.title: Rollback and Database Migrations: Code vs Data and Expand-Contract
cards.summary:
Rolling back stateless application code is usually straightforward—redeploy the previous image or shift traffic back—but rolling back **database changes** is much trickier. If a migration drops a column or rewrites existing rows and live traffic already wrote new data, simply reverting the schema can lose data or break running queries.

To keep code and schema compatible during rollouts and rollbacks, use **expand-and-contract** (parallel change) migrations. First, **expand** by adding a new nullable column or new table while keeping the old one working; deploy code that writes to both or reads safely; backfill data in batches; and only later **contract** by removing old columns after the new version is proven.

Keep migrations **backward-compatible** so both the old and new application versions can run against the same schema during transitions. Pair rollouts with **automated rollback signals**—such as spikes in HTTP `5xx` errors, latency breaches, or failed health checks—so unhealthy releases revert quickly without waiting for manual detection.

Destructive SQL operations—like `ALTER TABLE` locking large tables or dropping columns—can block queries or break rollbacks if run mid-traffic. In many production setups, teams prefer moving forward with a hotfix or feature-flag disable when data already changed, while keeping schema changes additive until safe to contract.
bullets: Rolling back application code is often quick, whereas reverting destructive database changes can lose live data.
**Expand-and-contract** stages schema changes across releases so old and new code stay compatible during rollouts.
Avoid dropping columns or renaming fields in lockstep with a single big-bang code release.
**Automated rollback signals** like elevated error rates help detect bad releases and revert faster.

glossary.meaning: Gradual schema migration adding new structures before retiring old ones.
Schema or API change that existing older code can still read and write.
Automated telemetry trigger like error spikes or failed checks initiating revert.

interview.q: Why is rolling back a database migration harder than rolling back application code?
interview.a: Application code is stateless once redeployed, but a database holds persistent state written by live traffic. Dropping a column or transforming data irreversibly means a rollback can fail or lose recent writes. Using expand-and-contract migrations keeps old and new code compatible across deployments so you can revert code safely.

interview.q: Walk through how you safely rename a database column with zero downtime.
interview.a: First expand by adding the new column while keeping the old one intact. Deploy code that writes to both columns and backfills existing rows in small batches, then switch reads to the new column. Once verified in production without rollback risk, contract by removing the old column in a later release.

cards.title: GitOps: Pull-Based Reconciliation, Drift Control, and Secrets
cards.summary:
**GitOps** treats a Git repository as the single **source of truth** for declarative cluster and environment state. Instead of a CI pipeline pushing credentials and `kubectl` or deployment commands directly into production clusters, a **pull-based** controller inside the cluster—such as **ArgoCD** or **Flux**—watches Git and reconciles live cluster state to match what is declared in Git.

This pull model reduces blast radius because the cluster does not expose inbound deployment credentials to external CI runners, and every change has a clear Git commit history and audit trail. Controllers continuously perform **drift detection**: if someone manually edits a live resource in the cluster, the controller flags or overwrites it back to the Git state.

Environment **promotion** typically moves a tested image tag or digest from `dev` to `staging` to `prod` via pull requests or automated manifest updates in Git. Never commit plaintext secrets to Git; instead use encrypted secret management (such as sealed secrets or an external secret store synced at runtime) so Git remains safe to read while real secrets stay protected.

A subtle GitOps pitfall is mutating tags like `latest` in Git: if the Git manifest does not change, the controller may not know a new image was pushed unless configured to watch digests or update pinned versions on each build. Also make sure controllers do not fight external autoscalers or controllers over the same live fields—ignore dynamically managed fields properly.
bullets: **GitOps** uses Git as the declarative source of truth with an in-cluster controller pulling changes rather than CI pushing.
Tools like **ArgoCD** and **Flux** run continuous reconciliation loops and handle **drift detection** automatically.
Promoting across environments via Git pull requests gives clear review, history, and easy Git-based rollbacks.
Keep plaintext secrets out of Git by using encrypted manifests or external secret stores injected at runtime.

glossary.meaning: Operating declarative infrastructure and apps using Git as the source of truth.
Controller cycle comparing live cluster state to Git and converging differences.
Detecting and optionally reverting out-of-band changes made outside Git.
Advancing a verified release configuration across environments like dev, staging, and prod.

cards.code:
# Pull-based GitOps flow (ArgoCD / Flux style)
# 1. CI builds image & pushes immutable tag/digest to registry
# 2. CI or PR updates manifest/tag in Git (e.g., staging -> prod)
# 3. In-cluster controller pulls Git change & reconciles live state
# 4. Controller detects manual cluster edits (drift) and converges back

interview.q: How does a GitOps pull model differ from traditional push-based CI/CD deployments?
interview.a: In push-based CI/CD, the pipeline holds cluster credentials and pushes changes outward into environments. In GitOps, CI builds the artifact and updates Git, while an in-cluster controller like ArgoCD or Flux pulls from Git and reconciles cluster state. Pulling keeps deployment credentials inside the cluster perimeter and gives continuous drift detection.

interview.q: How do you handle secrets safely in a GitOps workflow?
interview.a: Never store plaintext secrets in Git repositories, even in private repos. Instead, store encrypted secrets in Git or reference an external secret manager that syncs secrets into the cluster at runtime. That keeps Git auditable and declarative without exposing raw credentials.

cards.title: Cloud and AWS Basics: Regions, AZs, Edge, and Shared Responsibility
cards.summary:
Think of electricity from a power grid rather than buying your own diesel generator before turning on a lamp. Instead of racking servers in your own data center upfront, **cloud computing** lets you rent compute, storage, and networking over the internet and pay only for what you use.

**AWS** organizes its global network into **regions**—separate geographic areas such as `ap-south-1` (Mumbai)—each containing multiple isolated **Availability Zones** (**AZs**), which are physically separated data centers with independent power, cooling, and networking. Placing instances across multiple AZs protects an app if one facility has an outage, while **edge locations** cache content closer to users to lower latency.

Under the **shared responsibility model**, AWS secures the cloud hardware, facilities, and underlying infrastructure, while you secure what you put in the cloud—such as your code, data, and access settings. **Managed** services let AWS handle patching and scaling of the underlying engine, whereas **self-managed** compute gives you more control over the OS and software at the cost of extra maintenance.
bullets: AWS **regions** split global locations, and each contains multiple **Availability Zones** for fault isolation.
**Edge locations** sit closer to end users worldwide to speed up content delivery and lower latency.
The **shared responsibility model** splits duties: AWS secures underlying infrastructure while you secure your data and config.
**Managed** services reduce operational toil, while **self-managed** setups offer deeper control with higher maintenance effort.

glossary.meaning: Geographic AWS location containing multiple isolated Availability Zones.
One or more data centers within a region with independent power and network.
Division of security duties between AWS and the customer.
Cloud service where AWS handles underlying infrastructure patching and operations.

cards.code:
# AWS global layout mental model
# Region (e.g., ap-south-1) -> AZ-1, AZ-2, AZ-3 (isolated power/network)
# Edge locations -> global caching points near users

# Check current AWS CLI identity and configured region
aws sts get-caller-identity
aws configure get region

interview.q: Why do teams deploy across multiple Availability Zones inside one AWS region?
interview.a: Availability Zones are physically separated with independent power and network paths, so spreading instances across AZs protects an application if one data center experiences a failure. Keeping resources in one region also avoids high cross-region latency and data residency issues. A single AZ is a single point of failure for that workload.

interview.q: What does the shared responsibility model mean for a backend engineer deploying on AWS?
interview.a: AWS is responsible for security of the cloud—physical data centers, hardware, and core infrastructure—while you are responsible for security in the cloud, including IAM permissions, network rules, encryption choices, and app code. Even on managed services, you still control access and data protection. Misconfigured permissions remain a top cause of incidents.

cards.title: IAM: Users, Roles, Least Privilege, and Service Credentials
cards.summary:
Imagine handing out a master key to every room in an office when a contractor only needs to open one storage cabinet. **AWS Identity and Access Management** (**IAM**) controls who can authenticate to AWS and what actions they are allowed to perform on which resources.

An **IAM user** represents a human or legacy credential with long-term keys, while an **IAM role** provides temporary credentials assumed by trusted entities such as an EC2 instance, Lambda function, or federated user. **IAM policies** are JSON documents containing statements with an `Effect` (`Allow` or `Deny`), `Action` (like `s3:GetObject`), and `Resource` (like a specific bucket ARN).

Follow **least privilege** by granting only the exact permissions needed for a task, and attach **IAM roles** to compute workloads instead of hard-coding access keys in code or environment files. By default, access is denied unless explicitly allowed, and an explicit `Deny` overrides any `Allow`. A common mistake is using wildcard `*` permissions or committing long-lived keys to Git.
bullets: **IAM roles** supply temporary credentials to AWS services, avoiding hard-coded long-term access keys in code.
**IAM policies** evaluate permissions using default deny, explicit `Allow`, and explicit `Deny` taking precedence.
**Least privilege** scopes actions and resources tightly rather than granting broad `*` wildcards.
Never store static AWS access keys in source repositories or share the AWS root account for daily work.

glossary.meaning: Identity issuing short-lived credentials assumed by services or trusted callers.
JSON permission document specifying allowed or denied actions on resources.
Granting only the minimal permissions required to complete a job.

interview.q: Why should a service running on AWS use an IAM role instead of hard-coded IAM user access keys?
interview.a: An IAM role issues short-lived credentials that rotate automatically without storing static secrets inside code, config files, or container images. Hard-coded keys can leak in repositories or logs and stay valid until manually revoked. Roles make access safer and easier to audit.

interview.q: How does IAM decide whether a request is allowed when policies conflict?
interview.a: IAM starts with a default deny; an explicit `Allow` is needed to permit an action, and any explicit `Deny` overrides all allows. This means a broad `Allow` on `*` still loses if a matching explicit `Deny` applies. Always check both identity and resource policies when debugging access errors.

cards.title: S3: Buckets, Objects, Storage Classes, Versioning, and Presigned URLs
cards.summary:
Think of **Amazon S3** as a giant, durable cloud filing cabinet where every file is stored as an **object** inside a **bucket**. Each object holds data plus metadata and a unique key name within its bucket, and S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for object operations.

S3 offers multiple **storage classes**—such as `STANDARD` for frequent access, `STANDARD_IA` for infrequent access, and Glacier classes for archival—so you can match storage cost to access patterns. **Lifecycle rules** can automatically transition older objects to cheaper tiers or expire temporary files after a set number of days.

Enabling **versioning** keeps multiple variants of an object under the same key, protecting against accidental overwrites or deletes. To let a user upload or download a private file directly without giving them AWS credentials or making the bucket public, your backend can issue a time-limited **presigned URL**. Leaving buckets public or turning off Block Public Access is a frequent security pitfall.
bullets: S3 stores files as **objects** inside **buckets** and provides strong read-after-write consistency.
**Storage classes** and **lifecycle rules** lower cost by moving cold data to cheaper tiers or expiring old objects.
**Versioning** preserves previous object versions to help recover from accidental overwrites or deletions.
**Presigned URLs** grant temporary, scoped access to private objects without exposing AWS credentials or public buckets.

glossary.meaning: Top-level S3 container namespace holding stored objects.
File payload, metadata, and key stored inside an S3 bucket.
Time-limited signed link granting temporary access to a specific S3 object.
Automated policy transitioning or expiring S3 objects over time.

cards.code:
# List buckets, upload an object, and generate a 15-minute presigned download URL
aws s3 ls
aws s3 cp report.pdf s3://my-app-docs-bucket/reports/report.pdf
aws s3 presign s3://my-app-docs-bucket/reports/report.pdf --expires-in 900

interview.q: How can a mobile or web client upload a large file to a private S3 bucket without routing bytes through your backend?
interview.a: Your backend authenticates the user, checks authorization, and generates a short-lived S3 presigned upload URL scoped to a specific object key. The client uploads directly to S3 using that URL, saving backend bandwidth and compute. Presigned URLs remain valid until expiration, so keep lifetimes short.

interview.q: What does S3 versioning protect you against, and what cost trade-off does it bring?
interview.a: Versioning keeps prior versions when an object is overwritten or deleted, letting you restore earlier versions instead of losing data permanently. The trade-off is paying storage costs for retained versions and delete markers unless lifecycle rules clean up old versions. Deleting a specific version ID removes it permanently.

cards.title: VPC: Subnets, Route Tables, Gateways, Security Groups, and NACLs
cards.summary:
A **Virtual Private Cloud** (**VPC**) is your isolated virtual network inside AWS where you define IP address ranges, subnets, and routing rules. **Subnets** slice a VPC's CIDR block across Availability Zones: a **public subnet** has a route to an **Internet Gateway** (`igw`) so resources with public IPs can reach the internet directly, while a **private subnet** has no direct route to the internet gateway.

**Route tables** control where network traffic goes based on destination IP prefixes. To let instances in a private subnet reach external APIs or package repositories without exposing them to inbound internet traffic, route outbound traffic through a **NAT Gateway** placed in a public subnet.

**Security groups** are **stateful** firewalls attached to elastic network interfaces—if you allow inbound port `443`, return traffic is allowed automatically—whereas **Network ACLs** (**NACLs**) are **stateless** subnet-level rules that evaluate inbound and outbound traffic separately and support explicit `ALLOW` and `DENY` rules. A request to a private app instance typically enters via a public load balancer, crosses route tables to the private subnet, and passes security groups on both tiers.

NAT Gateways are deployed in a specific Availability Zone and incur hourly plus per-gigabyte processing charges, plus cross-AZ data transfer costs if private instances in another AZ route through it. For high availability across AZs, place a NAT Gateway in each AZ used by private workloads.
bullets: **Public subnets** route to an **Internet Gateway**, while **private subnets** keep instances off direct inbound internet paths.
A **NAT Gateway** lets private-subnet resources reach external endpoints outbound without giving them public IPs.
**Security groups** are stateful and allow-only, whereas **NACLs** are stateless per subnet and support explicit denies.
Traffic to a private backend typically hits a public load balancer first, then routes into a private subnet.

glossary.meaning: Subnet whose route table routes outbound internet traffic to an Internet Gateway.
Managed service enabling private-subnet instances to make outbound internet requests.
Stateful instance-level firewall controlling allowed inbound and outbound traffic.
Stateless subnet-level rule list evaluating inbound and outbound traffic separately.

cards.code:
# Typical request flow into a private backend instance
# Client -> Internet -> IGW -> Public Subnet (ALB)
#        -> Private Subnet (App EC2/ECS) -> Private Subnet (RDS)
# Outbound from Private App to external API -> NAT Gateway (in Public Subnet)

interview.q: What is the practical difference between a security group and a network ACL?
interview.a: Security groups are stateful and attached to instances or network interfaces, automatically permitting return traffic for allowed connections and supporting allow rules only. NACLs operate at the subnet level, are stateless—requiring explicit rules for both inbound and outbound traffic—and support `DENY` rules. Most teams rely primarily on security groups and use NACLs sparingly.

interview.q: How does a service in a private subnet download updates or call an external API securely?
interview.a: Its subnet route table sends `0.0.0.0/0` traffic to a NAT Gateway located in a public subnet, which translates the request and sends it out through the Internet Gateway. Because the instance has no public IP and no direct inbound route from the IGW, external hosts cannot initiate connections to it.

cards.title: EC2 and Auto Scaling: Instance Types, Pricing, ASGs, and Health Checks
cards.summary:
**Amazon EC2** provides resizable virtual servers launched from an **Amazon Machine Image** (**AMI**), which packages the OS and preinstalled software. **Instance families and sizes** balance vCPU, memory, network bandwidth, and local storage for compute-heavy, memory-heavy, or general-purpose backend workloads.

Pricing models trade discount against commitment or preemption risk: **On-Demand** charges per-second/hour with no commitment, **Spot** offers steep discounts on spare capacity that AWS can reclaim with a brief warning, and **Reserved / Savings Plans** lower unit cost in exchange for a 1-year or 3-year commitment on steady baseline usage.

An **Auto Scaling Group** (**ASG**) maintains a desired number of EC2 instances across subnets and scales out or in based on metrics or schedules. Paired with a load balancer, the ASG replaces unhealthy instances detected by **health checks**, though instances need graceful shutdown handling and enough warmup time so traffic does not hit unready apps.

When an ASG scales in or replaces an instance behind a load balancer, connection draining lets in-flight requests finish before terminating the instance. For Spot Instances, handle interruption notices cleanly by checkpointing work or draining traffic rather than holding long-running stateful connections on Spot alone.
bullets: Pick EC2 instance types to match workload CPU, memory, and I/O needs, launching from a curated **AMI**.
Use **On-Demand** for spiky or unpredictable workloads, commitments for steady baseline load, and **Spot** for fault-tolerant tasks.
An **Auto Scaling Group** scales capacity automatically and replaces instances that fail **health checks**.
Integrate ASGs with a load balancer and configure sensible health-check grace periods so startup does not trigger false kills.

glossary.meaning: Template image containing OS and software used to launch EC2 instances.
Discounted spare EC2 capacity that can be reclaimed by AWS on short notice.
EC2 group that automatically adjusts instance count to match demand and health.
Probe verifying whether an instance or target is healthy and ready for traffic.

cards.code:
# Inspect running EC2 instances and Auto Scaling groups
aws ec2 describe-instances \
  --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].{Id:InstanceId,Type:InstanceType,State:State.Name,AZ:Placement.AvailabilityZone}' \
  --output table

aws autoscaling describe-auto-scaling-groups \
  --query 'AutoScalingGroups[].{Name:AutoScalingGroupName,Min:MinSize,Desired:DesiredCapacity,Max:MaxSize}' \
  --output table

interview.q: How do On-Demand, Reserved/Savings Plans, and Spot differ when sizing EC2 capacity?
interview.a: On-Demand has no commitment and highest unit price, fitting variable or short-lived workloads. Savings Plans or Reserved Instances give lower rates for steady baseline capacity over one or three years. Spot offers big discounts on spare capacity but can be interrupted, making it great for stateless workers, batch jobs, or mixed ASG fleets rather than single-instance stateful nodes.

interview.q: Why can aggressive health checks cause trouble during Auto Scaling scale-out events?
interview.a: If a Java or backend app takes 30 seconds to boot and warm up, a health check that marks instances unhealthy too quickly can cause the ASG to terminate and replace them in a loop. Setting an appropriate health-check grace period and readiness path prevents premature replacement during normal startup.

cards.title: SQS: Queues, Visibility Timeout, DLQs, and Idempotent Consumers
cards.summary:
**Amazon SQS** is a managed message queue that decouples producers from consumers so traffic spikes buffer smoothly instead of overwhelming downstream workers. When a consumer reads a message, SQS hides it from other consumers for a **visibility timeout**; if the consumer finishes and deletes the message in time, it is removed, but if the consumer crashes or takes too long, the message becomes visible again for retry.

**Standard queues** offer high throughput and best-effort ordering with **at-least-once delivery**, meaning a message can occasionally be delivered more than once. **FIFO queues** preserve strict message ordering within a message group and provide **exactly-once processing** deduplication windows at lower throughput limits.

Messages that repeatedly fail processing can be routed to a **dead-letter queue** (**DLQ**) after a `maxReceiveCount` threshold so poison-pill messages do not block healthy traffic and can be inspected later. Because at-least-once delivery can send duplicates, consumers must be **idempotent**—processing the same event twice produces the same side effect without duplicate charges or double writes.

If a consumer takes 45 seconds to process a job and the visibility timeout is 30 seconds, SQS makes the message visible to another worker at second 30—causing duplicate concurrent work and potentially deleting the wrong receipt handle later. Tune visibility timeout to exceed worst-case processing time plus retry buffer, or heartbeat visibility extensions for long tasks.
bullets: SQS decouples producers and consumers, absorbing bursts without forcing synchronous coupling.
Set **visibility timeout** longer than expected processing time—or extend it—so slow jobs are not re-delivered mid-flight.
Route repeated failures to a **dead-letter queue** so bad messages do not loop infinitely and can be triaged.
Design consumers to be **idempotent** because **at-least-once delivery** can deliver duplicate messages.

glossary.meaning: Duration a leased SQS message stays hidden from other consumers while being processed.
Queue receiving messages that fail processing repeatedly after max retries.
Guarantee that a message arrives, with possible duplicate deliveries on retry.
Consumer safely handling duplicate messages without repeating harmful side effects.

cards.code:
# Create a standard SQS queue and inspect its attributes
aws sqs create-queue --queue-name orders-fulfillment-queue \
  --attributes VisibilityTimeout=60,MessageRetentionPeriod=345600

aws sqs get-queue-attributes \
  --queue-url "$(aws sqs get-queue-url --queue-name orders-fulfillment-queue --query QueueUrl --output text)" \
  --attribute-names All

interview.q: What happens if an SQS consumer's visibility timeout is shorter than the time it takes to process a message?
interview.a: SQS makes the message visible again while the first consumer is still working on it, so another consumer can pick up and process the same message concurrently. That causes duplicate work and can fail when the first worker tries to delete an expired receipt handle. Increase the visibility timeout or extend it while processing.

interview.q: Why must SQS consumers be idempotent even when using retries and DLQs?
interview.a: Standard SQS uses at-least-once delivery, and network timeouts or consumer crashes after completing work can cause a message to be redelivered. An idempotent consumer checks a deduplication key or uses conditional writes so replaying the event does not charge a card twice or insert duplicate orders.

cards.title: SNS: Topics, Push Subscribers, Filtering, and SQS Comparison
cards.summary:
**Amazon SNS** is a managed publish-subscribe (**pub/sub**) messaging service. A publisher sends a message once to an **SNS topic**, and SNS **pushes** that notification out to subscribed endpoints—such as SQS queues, Lambda functions, HTTP/HTTPS webhooks, SMS, or email.

**Message filtering** lets subscribers attach a JSON filter policy so a consumer only receives events matching specific attributes—for example, `order_status: ["PAID"]`—saving downstream processing and unnecessary invocations. SNS supports delivery retries and dead-letter targets for failed webhook or push deliveries, though it does not act as a durable pull buffer for slow consumers the way a queue does.

Compared with **SQS**, SQS is a pull-based point-to-point queue where consumers poll and delete messages at their own pace, whereas SNS is a push-based broadcast topic that delivers to multiple subscribers. When you want durable per-consumer buffering alongside pub/sub fan-out, pairing SNS with SQS gives you both.

When SNS pushes directly to a synchronous consumer like a Lambda function or HTTP endpoint, sudden traffic spikes fan out immediately to all subscribers. If a downstream service has tight concurrency or rate limits, placing an SQS queue between SNS and that consumer smooths burst load.
bullets: SNS uses a **push model** to broadcast messages from a **topic** to one or more subscribers.
**Message filtering** routes only relevant events to each subscriber, reducing noise and downstream work.
Unlike SQS, SNS does not hold messages for a consumer to poll on demand; consumers receive pushed deliveries.
Combine SNS with SQS when subscribers need independent durable queues, retries, and DLQs.

glossary.meaning: Named SNS pub/sub channel receiving published messages and forwarding to subscribers.
Subscription rule delivering only messages matching specified attribute criteria.
Delivery style where the broker pushes messages to subscribers rather than waiting for polls.

cards.code:
# Create an SNS topic and publish a message with a filterable attribute
TOPIC_ARN=$(aws sns create-topic --name order-events --query TopicArn --output text)

aws sns publish \
  --topic-arn "$TOPIC_ARN" \
  --message '{"orderId":"ord-101","status":"PAID"}' \
  --message-attributes '{"event_type":{"DataType":"String","StringValue":"ORDER_PAID"}}'

interview.q: When would you choose SNS over SQS, and when do you use both together?
interview.a: Choose SNS when one producer needs to broadcast an event to multiple independent subscribers via push, and SQS when a single consumer pool needs a durable queue to pull and buffer tasks at its own speed. Use SNS-to-SQS together when multiple downstream services each need their own durable queue and retry isolation from the same event.

interview.q: How does SNS message filtering help in an event-driven architecture?
interview.a: Subscribers define filter policies on message attributes so SNS only delivers matching events to that subscription. Downstream services do not have to wake up and discard irrelevant events. That lowers invocation costs and keeps consumer logic focused.

cards.title: SNS to SQS Fan-Out: Failure Isolation and Kafka Comparison
cards.summary:
Suppose placing an order should trigger billing, inventory reservation, analytics, and email notifications. If the order service calls all four services directly over HTTP, one slow or failing service can delay or break checkout, and adding a fifth consumer requires changing producer code.

The **SNS-to-SQS fan-out** pattern solves this: the producer publishes one event to an SNS topic, and each downstream service subscribes its own **SQS queue** to that topic. Each consumer pulls from its own queue independently, so if the email worker goes down or backs up, billing and inventory continue processing without impact, and each queue can have its own visibility timeout and DLQ.

How does this compare to **Kafka consumer groups**? In Kafka, multiple consumer groups can independently read the same topic stream with replayable offset logs and high-throughput partitioning, whereas SNS-to-SQS uses AWS managed push-to-queue delivery with per-queue DLQs and no multi-day stream replay log. Pick SNS-to-SQS for straightforward cloud event fan-out with per-queue retries; pick Kafka when you need log replay, partitioned stream ordering, or heavy streaming analytics.

Remember to attach an SNS topic policy allowing the SNS service principal to `sqs:SendMessage` to each subscribed SQS queue, and enable `RawMessageDelivery` if consumers expect the raw message body rather than the outer SNS envelope JSON.
bullets: **SNS-to-SQS fan-out** lets one published event feed separate queues for independent downstream consumers.
Per-consumer queues provide **failure isolation** and independent retry or DLQ settings without changing the producer.
Unlike Kafka consumer groups over a retained log, SNS-to-SQS delivers events forward to queues without stream offset replay.
Use SNS-to-SQS for decoupled AWS event fan-out; use Kafka when stream replay or partitioned log processing is key.

glossary.meaning: Delivering one published event to multiple independent downstream queues or consumers.
Preventing a slowdown or outage in one consumer from blocking others.
Kafka concept where independent groups read a topic stream with separate offsets.

cards.code:
# SNS -> SQS fan-out topology
# Order Service -> [SNS: orders-topic]
#                   |--(sub)--> [SQS: billing-q]   -> Billing Worker
#                   |--(sub)--> [SQS: inventory-q]-> Inventory Worker
#                   |--(sub)--> [SQS: notify-q]   -> Notification Worker

interview.q: Why is SNS-to-SQS fan-out better than having an order service call three downstream APIs synchronously?
interview.a: Synchronous calls couple checkout latency and availability to every downstream dependency—if one service times out, order creation can fail or stall. Fan-out via SNS and per-consumer SQS queues decouples them so each consumer processes at its own pace with independent retries and DLQs. The trade-off is eventual consistency rather than an immediate synchronous response from downstream workers.

interview.q: How does SNS-to-SQS fan-out compare with Apache Kafka consumer groups?
interview.a: Both let multiple independent consumers react to the same event stream, but Kafka retains an append-only partitioned log where consumer groups track offsets and can replay historical events. SNS-to-SQS pushes matching messages into separate SQS queues without a replayable stream log. SNS-to-SQS often wins for simple managed AWS event routing, while Kafka excels at high-throughput streaming and replay.

cards.title: RDS, Aurora, and DynamoDB: Relational vs Key-Value and HA
cards.summary:
Choosing the right database starts with your data model, consistency needs, and query patterns. **Amazon RDS** runs managed relational engines (such as PostgreSQL or MySQL) with SQL joins and ACID transactions; **Amazon Aurora** is AWS's cloud-native relational engine compatible with PostgreSQL or MySQL that separates compute from a fault-tolerant distributed storage layer; **Amazon DynamoDB** is a serverless key-value and document database built for predictable single-digit millisecond latency at scale.

For relational high availability, **Multi-AZ** maintains a synchronous standby replica in another AZ for automatic failover if the primary fails, while **read replicas** offload read queries asynchronously and can serve as promotion targets. In **DynamoDB**, every table uses a **partition key** (and optional sort key) to hash items across partitions—choosing a low-cardinality partition key like `status` creates **hot partitions** that throttle requests.

DynamoDB offers **on-demand** capacity (pay per request, great for spiky or unpredictable traffic) and **provisioned** capacity (set read/write capacity units with optional auto-scaling for steady, predictable load). Pick RDS or Aurora for complex relational joins and ad-hoc SQL queries, and DynamoDB for high-scale key-based lookups with known access patterns.

In DynamoDB, partitions are split automatically as data grows or throughput demands increase, but a single partition still has throughput ceilings (roughly 3,000 RCU or 1,000 WCU per partition historically). If many requests hit the exact same partition key at once—such as one viral tenant ID—you still hit a hot partition even across a large table.
bullets: Use **RDS** or **Aurora** for relational schemas, SQL joins, and complex queries; use **DynamoDB** for high-scale key access.
**Multi-AZ** provides high-availability failover across AZs, whereas **read replicas** scale read throughput asynchronously.
Pick high-cardinality **partition keys** in DynamoDB to spread load evenly and avoid **hot partitions**.
Choose DynamoDB **on-demand** for bursty traffic and **provisioned** capacity when steady throughput is predictable.

glossary.meaning: High-availability deployment keeping a standby replica in another AZ for failover.
Replica handling read traffic and helping scale reads beyond the primary.
Primary attribute hashed by DynamoDB to distribute data across partitions.
Uneven traffic hitting one partition key beyond that partition's throughput limit.

cards.code:
# Inspect RDS DB instances and DynamoDB table throughput/key schema
aws rds describe-db-instances \
  --query 'DBInstances[].{Id:DBInstanceIdentifier,Engine:Engine,MultiAZ:MultiAZ,Class:DBInstanceClass}' \
  --output table

aws dynamodb describe-table --table-name orders \
  --query 'Table.{Name:TableName,Status:TableStatus,Billing:BillingModeSummary.BillingMode}'

interview.q: What is the difference between a Multi-AZ deployment and a read replica in RDS?
interview.a: Multi-AZ is designed for high availability and automatic failover to a standby replica in another AZ during infrastructure or AZ failures, and the standby generally does not serve normal app reads. Read replicas replicate asynchronously and are used to scale read workloads or isolate analytics queries. Using both gives read scaling plus failover resilience.

interview.q: How do you choose between Aurora/RDS and DynamoDB for a new backend service?
interview.a: Pick RDS or Aurora when your domain relies on relational joins, flexible ad-hoc SQL queries, or multi-table relational integrity. Pick DynamoDB when access patterns are well-defined around primary/sort keys and you need serverless scaling with consistent low latency at high request rates. Force-fitting complex relational reporting into DynamoDB usually leads to painful workarounds.

cards.title: Lambda: Serverless Functions, Cold Starts, Concurrency, and Fit
cards.summary:
**AWS Lambda** runs event-driven code in stateless execution environments without you managing servers or OS patches. Events from API Gateway, S3, SQS, EventBridge, or schedules trigger your handler function, and Lambda scales instances up or down automatically based on incoming events.

A **cold start** happens when Lambda initializes a new execution environment—downloading code, starting the runtime (such as a JVM), and running initialization logic—before invoking your handler. Java and large deployment packages often experience noticeably longer cold starts than lightweight runtimes unless mitigated with smaller packages, snapshotting/warming strategies where supported, or **provisioned concurrency**.

**Concurrency** controls how many requests a function can handle simultaneously, and account-level or function-level limits protect downstream databases from sudden traffic bursts. Each invocation also has a configurable **timeout** (up to 15 minutes maximum). Lambda is a poor fit for long-running background jobs over 15 minutes, continuous stateful connections, or steady high-throughput workloads where dedicated containers or instances are cheaper and more predictable.

Because Lambda can scale out to hundreds or thousands of concurrent executions quickly, opening a brand-new database connection inside every invocation can exhaust RDS connection limits. Use an HTTP API, connection pooler/proxy, or keep connection creation outside the handler while capping function concurrency.
bullets: Lambda runs event-driven code with automatic scaling and zero server patching, bounded by a 15-minute max timeout.
**Cold starts** add initialization latency on new environments—often more visible for JVM apps—so keep init work lean.
**Concurrency** caps parallel executions, helping shield downstream databases from connection storms.
Avoid Lambda for jobs exceeding 15 minutes, persistent stateful sockets, or steady flat load better suited to containers.

glossary.meaning: Startup delay when Lambda initializes a fresh execution environment for a request.
Number of Lambda function executions running simultaneously at a moment.
Pre-warmed execution environments kept ready to reduce cold starts.

cards.code:
# List Lambda functions and inspect concurrency and timeout settings
aws lambda list-functions \
  --query 'Functions[].{Name:FunctionName,Runtime:Runtime,MemoryMB:MemorySize,TimeoutSec:Timeout}' \
  --output table

interview.q: Why do Java Lambda functions often face cold-start challenges, and how do you reduce their impact?
interview.a: Starting a JVM, loading classes, and initializing dependency-injection frameworks takes noticeably longer on a cold start than starting a lightweight interpreted runtime. You can keep initialization lean, avoid heavy unused dependencies, reuse static clients across warm invocations, or use provisioned concurrency for latency-sensitive paths. For steady traffic, containers may even be simpler and more cost-effective.

interview.q: When is AWS Lambda a bad fit for a backend workload?
interview.a: It is a poor fit when tasks run longer than Lambda's 15-minute timeout, rely on long-lived stateful connections, or run continuously at high steady utilization where containers or instances cost less. High-concurrency Lambda spikes can also overwhelm relational databases if connection limits are not managed.

cards.title: API Gateway: REST vs HTTP APIs, Auth, Throttling, and Integrations
cards.summary:
**Amazon API Gateway** acts as a managed front door for HTTP and WebSocket APIs, handling routing, request/response transformation, authentication, and **throttling** before forwarding requests to backends such as Lambda, HTTP services, or AWS integrations.

AWS offers **REST APIs** and **HTTP APIs**. **HTTP APIs** are lighter, faster, and lower cost for standard JSON/REST proxying, JWT/OIDC auth, and Lambda or HTTP integrations, while **REST APIs** provide richer features such as request/response body mapping templates, usage plans with API keys, and WAF integration options depending on setup.

**Throttling** enforces burst and steady rate limits (`requests per second`) so a misbehaving client or traffic spike cannot flood your backend, returning `429 Too Many Requests` when exceeded. Keep in mind that API Gateway adds network hop latency and per-request charges on top of backend costs, so evaluate whether direct ALB routing or HTTP API fits best for high-volume traffic.

If a backend already runs on ECS or EC2 behind an Application Load Balancer and does not need API Gateway's specific gateway features, routing directly through ALB can reduce per-request gateway fees and simplify architecture. Conversely, pairing API Gateway with Lambda or microservices gives centralized auth and rate limiting at the edge.
bullets: Choose **HTTP APIs** for lower cost and latency on standard routing; choose **REST APIs** when you need advanced mapping or features.
API Gateway centralizes authentication, CORS, and **throttling** (`429` responses) before hitting backend services.
It integrates smoothly with Lambda, HTTP endpoints, and direct AWS service calls.
Factor in per-million-request pricing and extra hop latency when designing high-throughput APIs.

glossary.meaning: Streamlined, lower-cost API Gateway option for modern HTTP and Lambda routing.
Full-featured API Gateway option supporting deeper transformations and request policies.
Rate limiting enforcing steady request rates and bursts to protect backends.

cards.code:
# List HTTP and REST APIs configured in API Gateway
aws apigatewayv2 get-apis \
  --query 'Items[].{Id:ApiId,Name:Name,Protocol:ProtocolType,Endpoint:ApiEndpoint}' \
  --output table

interview.q: How do you decide between an API Gateway HTTP API and a REST API?
interview.a: Start with an HTTP API when you need fast, cost-effective HTTP routing, JWT authorization, and Lambda or HTTP proxy integration without heavy transformation templates. Choose a REST API when you specifically need features like request/response payload transformations or richer legacy gateway capabilities. HTTP APIs are usually cheaper and lower latency for straightforward APIs.

interview.q: How does throttling in API Gateway protect downstream services?
interview.a: API Gateway caps steady request rates and bursts per route, stage, or client and rejects excess traffic with `429 Too Many Requests`. That shields downstream Lambda functions or databases from sudden surges. If limits are too tight, legitimate clients see `429` errors under normal peaks.

cards.title: CloudFront: CDN Caching, TTLs, Invalidation, and S3 OAC
cards.summary:
**Amazon CloudFront** is AWS's content delivery network (**CDN**) that caches static and dynamic content across global edge locations so users fetch data from a nearby location rather than hitting your **origin**—such as an S3 bucket or ALB—every time.

**Caching behaviour** controls which paths, headers, cookies, and query strings form the cache key, while **Time to Live** (**TTL**) settings determine how long edge nodes keep an object before revalidating with the origin. Longer TTLs improve cache hit ratio and reduce origin load and data transfer costs, whereas short TTLs keep content fresher at the cost of more origin requests.

If you update an asset before its TTL expires, you can trigger a cache **invalidation** or use versioned filenames (like `app.a1b2c3.js`). To serve private S3 content securely without opening the S3 bucket to the public internet, use an **Origin Access Control** (**OAC**) so only CloudFront can read from the bucket, and use **signed URLs** when individual users need time-restricted access to private files.

Including unnecessary headers, cookies, or query strings in the CloudFront cache key splits one file into many cache entries and tanks your hit ratio. Only forward and key on values that actually change the response body, and prefer content-hashed asset names for immutable static bundles.
bullets: CloudFront caches content at edge locations closer to users, reducing latency and load on the **origin**.
**TTL** and cache key rules govern freshness versus hit ratio; versioned filenames avoid frequent cache **invalidations**.
Use **Origin Access Control** (**OAC**) so a private S3 bucket is reachable through CloudFront rather than publicly.
Use **signed URLs** to gate access to private downloads or media for authorized users only.

glossary.meaning: Source server or S3 bucket from which CloudFront fetches content on cache miss.
Time to Live setting controlling how long CloudFront caches a response.
Mechanism restricting private S3 bucket access so only CloudFront can fetch objects.
Request telling CloudFront edge locations to clear cached paths before TTL expiry.

cards.code:
# Create a CloudFront cache invalidation for updated assets
aws cloudfront create-invalidation \
  --distribution-id E123456789ABCD \
  --paths "/index.html" "/assets/*"

interview.q: How do you keep an S3 bucket private while serving its files through CloudFront?
interview.a: Block public access on the S3 bucket and configure an Origin Access Control (OAC) on the CloudFront distribution with a matching bucket policy allowing only that distribution. Users cannot bypass CloudFront to hit the S3 URL directly. If user-level authorization is also required, layer signed URLs or signed cookies on top.

interview.q: When should you use versioned asset filenames instead of CloudFront cache invalidations?
interview.a: Content-hashed filenames like `main.9f86d0.js` are ideal for static bundles because each new build gets a unique URL with a long TTL and zero invalidation delay. Use invalidations for unhashed paths like `/index.html` or urgent fixes when TTLs are long. Relying on broad wildcards constantly adds operational overhead.

cards.title: ECS vs EKS and Fargate: Container Orchestration Trade-Offs
cards.summary:
Running dozens of containers across hosts requires scheduling, service discovery, health monitoring, and rolling deployments. **Amazon ECS** is AWS's native container orchestrator with a simpler mental model centered on task definitions, services, and clusters, while **Amazon EKS** runs managed **Kubernetes** control planes so you can use standard Kubernetes APIs, operators, and tooling.

With both ECS and EKS, you can run tasks on **EC2** worker instances—giving you direct control over instance types and node tuning—or on **AWS Fargate**, a serverless compute engine where AWS manages the underlying virtual machines per task or pod without you patching EC2 nodes.

Choose **ECS** when your team is already on AWS and wants fast setup, native IAM and ALB integration, and lower operational overhead without managing Kubernetes complexity. Choose **EKS** when you need the Kubernetes ecosystem, multi-cloud or hybrid portability, or complex platform custom controllers—keeping in mind that EKS brings higher cognitive and operational overhead.

Fargate is convenient and avoids node patching, but steady high-utilization workloads can sometimes cost more per vCPU/GB than well-sized EC2 or Spot instances. Many teams run stateless APIs on Fargate or Spot-backed nodes and keep steady baseline workloads tuned carefully.
bullets: **ECS** offers a simpler AWS-native container workflow, while **EKS** provides managed Kubernetes and its ecosystem.
**Fargate** removes EC2 host management per task or pod, whereas EC2 launch type gives deeper node control.
Pick **ECS** to ship fast on AWS with lower operational complexity; pick **EKS** when Kubernetes tooling or portability matters.
Factor in control-plane, add-on, and engineering maintenance costs before adopting Kubernetes for a small team.

glossary.meaning: AWS-native container orchestration service using tasks, services, and clusters.
Managed Kubernetes service running control planes on AWS.
Serverless compute option running containers without managing underlying EC2 hosts.

cards.code:
# List ECS clusters and services in the current AWS region
aws ecs list-clusters --output table
aws ecs list-services --cluster prod-backend-cluster --output table

interview.q: How do you decide between ECS and EKS for a backend team on AWS?
interview.a: If the team is focused on building product services on AWS and does not need Kubernetes-specific ecosystem tools or portability, ECS is often simpler, faster to operate, and tightly integrated with AWS primitives. Choose EKS when the organization already standardizes on Kubernetes, relies on Kubernetes operators, or needs cross-environment consistency. Over-engineering a small team on EKS can slow delivery.

interview.q: What does AWS Fargate change when running ECS or EKS workloads?
interview.a: Fargate runs each task or pod in an isolated serverless compute environment so you do not provision, patch, or scale EC2 worker nodes yourself. You still manage container images, networking, IAM permissions, and scaling rules. For steady heavy usage, EC2 instances can sometimes be more cost-effective than Fargate.

cards.title: EventBridge: Event Buses, Content Filtering, Rules, and SNS Comparison
cards.summary:
**Amazon EventBridge** is a serverless event bus service that routes JSON events from AWS services, custom applications, or SaaS partners to targets such as Lambda, SQS, Step Functions, or ECS tasks. Instead of a producer hardcoding every consumer's destination, the producer publishes an event to an **event bus**, and **rules** match events by source, detail type, or JSON payload attributes and forward them to configured **targets**.

EventBridge's **content-based filtering** can inspect nested fields inside the JSON event body—such as `{"detail": {"amount": [{"numeric": [">", 10000]}]}}`—and route only matching events to specific targets. It also supports **schema** discovery/registries and scheduled rules.

Compared with **SNS**, SNS is a fast, lightweight pub/sub fan-out topic where filtering primarily checks message attributes (with payload filtering supported on SNS too), whereas EventBridge excels at multi-source event routing, rich JSON payload pattern matching, and cross-service/cross-account event buses. Use EventBridge when routing diverse domain or AWS events with rich JSON rules, and SNS when simple high-throughput fan-out is your primary need.

EventBridge supports both the `default` bus (which receives many AWS service events) and custom event buses for specific domains or applications. Separating domain buses helps isolate permissions and rules across teams while keeping event schemas clear.
bullets: EventBridge routes events from AWS, custom apps, or SaaS sources through an **event bus** using **rules** and **targets**.
**Content-based filtering** matches nested JSON fields so consumers only receive relevant events.
EventBridge supports rich event routing and cross-service integration, while SNS focuses on straightforward pub/sub fan-out.
Attach dead-letter targets and retry policies to EventBridge rules so failed target deliveries are not lost.

glossary.meaning: EventBridge router receiving events and evaluating rules to dispatch to targets.
EventBridge pattern or schedule matching events and routing them to targets.
Matching rules against values inside a JSON event payload.

cards.code:
# List EventBridge event buses and rules on the default bus
aws events list-event-buses --output table
aws events list-rules --event-bus-name default --output table

interview.q: When should you choose EventBridge over SNS for event-driven communication?
interview.a: Choose EventBridge when you want a central event bus routing events from multiple producers using rich JSON payload content filtering, scheduled triggers, or cross-account/cross-service event rules. Choose SNS when you want straightforward pub/sub broadcasting from a topic to subscribers with minimal indirection. Both pair well with SQS queues for durable consumer buffering.

interview.q: How does content-based filtering in EventBridge help decoupled microservices?
interview.a: Rules can inspect specific fields inside an event's JSON structure—such as event type, region, or numeric thresholds—and send only matching events to a consumer's queue or function. Producers stay unaware of downstream consumers and their filtering logic. That keeps services loosely coupled.

cards.title: Well-Architected and Cost: Resilience, Cost Levers, and Surprise Bills
cards.summary:
The **AWS Well-Architected Framework** groups architecture best practices into six pillars: **operational excellence**, **security**, **reliability**, **performance efficiency**, **cost optimization**, and **sustainability**. Designing for failure in production means assuming components—single AZs, instances, dependencies, or networks—will fail, spreading workloads across multiple AZs, using retries with backoff and jitter, isolating failures with timeouts and circuit breakers, and automating recovery.

On the **cost optimization** pillar, major levers include **right-sizing** over-provisioned instances and storage, using **Savings Plans** or Reserved capacity for steady baseline usage, leveraging **Spot** capacity for fault-tolerant workloads, and eliminating idle resources like unattached volumes or over-retained snapshots.

**Data transfer** is one of the most common sources of surprise AWS bills: cross-AZ traffic, NAT Gateway data processing, and egress to the internet add up quickly when chatty services talk across AZs or move large payloads through NAT gateways. Keep chatty components in the same AZ when possible without sacrificing HA, monitor billing alerts and Cost Explorer regularly, and keep data transfer visible during design reviews.

A classic production cost trap is pairing a chatty microservices call chain or large data transfer across AZs with a NAT Gateway or public IP path when a VPC endpoint (Gateway endpoint for S3, Interface endpoints where appropriate) or co-located processing could avoid unnecessary hops. Always measure real bytes transferred per request path during load and cost reviews.
bullets: Design for failure across multiple AZs with timeouts, bounded retries, and graceful degradation rather than assuming perfection.
Cut waste via **right-sizing**, **Savings Plans** for steady baseline load, **Spot** for flexible workers, and cleanup of idle assets.
Watch **data transfer** across AZs, NAT gateways, and internet egress—a frequent cause of unexpected cloud bills.
Set billing alarms and review cost drivers early so architecture choices stay aligned with budget.

glossary.meaning: Six-pillar guide covering operational, security, reliability, performance, cost, and sustainability design.
Matching instance size or resource capacity to actual observed workload demand.
Charges for moving network traffic across AZs, regions, NAT gateways, or out to internet.

cards.code:
# Check current-month AWS cost and usage by service using Cost Explorer
aws ce get-cost-and-usage \
  --time-period Start=$(date -u +%Y-%m-01),End=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%d) \
  --granularity MONTHLY \
  --metrics "UnblendedCost" \
  --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=SERVICE

interview.q: What are the most common sources of surprise AWS bills for backend teams, and how do you prevent them?
interview.a: Surprise bills often come from data transfer—especially NAT Gateway processing fees, cross-AZ traffic, and internet egress—alongside over-provisioned instances, unattached EBS volumes, and runaway logs or retries. Prevent them by right-sizing from metrics, using Savings Plans or Spot appropriately, keeping chatty calls efficient, and setting budget alerts with regular cost reviews.

interview.q: How do reliability and cost optimization interact in a multi-AZ production design?
interview.a: Multi-AZ redundancy increases cost compared to a single-AZ setup because you run capacity across multiple zones and may pay for cross-AZ traffic or multiple NAT gateways. You balance them by keeping critical availability across AZs while right-sizing instances, using Spot or commitments where appropriate, and avoiding chatty cross-AZ loops on hot paths.

cards.title: How the Internet Works from URL to Response
cards.summary:
Sending data across the internet works like mailing a letter inside nested envelopes. You write your message, put it in an envelope with an apartment number, put that in a box with a street address, and hand it to a courier who knows the roads.

Computers standardize these nested envelopes using two models: the seven-layer **OSI model** (a teaching framework) and the four-layer **TCP/IP model** (what the internet actually runs). When you type a URL, your browser first uses **DNS** to translate the domain name into an **IP address** (the server's street address). It then opens a connection to a specific **port** (the apartment number for that app, like `443` for HTTPS) using **TCP**, secures it with **TLS**, and sends an **HTTP** request.

The message is chopped into small chunks called **packets**, routed across independent switches and routers, and reassembled at the destination before the server returns the web page.
bullets: The four-layer **TCP/IP model** maps directly to real internet protocols, while the seven-layer **OSI model** helps engineers isolate where failures occur.
An **IP address** identifies the target machine, whereas a **port** (`80`, `443`, `8080`) identifies the exact process listening on that machine.
Typing a URL triggers **DNS** lookup, **TCP** handshake, **TLS** encryption setup, and finally an **HTTP** request-response exchange.
Large payloads are split into **packets** that can travel different network paths and arrive out of order before reassembly.

glossary.meaning: A unique numerical label identifying a device on a network.
A 16-bit number directing traffic to a specific application on a host.
A small formatted unit of data sent across a packet-switched network.
A seven-layer conceptual framework describing how network protocols interact.

cards.code:
# End-to-end flow when opening https://api.example.com/users
1. DNS Lookup:   api.example.com  -->  93.184.216.34
2. TCP Connect:  Client:51432     <-> 93.184.216.34:443 (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK)
3. TLS Setup:    Verify certificate & agree on symmetric session keys
4. HTTP Request: GET /users HTTP/1.1 (encrypted inside TLS)
5. Encapsulation:
   [ Ethernet Frame | IP Header (Src/Dst IP) | TCP Header (Src/Dst Port) | TLS + HTTP ]
6. Response:     200 OK + JSON body returned in packets and reassembled

interview.q: Walk me through what happens when you type a URL into a browser and press Enter.
interview.a: First, the browser checks caches and queries **DNS** to resolve the hostname to an **IP address**. Next, it opens a **TCP** connection to port `443` via a three-way handshake and negotiates a **TLS** session to verify the server certificate and encrypt traffic. Finally, it sends an **HTTP** `GET` request, and the server streams back the response packets for rendering.

interview.q: Why do we still talk about the OSI model if the internet uses TCP/IP?
interview.a: The **OSI model** is a diagnostic vocabulary rather than a literal implementation. Separating Layer 3 (IP routing), Layer 4 (TCP/UDP transport), and Layer 7 (HTTP application logic) lets engineers pinpoint whether an outage is a firewall blocking a port, a bad route, or an application returning `500` errors.

cards.title: TCP vs UDP: Reliability Against Raw Speed
cards.summary:
**TCP** is like a certified courier who calls ahead to confirm you are home, numbers every box, and resends any box lost in transit. **UDP** is like tossing postcards into a mailbox: fast and lightweight, with no guarantee they arrive or stay in order.

**TCP** (Transmission Control Protocol) solves the problem of unreliable networks by establishing a stateful connection using a three-way **handshake** (`SYN`, `SYN-ACK`, `ACK`). It guarantees in-order, lossless delivery using sequence numbers, acknowledgments, retransmissions, and **congestion control** so senders do not overwhelm slow links. However, waiting to retransmit one dropped packet stalls every packet behind it, a delay called **head-of-line blocking**.

**UDP** (User Datagram Protocol) skips handshakes, ordering, and retransmissions entirely. That zero-overhead design makes UDP ideal when fresh data beats perfect data, such as live video, online games, and **DNS** lookups, and lets modern protocols like **QUIC** build custom reliability on top.
bullets: **TCP** guarantees ordered, reliable delivery via sequence numbers and acknowledgments, making it the default for web APIs, databases, and file transfers.
**UDP** is connectionless and fire-and-forget, cutting handshake latency and avoiding retransmissions of stale real-time frames.
TCP suffers from **head-of-line blocking** because the operating system cannot deliver packet 5 to the app until lost packet 4 is retransmitted.
Protocols like **QUIC** run over **UDP** to eliminate TCP head-of-line blocking while still offering reliable, encrypted streams.

glossary.meaning: The SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK exchange that initializes a TCP connection.
Algorithms that throttle sending speed when network packet loss or delay rises.
A single lost packet delaying delivery of all subsequent packets in a stream.
A UDP-based transport protocol providing multiplexed streams and built-in TLS encryption.

cards.code:
# TCP 3-Way Handshake vs UDP Fire-and-Forget
# TCP (Stateful, ordered, reliable)
Client                            Server
  | -------- SYN (seq=100) --------> |
  | <--- SYN-ACK (seq=300, ack=101) -|
  | -------- ACK (ack=301) --------> |
  | ==== Data Transfer + Retries === |

# UDP (Stateless, no handshake, no retransmit)
Client                            Server
  | ---- Datagram 1 (DNS query) ---> |
  | <--- Datagram 2 (DNS answer) --- |

interview.q: Why do video calls and online multiplayer games prefer UDP over TCP?
interview.a: In real-time audio, video, or gaming, a packet arriving 300 milliseconds late is useless because the live moment has already passed. **TCP** would pause the entire stream to retransmit that lost frame due to **head-of-line blocking**, causing noticeable freezes. **UDP** lets the app skip the glitch and immediately render the newest frame.

interview.q: If UDP is unreliable, how does QUIC provide reliable delivery over it?
interview.a: **QUIC** moves reliability, congestion control, and **TLS 1.3** out of the OS kernel and into user space on top of **UDP**. It splits data into independent streams, so a dropped packet only pauses the single stream it belongs to rather than blocking every parallel request.

cards.title: HTTP Evolution from HTTP/1.1 to HTTP/3
cards.summary:
**HTTP** is the common language web browsers and servers speak, structured like a restaurant order slip: you state what action you want (**method**), any extra notes (**headers**), and the kitchen replies with a result code (**status code**) and your dish (**body**).

Because HTTP itself is **stateless**, servers use **cookies**—small tokens stored by the browser and sent back on each request—to remember logged-in users. Early **HTTP/1.1** added **keep-alive** connections so browsers did not open a fresh TCP connection per file, yet each connection could still handle only one request at a time, forcing browsers to open six parallel connections per domain.

**HTTP/2** fixed application-level blocking using binary framing and **multiplexing**, letting dozens of requests share one TCP connection simultaneously. However, TCP still blocked every stream when a single packet dropped. **HTTP/3** solved this by running over **QUIC** (UDP), giving independent streams and faster connection setup.
bullets: Standard HTTP **methods** (`GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`) express intent, while **status codes** (`2xx`, `3xx`, `4xx`, `5xx`) signal outcomes cleanly to clients.
HTTP is **stateless**, so **cookies** or `Authorization` headers carry session identity on every request.
**HTTP/2** introduced binary framing, header compression (`HPACK`), and **multiplexing** over one TCP connection, eliminating HTTP/1.1 request queuing.
**HTTP/3** replaces TCP with **QUIC** over UDP, removing transport-level head-of-line blocking on lossy mobile networks.

glossary.meaning: An HTTP method like GET or PUT whose repeated execution produces the same state.
Reusing an existing TCP connection across multiple sequential HTTP requests.
Interleaving multiple independent request and response streams over a single connection.
A protocol where the server retains no session state between independent requests.

cards.code:
# HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 Multiplexing over One Connection
# HTTP/1.1 (Sequential on a single connection - Req 2 waits for Req 1)
Conn 1: [ Req 1 ] ---> [ Resp 1 ] ---> [ Req 2 ] ---> [ Resp 2 ]

# HTTP/2 (Interleaved binary frames on a single connection)
Conn 1: [Req1:H][Req2:H][Req1:Data][Resp2:H][Resp2:Data][Resp1:Data]

# Common HTTP Status Families
# 200 OK | 201 Created | 304 Not Modified | 400 Bad Request
# 401 Unauthorized | 403 Forbidden | 404 Not Found | 429 Too Many Requests | 503 Unavailable

interview.q: What problem did HTTP/2 solve over HTTP/1.1, and what bottleneck remained?
interview.a: **HTTP/2** solved HTTP-level head-of-line blocking by introducing **multiplexing** and header compression (`HPACK`), allowing multiple concurrent requests over a single TCP connection instead of opening six connections per host. However, because HTTP/2 still runs over **TCP**, a single lost packet stalls all multiplexed streams at the transport layer until TCP retransmits it.

interview.q: What is the difference between 401 Unauthorized and 403 Forbidden?
interview.a: `401 Unauthorized` actually means unauthenticated: the server does not know who you are because credentials or a token are missing or expired. `403 Forbidden` means authenticated but not authorized: the server verified your identity, yet your role lacks permission for that resource.

cards.title: TLS and HTTPS: Encryption, Handshakes, and Certificates
cards.summary:
**HTTPS** wraps standard HTTP inside **TLS** (Transport Layer Security), providing three guarantees: **confidentiality** (eavesdroppers cannot read payloads), **integrity** (tampering breaks the message authentication code), and **authentication** (you are talking to the real domain, not an impostor).

During a **TLS handshake**, the client and server use slow **asymmetric cryptography** (public and private keys) to prove identity and safely agree on a shared secret, then switch to fast **symmetric encryption** (like `AES-GCM`) for actual data transfer. The server proves its identity by sending an **X.509 certificate** signed by an intermediate **Certificate Authority (CA)**, which chains up to a **root CA** pre-installed in your OS or browser trust store.

**TLS 1.3** cut the handshake down to a single round trip (`1-RTT`), removed weak legacy ciphers, and mandated **forward secrecy** so compromising a server's private key later cannot decrypt past traffic. Avoid terminating TLS blindly without certificate validation in production clients, as disabling verification exposes apps to man-in-the-middle attacks.

In TLS 1.3, the client guesses the key-exchange curve and sends its `KeyShare` inside the very first `ClientHello` message. That allows the server to derive the symmetric traffic keys immediately, encrypt its own certificate, and reply in one round trip. TLS 1.3 also supports `0-RTT` resumption for repeat visitors, though `0-RTT` data is vulnerable to replay attacks and must only carry idempotent `GET` requests. When a server forgets to bundle its intermediate CA certificate, desktop browsers might cache it from other sites while Java `HttpClient` or `curl` fails with `PKIX path building failed`.
bullets: **TLS** combines asymmetric key exchange for authentication with fast symmetric ciphers (`AES-GCM`, `ChaCha20-Poly1305`) for bulk data encryption.
Browsers validate a **certificate chain** from the leaf server certificate through intermediate CAs up to a locally trusted **root CA**.
**TLS 1.3** completes handshakes in **1-RTT** (saving ~20 to 100 ms over TLS 1.2) and enforces **forward secrecy** via ephemeral Diffie-Hellman keys.
Common production TLS failures stem from **expired certificates**, missing intermediate certificates, hostname mismatches, or skewed server system clocks.

glossary.meaning: A trusted entity that cryptographically signs digital certificates verifying domain ownership.
Generating ephemeral session keys so compromising long-term private keys never exposes past traffic.
Encryption using a public key to encrypt or verify and a private key to decrypt or sign.
A TLS extension telling the server which hostname the client wants before certificate selection.

cards.code:
# TLS 1.3 Handshake (1-RTT) & Quick Certificate Inspection
Client                                          Server
  | -- ClientHello (TLS 1.3, SNI, KeyShare) -----> |
  | <-- ServerHello, KeyShare, Cert, Finished ---- |
  | -- Finished + Encrypted HTTP Request --------> |

# Inspect live certificate chain and expiry with openssl
openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates

interview.q: Why does TLS use both asymmetric and symmetric encryption instead of just one?
interview.a: Asymmetric cryptography solves the key-distribution and identity problem over an untrusted network, allowing two strangers to verify a **CA-signed certificate** and agree on a secret. However, asymmetric math is orders of magnitude slower than symmetric ciphers. Once the handshake establishes a shared session key, switching to **symmetric encryption** keeps throughput high and CPU cost low.

interview.q: Your Java service throws `PKIX path building failed` when calling a partner API, even though the URL works in Chrome. Why?
interview.a: The partner server likely omitted an **intermediate CA certificate** from its TLS chain. Browsers work around this using cached intermediates or `AIA` fetching, whereas Java's default `TrustManager` strictly requires the server to send the complete chain up to a root CA in `cacerts`. The fix is having the server send the full certificate bundle.

cards.title: DNS Resolution, Record Types, Caching, and Outages
cards.summary:
**DNS** (Domain Name System) is the internet's distributed phonebook, translating human-readable names like `api.example.com` into IP addresses. Rather than one giant database, DNS uses a hierarchical tree.

When your app queries a **recursive resolver** (often run by your ISP, `1.1.1.1`, or `8.8.8.8`), and the answer is not cached, the resolver walks the hierarchy: it asks a **root server** where `.com` lives, asks the `.com` **TLD (Top-Level Domain) server** where `example.com` lives, and finally asks `example.com`'s **authoritative nameserver** for the exact record. Responses carry a **TTL (Time to Live)** in seconds telling resolvers how long to cache the answer.

Different **record types** serve distinct roles: `A` maps to IPv4, `AAAA` maps to IPv6, `CNAME` aliases one domain name to another, `MX` routes email, and `TXT` holds verification or SPF policies. Avoid setting ultra-low TTLs (like `5s`) everywhere, which spikes authoritative query load, and remember DNS caching means rollback changes are never instant.

Engineers joke 'it is always DNS' because DNS sits on the critical path of every outbound call yet hides behind multi-layer caching. A broken deploy often looks like a DNS failure when an expired domain, misconfigured `CNAME`, or dead IP cached beyond its TTL blocks connectivity. Worse, older Java runtimes cached positive DNS lookups indefinitely when a `SecurityManager` was enabled, forcing pods to keep hitting terminated backend IPs after a cloud load balancer scaled or rotated nodes. Setting `networkaddress.cache.ttl=30` in JVM security properties prevents stale IP pinning.
bullets: Uncached **DNS** lookups traverse **recursive resolver**, **root**, **TLD**, and **authoritative** servers, usually over UDP port `53` (or TCP for large responses).
`A` and `AAAA` records point directly to IPv4/IPv6 addresses, while `CNAME` points to another domain name and cannot coexist with other records at the zone apex.
**TTL** governs how quickly traffic shifts during failovers: lowering TTL to `30s` hours before a migration speeds cutover without permanently hammering nameservers.
DNS enables **geographic and weighted routing**, though stale caches on client OSes or JVM `InetAddress` caches can delay failover.

glossary.meaning: A DNS server that queries root, TLD, and authoritative servers on a client's behalf.
The server holding the actual DNS zone records for a specific domain.
Duration in seconds a DNS record may be cached before re-querying.
A canonical name record aliasing one hostname to another hostname rather than an IP.

cards.code:
# Iterative DNS Walk & Common Record Types
App -> Recursive Resolver (8.8.8.8)
         |-- 1. Ask Root (.)         --> Referral to .com TLD
         |-- 2. Ask .com TLD         --> Referral to ns1.example.com
         |-- 3. Ask Authoritative    --> api.example.com. 300 IN A 93.184.216.34

# Record Examples in a Zone File
example.com.      3600  IN  A      93.184.216.34
example.com.      3600  IN  AAAA   2606:2800:220:1:248:1893:25c8:1946
www.example.com.  300   IN  CNAME  example.com.
example.com.      3600  IN  MX     10 mail.example.com.
example.com.      3600  IN  TXT    "v=spf1 include:_spf.example.com ~all"

interview.q: Why can you not put a CNAME record on the root domain (zone apex) like `example.com`?
interview.a: By DNS specification, a `CNAME` aliases all record types for a name to its target. Because a zone apex like `example.com` must already hold `SOA` and `NS` records, adding a `CNAME` creates a conflict. Cloud providers solve this with proprietary `ALIAS` or `ANAME` records that resolve the target internally and return a flat `A` record.

interview.q: You updated a DNS `A` record to fail over to a healthy region, yet traffic still hits the dead region for 20 minutes. Why?
interview.a: The previous record likely had a high **TTL** (such as `1800` or `3600` seconds), so recursive resolvers, operating systems, and JVM `InetAddress` caches are still serving the cached IP. Also, some ISP resolvers ignore tiny TTLs. Always lower TTLs ahead of planned migrations and ensure clients honor short DNS cache lifetimes.

cards.title: CDN and HTTP Caching: Edge Delivery and Freshness
cards.summary:
A **CDN (Content Delivery Network)** places thousands of **edge servers** (Points of Presence) physically close to users worldwide.
